news.title: Bruce Springsteen Urges Officials to Protect the Vote on Election Day: ‘Our Vote Is Our Voice’
news.text:
Skip to main content

Bruce Springsteen performs at the AFI FEST 2025 Presented By Canva Opening Night "Springsteen: Deliver Me From Nowhere" Premiere at TCL Chinese Theatre on October 22, 2025 in Hollywood, California.

Rodin Eckenroth/Getty Images for AFI

Bruce Springsteen has a message for election officials on Election Day.

On Tuesday (Nov. 3), the 77-year-old music icon and longtime political activist shared a brief video message on social media, urging “election officials and representatives of our government” to ensure votes are securely counted.

Bruce Springsteen Has No Regrets About His Political Tour: ‘I Do What I Want to Do’

Bruce Springsteen Slams ICE at New Jersey Benefit Show: ‘Get the F—k Out of Minneapolis’

Bruce Springsteen Backs Michigan’s Dr. Abdul El-Sayed for U.S. Senate Amid Haley Stevens Reversal: ‘He’s a Fighter’

Standing in front of a stone wall and dressed in a flannel shirt, Springsteen delivered a direct appeal to those overseeing the electoral process.

“I’m speaking to election officials and representatives of our government on Election Day,” Springsteen said on Instagram. “You have sworn an oath to preserve, protect, and defend our Constitution. That means you have a solemn duty to ensure that our votes are securely counted.”

He continued, “Thomas Jefferson said, ‘Government requires a consent of the governed.’ You who represent us must never consent to any directives that undermine our constitutional right to a free and fair election.”

Election Day marks the 2026 midterm elections, with voters across the country casting ballots in congressional races that will determine control of the House of Representatives and Senate. Voters are also deciding a number of gubernatorial, state legislative and local contests.

“Our vote is our voice,” Springsteen said in conclusion. “And it’s up to you to ensure that our voice is heard. I wish you all a good Election Day, and thank you for your service.”

In the caption accompanying the 45-second clip, Springsteen thanked those voting on Election Day and encouraged his followers to continue supporting democracy by taking the Oath to the Constitution at oathproject.org.

Merck Mercuriadis, founder of the influential music catalog investment group Hipgnosis, took to the comments, writing, “The boss has spoken – for 50 years he has spoken truthfully about the cracks in ‘merica in order to help us become the best version of ourselves that we can be. Born to vote!!!!!!!!!”

This isn’t the first time Springsteen has spoken out about voting rights and election integrity. In 2012, the “Dancing in the Dark” singer-songwriter criticized voter suppression efforts in several states, writing that Americans of all political views should oppose what he described as “anti-voter, anti-citizen efforts.” He also raised concerns about the future of American democracy during the 2024 presidential election, when he endorsed Kamala Harris and Tim Walz.

A vocal critic of President Donald Trump and longtime Democratic supporter, Springsteen released his protest anthem “Streets of Minneapolis” earlier this year in response to the fatal shootings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti amid the administration’s immigration crackdown. He also performed the song during his recent Land of Hope and Dreams Tour.

During a January 2026 benefit concert in New Jersey, Springsteen also spoke out about the Trump administration, saying, “The United States, the ideals and the values for which it stood for the past 250 years, is being tested like it has never been in modern times. Those values and those ideals have never been as endangered as they are right now.”

On Monday (Nov. 2), Springsteen also threw his support behind Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in the Michigan Senate race.

“Dr. El-Sayed is a fighter for our American Constitution, he’s a fighter for our American Democracy, and he’s a fighter against the corrupt, lawless, and anti-American leadership currently in the White House,” he wrote on Instagram. “That’s why I’m in his corner 100%.”

news.title: Katie Miller is already spreading election conspiracies as polling site issues are reported in New York
news.text:
Katie Miller is already jumping on baseless election conspiracy theories and spreading them to her MAGA followers after voting issues were reported in New York. 

Election officials in Westchester County, New York, said they were aware of problems with voting scanners - and ballots not being scanned properly - and assured the public that every vote would be counted. 

But Miller, the wife of White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, seized on the social media post of a voter in Westchester County - where Republican incumbent Rep. Mike Lawler in a tight race against Democrat Cait Conley in New York’s 17th Congressional District race - and used it to cast doubt on election integrity. 

“This is how the Left steals elections,” Miller said Tuesday morning. “Mike Lawler’s competitive district and they are turning away voters.”

The X user, named Ben Hort according to the profile, said he was initially unable to cast his vote in his district and was told to come back later. 

“I just went to vote in Westchester & machines are apparently broken county wide,” Hort said. “They said choice is vote absentee or come back later. This is going to be crazy. Our country is in trouble.”

Other users swiftly challenged Hort, who then clarified, “That is what she said. She just misspoke by calling it an absentee ballot,” he said, referring to a poll worker. “I don’t feel like I was turned away but it’s not ideal.”

Hort’s post has received over 400,000 views since it was shared by Miller, who was accused of being “wildly irresponsible” by some.

“That is literally not what is happening and you are spreading known lies,” writer and activist Amy Siskind replied to Miller.

“The reason people say maga's a cult is precisely because cults require adherents to believe in stupid falsehoods in order to make the cult leader right,” said journalist Robert Lusetich.

Other journalists and pundits pointed to another flaw in Miller’s theory. 

“Ah yes. Textbook election-rigging by Dems, suppressing the vote in a county Kamala Harris carried by 26 pts,” said The Atlantic’s Tim Alberta. 

“This is the Democratic part of the district,” said Semafor’s Ben Smith.

Adam Carlson of polling firm Zenith Polls also highlighted that Westchester County is “the most Democratic part of the district,” backing it up with data. 

Westchester County executive Ken Jenkins said his office was aware of the issues with voting scanners in the area and said the situation was “unacceptable.”

“Voters should remain in line and exercise their right to vote,” Jenkins said in a statement. “Every eligible voter will have the opportunity to cast their ballot, and every vote must be counted. I have directed County officials, including representatives from our Law Department, to monitor the voting process and ensure that voters can cast their ballots without interference and that every vote is properly and accurately counted.”

Jenkins said a bipartisan group would review what went wrong once the voting machine issues are resolved.

“Westchester County voters deserve a fair, secure and seamless election process. Today, we have fallen short of that standard,” Jenkins concluded. “The voters deserve better, and I intend to make sure they get it.”
news.summary: Election officials in Westchester County said they were aware of issues with voting scanners and assured the public that every vote would be counted

news.title: Trump's Dismissed Epstein Letter Lawsuit Is the Latest Example of His Failure To State Cognizable Claims
news.text:
On July 17, 2025, The Wall Street Journal reported that a 2003 album marking the 50th birthday of financier Jeffrey Epstein, who would later be implicated in state and federal sex offenses involving underage girls, included a letter from Donald Trump, a longtime friend. The very next day, Trump sued the Journal in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida, saying "the supposed letter is a fake and the Defendants knew it when they chose to deliberately defame President Trump." The complaint sought compensatory and punitive damages "not less than $10 billion."

Last April, U.S. District Judge Darrin Gayles dismissed that lawsuit but let Trump try again with an amended complaint. On Saturday, Gayles dismissed the lawsuit again, this time with prejudice. In both cases, Gayles concluded that Trump's lawyers had fallen far short of alleging "actual malice," a crucial element of defamation cases involving public figures. That abject failure illustrates a persistent pattern in Trump's long history of frivolous lawsuits: As far as Trump is concerned, the point is to punish people for saying things he does not like, as opposed to seeking compensation for a legally cognizable injury.

What does "actual malice" mean? Trump seems to think it means that someone published a false statement "out of hatred and ill-will"—a phrase that appears in both Trump's original complaint against the Journal and in his amended complaint, which he filed on May 27, 2026. But as Gayles explains in his order, that is not what "actual malice" means.

"To plead actual malice," Gayles notes, quoting a 2018 decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 11th Circuit (which includes Florida), Trump "must allege facts sufficient to give rise to a reasonable inference that the false statement was made with knowledge that it was false or with reckless disregard of whether it was false or not. This is a subjective test, focusing on whether the defendant 'actually entertained serious doubts as to the veracity of the published account, or was highly aware that the account was probably false.'"

The Supreme Court established that standard in the 1964 case New York Times v. Sullivan, saying it was required by the First Amendment. "In these cases," the 11th Circuit noted in 2016, "there is a powerful interest in ensuring that free speech is not unduly burdened by the necessity of defending against expensive yet groundless litigation."

The actual malice standard "was designed to allow publishers the 'breathing
space' needed to ensure robust reporting on public figures and events," the 11th Circuit explained. "Forcing publishers to defend inappropriate suits through expensive discovery proceedings in all cases would constrict that breathing space in exactly the manner the actual malice standard was intended to prevent. The costs and efforts required to defend a lawsuit through that stage of litigation could chill free speech nearly as effectively as the absence of the actual malice standard altogether."

That explains why Gayles, after dismissing Trump's first complaint, rejected his motion for discovery "on issues related to actual malice." Specifically, Trump was keen to find evidence that might illuminate the defendants' "state of mind," which was sorely lacking in his original complaint. "President Trump's request to conduct discovery on issues related to actual malice before filing a well-pleaded complaint contravenes the purpose behind the actual malice standard," Gayles wrote.

Denied a license for that fishing expedition, Trump's lawyers tried again to file "a well-pleaded complaint," meaning their allegations, if true, would be sufficient to infer actual malice. But according to Gayles, they did not do any better this time around. "President Trump's conclusory allegations that Defendants acted with malice because they 'knew or should have known' the statements in the Article were false are insufficient to state a claim," he writes.

The amended complaint "appears to allege that by choosing to publish the Article despite President Trump's and his team's denials, Defendants acted with actual malice," Gayles says. "In effect, President Trump argues that once he declared the Letter a 'fake,' Defendants should have disregarded everything else they learned in their investigation and not published the story. But that is not what the actual malice standard requires and runs afoul of the First Amendment. Indeed, were that the law, any time a public figure or his team denies an accusation, journalists would be immediately blocked from publishing negative or contradictory press."

Trump argued that the Journal's investigation was inadequate. "A failure to investigate, without more, does not establish actual malice," Gayles notes. "Rather, 'a plaintiff must show the defendant deliberately avoided investigating the veracity of the statement in order to evade learning the truth.' The Amended Complaint comes nowhere close to this standard."

In fact, the Journal's article "details a thoughtful and detailed investigation," Gayles writes. "Before running the story, Defendants contacted President Trump and his team, Justice Department officials, and the FBI for comment. President Trump and his team responded with his denial [which was quoted in the article], the Justice Department did not respond at all, and the FBI declined to comment."

Journal reporters Khadeeja Safdar and Joseph Palazzolo tried to interview Ghislane Maxwell, the Epstein associate who solicited the messages for his birthday album, but she did not respond, and "her attorney stated that she was focused on her case before the Supreme Court" involving her federal sex trafficking conviction. In a July 2025 interview with the Justice Department, according to Trump's lawyers, Maxwell said "she did not remember President Trump submitting a letter for Epstein's 50th Birthday." Judging from that statement, Gayles says, "Maxwell had little to offer to Defendants' investigation."

Safdar and Palazzolo also "reached out to other individuals named in the Birthday
Book, including Leslie Wexner and Alan Dershowitz, and to individuals involved in binding the Birthday Book," Gayles notes. "In short, President Trump's allegation that Defendants failed to conduct an adequate investigation is rebutted by the Article
and is insufficient to establish actual malice."

The amended complaint "attempts to manufacture flaws" in the Journal's investigation, Gayles says, describing those efforts as "grasping at straws." The complaint, for example, faults Safdar and Palazzolo for "reviewing the Letter before publication" rather than "obtaining a copy of the Letter." But "nothing in the law suggests that Defendants needed to obtain, retain, or publish a copy."

Speaking of grasping at straws, the complaint charges Safdar and Palazzolo with "the intentional omission of the denial from President Trump regarding whether he signed the alleged letter or whether the signature on the alleged letter is authentic." Yet the article "states, multiple times, that President Trump denies writing the Letter and that '[i]t isn't clear how the letter with Trump's signature was prepared,'" Gayles notes. "This is more than sufficient to encompass any denial that he 'signed' the Letter or that the signature on the Letter is authentic."

In addition to Safdar, Palazzolo, and Dow Jones, which owns the Journal, Trump sued News Corporation, which owns Dow Jones; News Corporation CEO Robert Thomson; and Rupert Murdoch, the company's majority owner and emeritus chairman. But "other than stating that Dow Jones and News Corp published the Article 'at the direction of Defendants Murdoch and Thomson,'" Gayles notes, "the Amended Complaint is devoid of any allegations about how Thomson acted with actual malice."

Trump's disdain for meeting minimum legal requirements is part of a longstanding pattern. He has never been much concerned about actually winning in court, as opposed to inflicting pain on his enemies, whether he was demanding $500 million from an architecture critic who said unkind things about his plan for a Manhattan skyscraper, seeking $5 billion from a financial journalist who dared to question the extent of his wealth, suing a comedian for breach of contract based on a joke likening Trump to an orangutan, asserting that CNN defamed him by describing his reality-defying claims about the 2020 presidential election as "the Big Lie," alleging that The Des Moines Register committed consumer fraud by publishing poll results he did not like, or averring that CBS caused him $20 billion in damages by editing a 60 Minutes interview with Kamala Harris to make her seem slightly more cogent.

Although Trump plans to appeal Gayles' ruling, the Journal's editorial board said on Sunday, "the appeal isn't likely to succeed. A letter matching the Journal's description was released by Congressional investigators. Mr. Trump said he never wrote or signed the letter, but the Journal never claimed he did. It said only that the letter with the signature existed, and the Journal's stories have always included Mr. Trump's denials."

Trump "has long used lawsuits to intimidate the press, and most of the time he ends up losing," the editorial noted. "Mr. Trump, like other politicians, uses lawsuits to coerce settlements that he can tout as legal victories. He failed in this case because the Journal didn't roll over. A free press requires owners who back editors, and we couldn't do what we do without that support."
news.summary: The president's defamation case against The Wall Street Journal fits a pattern of frivolous litigation aimed at punishing speech that irks him.
news.author: Jacob Sullum

news.title: US voters head to polls to deliver midterm verdict on Trump
news.text:
DETROIT: Americans headed to the polls in Tuesday’s midterm elections to deliver a verdict on the first two years of President Donald Trump’s second term, with surveys and nonpartisan analysts favoring Democrats to wrest the House of Representatives from Republicans while control of the Senate remains uncertain.

The battle for the Senate is unfolding across nearly 10 closely contested statewide races, most in Republican strongholds.

History is against Trump’s Republicans: the sitting president’s party has lost ground in Congress in all but two midterm elections since World War Two. Trump’s approval rating is hovering near his all-time lows, dragged down by deep voter frustration over the war with Iran and the resulting rise in fuel prices.

There is little doubt this year’s election is all about Trump, who is nearly two years into his second term. Trump himself has told his supporters repeatedly to “pretend I’m on the ballot,” a message Democratic leaders have happily echoed.

Trump touted in a television interview on Tuesday morning what he billed as his achievements in Venezuela and Iran and declared optimism for fellow Republicans.

In remarks that appeared aimed at swaying voters unhappy with US support for Israel, Trump said that he intended to stop $3.8 billion in promised annual funding to Israel after the end of this year, but it was unclear how he would do so, given a 2020 law mandating the funding levels in the agreement with Israel.

US policy toward Israel has been a particular focus in Michigan, where progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed is running a closely watched campaign for Senate.

The president has sought to energize his base with more than two dozen campaign rallies since the start of October, most in states he easily won in 2024.

Led by Trump, Republicans have portrayed Democratic candidates as radical, un-American and even communist.

But opinion polls show voters are most concerned about affordability, and disapprove of Trump’s handling of the issue after his sweeping tariffs on imports, many of which were thrown out as illegal by the courts, and his decision to attack Iran in February increased domestic costs.

Republican candidates, meanwhile, have struggled to distance themselves from a president who demands fealty and rarely acknowledges mistakes.

At a voting center in a predominantly Black neighborhood in northwest Detroit, Natalia Towns, 34, said she did not find efforts by Mike Rogers, the Republican Senate candidate, to court Black voters sincere, and felt El-Sayed would do more to bring down costs.

“I do feel like health matters, gas prices are high, food is too high,” she said.

Doj deploys election monitors

Democrats have warned that Trump, who has long falsely claimed that US elections are rigged, may attempt to challenge Tuesday’s results if Republicans lose.

The US Justice Department said on Tuesday it was deploying 1,000 election monitors and observers to all 50 states in what it called the largest Election Day monitoring effort in history.

Democrats have criticized the plan as potential voter intimidation. Roughly two-thirds of the jurisdictions the department listed are in places where voters supported Democrat Kamala Harris over Trump in the 2024 presidential election, a Reuters analysis found.

All 435 seats in the US House of Representatives are up for election, along with 35 of the Senate’s 100 seats, though most contests are not considered competitive. Democrats must flip at least three House seats and four Senate seats to win a majority in each chamber.

Democrats have little margin for error. The party must defend all of its current seats while winning at least two states that voted for Trump by a double-digit margin two years ago: Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, Ohio, South Carolina and Texas.

Opinion polls show Democrats either narrowly leading or within striking distance in all of those states.

Election drama in michigan, alaska, texas

The Michigan Senate contest between El-Sayed, 42, and Rogers, 63, represents a high-profile test of whether Republicans’ identity-based attacks û El-Sayed would be the nation’s first Muslim senator ù prove effective in a battleground state.

A win for El-Sayed, who has criticized Israel and supports policies such as universal healthcare, would also be seen as a boost for the Democratic Party’s left wing ahead of the 2028 presidential election.

The Alaska Senate race has been thrown into turmoil after the New York Times reported that the campaign of Democratic candidate Mary Peltola, 53, helped recruit a third candidate who shares the first and last name of her Republican opponent, Dan Sullivan, 61.

Peltola has denied involvement. Trump’s Justice Department has launched a criminal probe into the allegations and filed a lawsuit to block certification of the election results, though a judge dismissed the latter effort.

In addition to its actions in Alaska, Trump’s Justice Department also filed a lawsuit in California to block ballots it says may be invalid, a break from decades of practice meant to insulate elections from political interference. The US Supreme Court on Monday rejected the administration’s request for an emergency order in the case.

In Texas, Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico, 37, has his party once again dreaming of winning the biggest Republican state after decades of heartbreak. His scandal-plagued opponent, Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton, 63, has benefited from a nine-figure investment from the world’s richest man, Elon Musk, who has spent hundreds of millions of dollars boosting Republicans.

In Kansas, Democrat Adam Hamilton, 62, a megachurch pastor, holds a narrow polling lead over Republican US Senator Roger Marshall, 66. The state voted for Trump by more than 16 percentage points in 2024 and has not elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century.

And in Maine, Republican US Senator Susan Collins, 73, is once again seeking to defy the Democratic leanings of her home state and win a sixth term. She faces Democrat Troy Jackson, 58, a former state senate president who unexpectedly became the nominee after Democratic oyster farmer Graham Platner dropped out amid accusations of misconduct, which he denied.

There are 47 US House races widely seen as competitive, according to a Reuters analysis of the leading election forecasters. If the other contests all proceed as predicted, Democrats would need to win only 13 of those races to secure a majority.

The fight for the House has been waged largely on Republican turf, including some districts Trump carried by double digits in 2024. A Trump-backed Republican effort to redraw districts in several states to make them safer for the party appears not to have yielded the gains the president expected.

news.title: America votes: Democrats hope for midterm 'blue wave' as Trump faces test of his presidency
news.text: In-person voting is underway Tuesday in the U.S. midterm elections, widely seen as a referendum on President Donald Trump's second term. With his approval ratings at a low point, Democrats are hoping to capture both chambers of Congress - the House of Representatives and the Senate - whcih would make it much harder for the president to advance his agenda during his remaining two years in office and strengthening their position ahead of the 2028 presidential election. The first polling stations on the U.S. East Coast opened at noon Israel time, with voting beginning later in the day across the central and western United States. Even before Election Day, more than 57 million Americans had cast ballots through early in-person voting or by mail. That represents a significant increase from the 45 million who voted early in the 2022 midterms and offers an encouraging sign for Democrats, who hope frustration with Trump's policies, particularly the war in Iran and the resulting surge in gasoline prices, will drive large numbers of their supporters to the polls. Nevertheless, the outcome could still change significantly during Election Day itself, when Republicans traditionally account for a larger share of votes than they do during early voting. The first results are expected to begin arriving at 1 a.m. Wednesday Israel time, when polling stations close in parts of Indiana and Kentucky. The final polls will close in Alaska at 8 a.m. Israel time. An initial picture of the balance of power in Congress could emerge overnight or Wednesday morning. However, close races, particularly in states where counting mail-in ballots takes longer, may not be decided for several days. Polls point to a 'blue wave,' but Republicans could still surprise Midterm elections take place every four years, halfway through a president's term. Americans vote for representatives to numerous federal and state offices, including Congress, state legislatures, governorships and attorneys general. The elections are widely regarded as a referendum on the sitting president's performance, and historically, the president's party tends to lose ground. An initial picture of the balance of power in Congress could emerge overnight or Wednesday morning. However, close races, particularly in states where counting mail-in ballots takes longer, may not be decided for several days. The greatest attention is focused on the races for the Senate and House of Representatives. When the president's party controls both chambers, it is easier for the administration to advance legislation and policy initiatives. When the opposing party holds a majority, the president's ability to govern is significantly constrained, potentially turning him into a "lame duck." Republicans enter the elections holding majorities in both chambers. In the outgoing House, they have 218 seats compared with 214 for Democrats. Another lawmaker identifies as an independent but leans Republican, while two seats are vacant. In the Senate, Republicans hold a stronger 53-47 majority and can afford to lose up to three seats. In the event of a 50-50 tie, Vice President JD Vance would cast the deciding vote. But the Republican Party enters Election Day under considerable pressure. For months, polls have suggested that Democrats could regain control of the House. Since gasoline prices surged following the war in Iran, polling has also indicated a more competitive battle for the Senate. With a Democratic takeover of the House widely anticipated in pre-election assessments, much of the attention Tuesday night will focus on the closely contested Senate races. Thirty-five Senate seats are up for election, but only a handful of races are considered truly competitive. Their outcomes will determine control of the upper chamber. Polling on the eve of the vote showed unexpectedly close races in deeply conservative states that Trump carried by double-digit margins against Kamala Harris two years ago, including Alaska, Iowa, Ohio and South Carolina. Competitive contests are also unfolding in Texas, a major Republican stronghold that has not elected a Democrat to the Senate in 38 years, and Kansas, where Democrats have not won a Senate seat in 94 years. Some recent polls gave Democratic candidates substantial leads in several of these races. However, pollsters have warned that conservative voters in rural areas can be difficult to reach and that surveys may once again be underestimating Republican support. Others point out that polls underestimated Democratic strength in the previous midterm elections. Democrats are hoping that a surge in support from independent voters and moderate Republicans will produce a sweeping "blue wave," allowing them to capture both chambers of Congress simultaneously. Such an outcome has occurred in only three previous midterm elections, most recently 20 years ago, when public frustration over the Iraq war helped Democrats make major gains. In an effort to preserve Republican control of at least the Senate, Trump spent the past month holding a series of campaign rallies designed to energize his supporters and drive turnout. Many of those rallies took place in conservative states he won comfortably two years ago, reflecting the defensive position in which his party now finds itself. One of his central messages was a warning that the "radical left" could seize control of Washington, both now and in 2028. He argued that Democrats could then entrench their power for generations by appointing new Supreme Court justices and granting statehood to Washington, DC, and Puerto Rico, changes he said would give Democrats an advantage in the Senate. Israel at the center of Trump's 'election surprise' With gasoline prices and inflation still high, however, Trump's warnings about Democratic control have struggled to gain traction. The president has done little to help Republicans on that front, frequently appearing dismissive of Americans' economic difficulties. He has repeatedly described the surge in gasoline prices as a "small price" to pay for preventing Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons. Trump has also insisted that the economy is performing exceptionally well. In an interview with Fox News on Tuesday afternoon, he claimed that "inflation has been solved," even though annual inflation is expected to reach approximately 3.7% this year, well above the Federal Reserve's 2% target. Israel has also become a major issue in the elections, with American support for the country declining sharply following the wars in Gaza and Iran. In Michigan, for example, a close Senate race is underway between progressive Muslim Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, who has emphasized his opposition to continued US military assistance to Israel, and pro-Israel Republican Mike Rogers. Perhaps in an attempt to help the Republican candidate, Trump made a surprise announcement during his Fox News interview Tuesday, claiming that he had reached an agreement with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to end approximately $4 billion in annual US military aid to Israel. During the interview, Trump appeared to address arguments made by Democrats such as El-Sayed, who have criticized the assistance as a burden on American taxpayers, even though the funds are used to purchase U.S.-made weapons and military equipment. "The left uses the $4 billion payment, which everybody knows about and is no secret, to portray it as a symbol of unfairness, and we can't allow that to happen," Trump said. CNN suggested Tuesday evening that Trump's announcement was directly connected to the Michigan race. The president's campaign account on X later amplified the statement, posting an image with a large headline announcing the end of aid to Israel alongside the words "America First." Earlier, CNN reported, citing a White House source, that Trump had been optimistic during the initial stages of the campaign about Republicans' chances of defying expectations Tuesday night, but had grown more pessimistic in recent days, leaving him in a subdued mood. Later, however, CNN quoted a presidential adviser who insisted that Trump was in "great spirits." The adviser said the White House remained "cautiously optimistic." 'It's scary. We need change': Michigan voters voice frustration For many Americans, Tuesday's elections offer an opportunity to express dissatisfaction with Trump's policies. Beyond the unpopular war in Iran, the president has launched a mass deportation campaign against undocumented immigrants, which has sparked widespread anger and unrest in American cities. His administration has imposed tariffs on numerous countries, is engaged in a trade war with Canada and has pursued legal action against political opponents. "I feel I have a duty to do everything I can to change the direction our country is heading right now, to put it back on the path of democracy and away from autocracy," said Jane Callum, a 77-year-old retired teacher who voted for Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff in an Atlanta suburb. Georgia is considered a swing state, and Ossoff won his seat by a narrow margin six years ago. This time, amid frustration with Trump, polls show him holding a substantial lead over his Republican opponent, and the race is no longer considered competitive. In Macomb, Michigan, north of Detroit, 62-year-old voter Arnes Rogers told CNN he was hoping for change. "It's never been this bad. Gas prices are high. The economy is terrible. We've been losing jobs for the past two years, since he took office," he said. "I hope my company, one of the Big Three US automakers, can keep operating because our parts come from Canada. He's picking fights with everybody, and it's terrible to see where things are going in America right now. It's just scary." Another voter, Hayden Mendez, said he had cast his ballot for Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan. Alongside his criticism of Israel, El-Sayed has focused his campaign on the cost of living and health care. Mendez also cited the war in Iran as one of the reasons behind his decision. "I just think things never should have gotten this bad in the first place," he said. "But I hope whoever wins today actually looks out for the American people and chooses to do things that serve Americans instead of just making things worse for them." Election fraud fears and questions over whether Trump will accept the results Tuesday's elections are also taking place amid concerns that Trump, who continues to refuse to acknowledge his defeat to Joe Biden in the 2020 presidential election and has repeatedly made unsubstantiated claims of widespread voter fraud, could attempt to challenge or obstruct the midterm results. In recent months, Trump has raised numerous allegations of election fraud, while the federal administration has taken several steps that have alarmed election officials across the United States. California Gov. Gavin Newsom warned over the weekend that the Trump administration might attempt to seize ballots and other election materials, allegedly to interfere with the vote-counting process. 1,000 election monitors deployed, but no immigration agents near polling places On Monday night, the administration filed an emergency petition with the Supreme Court demanding that approximately 20,000 mail-in ballots in California be separated from the count until the eligibility of the voters could be established. The administration claimed that some of those voters might not be US citizens. California authorities countered that the list submitted by the federal government was unreliable and contained numerous errors. The Supreme Court quickly rejected the request. Another federal court challenge, filed last month, sought to prevent recognition of a possible defeat by Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska. The administration argued that a "spoiler candidate" with the same name as the senator was running in the race and could confuse voters. Trump claimed the candidacy amounted to "election fraud of the highest order," but the court rejected the petition. Asked last week whether he would accept the midterm election results, Trump offered only a conditional response: "I'll accept them if they're fair." The U.S. Justice Department also announced Tuesday that it had deployed 1,000 election monitors to polling locations across the country, primarily in Democratic strongholds, to ensure that voting procedures were conducted properly. More dramatic measures feared by Democrats, including the possible deployment of immigration enforcement agents or National Guard troops near polling stations to allegedly intimidate voters, have not materialized.

news.title: US voters to determine control of Congress in Tuesday’s midterm elections
news.text:
Voters are going to the polls across the United States on Tuesday, casting ballots in a midterm election that will determine the control of U.S. Congress during the remaining two years of President Donald Trump’s term.

All 435 seats in the U.S. House of Representatives are up for election along with 35 of the Senate’s 100 seats.

The Republican Party held majority in both chambers heading into the election, while the Democratic Party is hoping to flip enough seats in its favor to take back control of the legislative body.

Voters in many states were able to cast ballots ahead of Tuesday’s Election Day, with a combination of in-person early voting and mail-in ballots available in most areas. More than 57 million people cast early ballots, according to the University of Florida Election Lab.

In addition to the U.S. congressional races, there are also elections for governor in 36 of the country’s 50 states, as well as members of state legislatures and other local races.

More than 54 million voters had already cast their ballots either in person or by mail by Monday, according to the University of Florida Election Lab. During the last midterm election in 2022, there were about 112 million total votes.

Prominent figures used weekend rallies to push for support, including former Vice President Kamala Harris boosting Democratic candidates in California. President Trump promoted Republicans in Kansas and Iowa, and he made a final pitch for support Monday during an event in Washington.

Republicans held a 53-47 Senate majority heading into the election. Some of the most closely watched races for control of the Senate are in Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio, and Texas.

In the House, Republicans hold a 219-214 advantage. History suggests Republicans could have a more difficult time holding their House majority, as the party of the president has lost an average of 23 seats during midterm elections dating back to 1934.

Those elected Tuesday will take office on January 3, 2027.

news.title: Explainer: Key election races in the battle to control the U.S. Congress
news.text:
There are 470 total seats in the U.S. House of Representatives and Senate that are up for election in November, but control of both chambers will likely be determined by a small group of competitive races. Democrats and Republicans each have a certain block of seats that they consider safe, with long hoping to get a w standing patterns of voters in those districts supporting one party or the other.

That leaves the so-called battleground areas where either party could win. These are the areas where the two major parties have spent millions of dollars in and in turn deliver an important House or Senate majority.

Key Senate races 

Heading into the election, Republicans hold a 53-47 Senate majority. Thirty-five of the chamber’s seats are on the ballot in November: 22 currently held by Republicans and 13 held by Democrats.

In Alaska, Republican Dan Sullivan is seeking reelection to the seat he has held since 2015. Democrat Mary Peltola, a former House representative for the state, is seeking to flip the seat for her party. One wrinkle to this race: An independent candidate, also named Dan Sullivan, is on the ballot as well.

In Georgia, Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff is seeking his second term after being elected to this seat in 2021. Republican Congressman Mike Collins is trying to move up from the House to the Senate representing a state that President Donald Trump won in 2024.

In Iowa, Republican Senator Joni Ernst is retiring after two terms, leaving an open race between Republican Congresswoman Ashley Hinson and Democrat Josh Turek, a state legislator.

In Kansas, Democrat Adam Hamilton, who leads the country’s largest United Methodist church, is trying to become the first Democrat elected to the senate from the state since 1932. He is trying to unseat Republican Senator Roger Marshall, who was elected to this seat in 2020.

Maine Republican Susan Collins is seeking another term for the Senate seat she has held since first being elected in 1996. Democrats have made unseating her a top priority, with Troy Jackson, a former state Senate President, as their candidate.

In Michigan, the retirement of Democratic Senator Gary Peters has given way to a tight battle between Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, a former public health official, and Republican former Congressman Mike Rogers. 

Another Democratic retirement has opened a seat in New Hampshire, with Senator Jeanne Shaheen not running for reelection. Former Republican Senator John Sununu, who lost this seat in 2008, has returned to face Democratic Congressman Chris Pappas.

In North Carolina, Republican Thom Tillis’ retirement has opened a race between Republican Michael Whatley, the former chairman of the Republican National Committee, and Democrat Roy Cooper, the state’s former governor.

A special election in Ohio has drawn some of the highest spending by the two parties, as they seek to fill the final two years of the Senate term Vice President JD Vance vacated upon taking office in 2025. Republican Jon Husted was appointed to the seat and is now seeking election to finish the term. Democrat Sherrod Brown is trying to return to the Senate after losing his seat in 2024.

In Texas, Republican state Attorney General Ken Paxton is facing Democrat James Talarico, a state representative. Democrats are trying to reverse a longstanding conservative hold in the state where they have not won a Senate seat since 1988.

The race for the House of Representatives

Republicans hold a slim majority in the House of Representatives as well, with Democrats seeking to gain a net of four seats to flip control.

Among the races to watch are seats in three districts that Republicans won in 2024, but also where a majority of voters supported Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris.

In New York’s 17th district, incumbent Republican Mike Lawler is seeking reelection against Democrat Cait Conley, a former national security official in the Biden administration.

In Nebraska’s 2nd district, Democrat Denise Powell, a political activist, is facing Republican Brinker Harding, a city council member, in an open race following the retirement of Republican Congressman Don Bacon.

And in Pennsylvania’s 1st district, incumbent Republican Brian Fitzpatrick is facing Democrat Bob Harvie, a county commissioner.

In a case of a Democrat-held seat in a district that supported President Trump in 2024, incumbent Democrat Marie Gluesenkamp Perez is running for reelection against Republican John Braun, the state senate’s Republican leader in Washington's third district.

The lead-up to this election cycle featured a battle in multiple states over congressional district maps, with Republicans and Democrats seeking to redraw districts in a way that could make them more favorable to candidates from their party.

One such area is Texas’ 34th district, where Republicans redistricted to try to gain an advantage. Democratic Congressman Vicente Gonzalez is seeking a sixth term in office and is facing Republican Eric Flores, a former federal prosecutor. 

In California’s 22nd district, it was Democrats who tried to use a new map to gain an edge. Republican Congressman David Valadao is trying to hold his seat for another term with Democrat Randy Villegas, a professor, as his challenger.

Other races to watch include Maine’s 2nd district, where the retirement of Democratic incumbent Jared Golden has opened a race between Republican Paul LePage, a former state governor, and Democrat Matt Dunlap, a state auditor.

And in Ohio, the state’s 7th district features a race between Republican Congressman Max Miller and Democrat Brian Poindexter, an ironworker.

Election day is November 3. The elected members of Congress will be sworn in on January 3.

news.title: 18 races results to watch to see if Democrats or Republicans control Wisconsin legislature
news.text:
Here are key races to watch for control of the state Legislature as results come in on Nov. 3.

Democrats, who have been in the minority in both legislative chambers for 15 years, need to flip two Senate seats and five seats in the Assembly to take over as the majority party. This is the second set of elections under new legislative maps enacted in 2024.

Results will begin to come in after polls close at 8 p.m. See results for all statewide offices, including governor and attorney general, review full results for all Wisconsin state Senate and Assembly seats and follow our live coverage for news and updates.

Senate District 5

Republican Mike Roberts vs. Democratic state Rep. Robyn Vining.

Senate District 5 encompasses communities west of Milwaukee running from Pewaukee through Brookfield, into Wauwatosa and West Allis. The retirement of Republican Sen. Rob Hutton created an open seat.

The district has not been represented by a Democrat since 2010. It broke for Democratic former Vice President Kamala Harris over Republican President Donald Trump by 5.9 points in the fall 2024 presidential election.

Senate District 17

Democratic state Rep. Jenna Jacobson vs. incumbent Republican Sen. Howard Marklein.

The district runs along the western part of the state into Crawford County, ending just north of Soldiers Grove. It includes portions of Grant, Iowa, Lafayette and Green counties with the Wisconsin River as a northern border, and now covers the southwestern portion of Dane County.

Harris won the newly drawn district by 1 percentage point in the 2024 presidential election. Marklein has held the seat since 2015, defeating challengers under its previous boundaries by eight points or more in each of his Senate races.

Senate District 21

Republican Jim Croft vs. Democrat Trevor Jung.

Senate District 21 includes part of the city of Racine and parts of northern Racine County, along with Franklin, Greenfield and Hales Corners in Milwaukee County. The retirement of Republican Rep. Van Wanggaard created a competitive open seat.

The district voted for Harris by a 1.3-point margin in 2024.

Senate District 25

Democrat Charly Ray vs. Republican Erik Severson.

Senate District 25 includes areas of Douglas, Bayfield, Burnett, Washburn and Sawyer counties.

The seat is open because its current state Sen. Romaine Quinn, R-Birchwood, is seeking reelection in the 23rd District under the changed maps. Trump won the district by 13.6 points in 2024, but both parties have directed resources toward the race this year.

Senate District 31

Republican Michele Magadance Skinner vs. incumbent Democratic Sen. Jeff Smith.

Senate District 31 includes areas of Dunn, Chippewa, Eau Claire and Trempealeau counties. Harris won the district by 2.2 points in 2024, and Republicans have made it a target this year.

Assembly District 21

Democrat Dan Bukiewicz vs. Republican Dylan Pfaffenbach.

Assembly District 21 includes Oak Creek and portions of Milwaukee and Greenfield.

Rep. Jessie Rodriguez, R-Oak Creek, decided not to run for reelection in the district that broke for Harris by 4.1 points in 2024.

Assembly District 26

Republican John Belanger vs. incumbent Democratic state Rep. Joe Sheehan.

Assembly District 26 includes parts of Sheboygan County. Sheehan was first elected to the seat in 2024, ousting GOP Rep. Amy Binsfeld, who is running in the 9th Senate District this year. Sheehan won his 2024 race by 2.9 points, running just ahead of Harris at 2.6 points.

Assembly District 30

Democrat Kevin Knoke vs. incumbent Republican Rep. Shannon Zimmerman.

Assembly District 30 includes areas of St. Croix and Pierce counties. Trump carried the seat by 4.4 points in 2024, and both parties have invested in the legislative contest this year.

Assembly District 51

Democrat Ben Gruber vs. incumbent Republican Rep. Todd Novak.

Assembly District 51 includes areas of Grant, Iowa and Dane counties. Novak was first elected in 2014 and has fended off challenges in the district, which broke for Harris by 3.5 points, in each election since.

Assembly District 53

Republican David Daniels vs. Democrat Becky Nichols.

Assembly District 53 includes areas of Outagamie and Winnebago counties. The retirement of Republican Rep. Dean Kaufert created an open seat.

The district went for Harris by 4.4 points in 2024.

Assembly District 61

Democrat Ben Brist vs. incumbent Republican Rep. Bob Donovan.

Assembly District 61 includes Greendale, Hales Corners, Greenfield as well as parts of Milwaukee and Franklin in Milwaukee County. Voters backed Harris with a 2.2-point lead in 2024.

Assembly District 82

Democrat Rico Camacho vs. Republican Bryson Reyes.

Assembly District 82 covers most of the City of Waukesha as well as a smaller piece of the Village of Waukesha. The retirement of Republican state Rep. Scott Allen created an open seat.

Trump won the seat by 8 points in 2024.

Assembly District 85

Democrat John Kroll vs. incumbent state Rep. Pat Snyder.

Assembly District 85 is in Marathon County. Trump barely carried the district in 2024, winning it by less than a percentage point. Both parties have spent heavily to contest the seat.

Assembly District 88

Incumbent Republican state Rep. Ben Franklin vs. Democrat Brandy Tollefson.

Assembly District 88 is in Brown County. Harris barely won it in 2024, holding a lead of less than a percentage point over Trump. The seat has been actively targeted by both parties.

Assembly District 89

Republican Bobby Lindsey vs. incumbent Democratic Rep. Ryan Spaude.

Assembly District 89 is in Brown County. Harris won the seat by 2 points in 2024, and Republicans have put significant effort into ousting Spaude after his first term.

Assembly District 91

Incumbent Democratic state Rep. Jodi Emerson vs. Republican Bruce Stabenow.

Assembly District 91 includes parts of Chippewa and Eau Claire counties. Harris won the district by 4.5 points in 2024, but it sits within the 31st Senate District where Republicans are aiming to oust Smith.

Assembly District 92

Democrat Jeremiah Frederickson vs. incumbent Republican state Rep. Clint Moses.

Assembly District 92 includes areas of Dunn and Chippewa counties. It supported Trump by a 7-point margin in 2024, but Republicans and Democrats have both flooded the airwaves with ads targeting the race.

Assembly District 94

Incumbent Democratic state Rep. Steve Doyle vs. Republican Kevin Purnell.

Assembly District 94 includes parts of Trempealeau and La Crosse counties and broke for Trump by 2.2 points in 2024. Republicans are seeking to boot Doyle, who has represented the district since 2011.

news.title: How political candidates charter jets to travel across battleground states during election cycles
news.text: It's been a busy year for campaign travel as state and federal lawmakers — and their challengers — crisscross the country for rallies and fundraisers for the 2026 midterm elections. But moving candidates and their staff, donors, press, and, in some cases, armed security, from one stop to the next isn't as simple as booking a commercial flight. Political travel has become a niche of its own within aviation. One pro in that realm is Gregg Brunson-Pitts, the founder and CEO of Advanced Aviation Team. Founded in 2015, the Washington, DC-based firm arranges VIP travel for ultrawealthy families, celebrities, and corporate C-suites, with a particular specialty in campaign travel. Brunson-Pitts' company manages every step of political travel — from scheduling flights and sourcing crews to branding planes, coordinating security, and adapting to rapidly changing itineraries. Advanced Aviation handles hundreds of thousands of dollars in contracts over a single election cycle and describes itself as nonpartisan. This year, Federal Election Commission (FEC) filings show it received roughly $58,000 from Sen. Susan Collins' leadership PAC and $66,000 from Rep. Hakeem Jeffries' campaign committee for 2026 travel, among others. All 435 House seats, 35 Senate seats (including two special elections), 36 governorships, three territorial governorships, numerous state offices, and thousands of state legislative seats nationwide will be on Tuesday's ballot. "We are hyper-focused on client satisfaction, which means seeing around corners, being problem solvers, and being solutions-oriented," Brunson-Pitts told Business Insider in early 2026. "We're seeing organizations plan earlier and lock in travel support sooner, because once the calendar tightens, capacity disappears quickly." Brunson-Pitts previously ran the White House Travel Office for eight years under former President George W. Bush. He said a charter jet carrying the White House press corps, Secret Service personnel, and other staff would almost always fly in tandem with Air Force One. That experience — blending chartered aircraft, armed security, and government protocols — helped him build a specialty focused on the logistical demands of modern campaigns: "Our approach allows us to support clients affiliated with any party," he said. Unlike charter operators or fractional owners such as NetJets or Flexjet, which operate and maintain their own planes, Advanced Aviation Team functions as a broker with access to contracted aircraft. "We can source smaller private jets, but we can also do group travel for 100 or more people and customize an airliner," he said. "Not a lot of brokers can do that; that's what sets us apart." Brunson-Pitts said he built a team drawing from inside and outside the aviation industry, bringing together experience in politics, campaign travel, logistics, and private aviation chartering, brokerage, and sales. For example, Peter Newell, the former director of the White House travel office under President Barack Obama, joined as company president in March. Meanwhile, before joining Advanced Aviation, company vice president Jonathan Tasler organized the McDonnell Douglas MD-83 chartered by Mitt Romney's 2012 presidential campaign. This logistical expertise is imperative to a successful campaign, as winning can come down to how fast, cheaply, and visibly candidates can move across battleground states. "The campaign plane is an important tool to help candidates safely meet with voters and get out their message. Down the homestretch, it becomes a working office and a home away from home," Brunson-Pitts told Business Insider ahead of the midterms. "Our team works behind the scenes coordinating crews, airports, ground transportation, security and last-minute changes so the candidate can keep moving." Brunson-Pitts' client list spans two decades of election cycles and includes officials from both parties. Beyond Sen. Collins and Rep. Jeffries, 2026 FEC filings show the campaigns of Arkansas Sen. Tom Cotton and West Virginia Sen. Jim Justice also paid AAT for air travel. In 2024, the firm worked with Doug Emhoff, the husband of former Vice President Kamala Harris, and Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz, Harris' 2024 running mate. He has also handled contracts for politicians such as former President Joe Biden, Hillary Clinton, John Kerry, Sen. Bernie Sanders, Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, and "many more." Brunson-Pitts said AAT arranges flights on aircraft ranging from regional jets to full-size airliners: Emhoff traveled on a Bombardier CRJ-200, and Walz used a Boeing 757 in 2024. Biden used a Boeing 737 during his 2020 campaign. The team may modify aircraft inside and out — from changing seat layouts to adding campaign logos — in coordination with design teams and third-party vendors. Branding can range from simple decals to fully repainted liveries. "From Labor Day to Election Day, the travel gets really intense," he said. "So we try to make it a home away from home with WiFi, power, and catering; maybe their favorite food or a meal from their favorite local restaurant." Comfort, however, is only part of the challenge. Security is often the most complex variable. Brunson-Pitts said sitting members of Congress sometimes receive Capitol Police protection, while governors may rely on state details. Most first-time House or Senate candidates, however, hire private security. A smaller group of high-profile candidates receives Secret Service protection due to national prominence or credible threats. That can dictate everything from airport choice to how close an aircraft can park to a terminal. While expensive charter flights may frustrate some voters, candidates argue the aircraft offer speed, security, and flexibility that commercial travel can't match. Sen. Bernie Sanders, an independent from Vermont, faced criticism earlier this year for using private planes during his coast-to-coast "Fighting Oligarchy" tour, which covered 25 US cities. Campaign finance records show the flights cost more than $221,000. Sanders defended the decision on Fox News in May, saying the packed rally schedule made flying commercially impractical and that charters were necessary to reach the tens of thousands of voters. Biden expressed a similar sentiment during his 2008 presidential run. "If I had a plane, I would make 30% more appearances in the state of Iowa, in New Hampshire, in Nevada," he said, according to ABC News. "That's where money does make a difference." Campaign resources often determine travel options. Well-funded operations can afford charters that allow multiple stops and last-minute schedule changes. These charters can cost millions of dollars over a campaign season once crews, aircraft rental, fuel, repositioning flights, landing fees, branding, and other expenses are factored in. Financial documents show the 2020 Biden campaign spent about $2.2 million on private charters. Forbes estimated Vice President JD Vance's 2024 campaign Boeing 737 — not chartered by Advanced Aviation — likely cost around $30,000 an hour. Brunson-Pitts said pricing varies by season, passenger count, and onboard experience. He added that the press and the Secret Service typically pay for their own seats. Charters often bypass crowded terminals for private aircraft service stations with minimal security screening and low crowds, allowing for faster boarding and quicker turnarounds. Smaller campaigns sometimes rely on less expensive commercial flights, even if they are less efficient. Some candidates do so for the sake of public perception. Either way, Brunson-Pitts said the logistics for these commercial flyers can be complicated. Candidates often have an entourage of armed guards and sometimes drive directly onto the tarmac to board the plane from their motorcade. "We usually pick the operator from a pool that is familiar with the process for an armed detail," he said. "There's a lot of behind-the-scenes coordination and paperwork, and the pilots need to be aware, but we know how it should flow so there are no day-of surprises." Editor's note: This story was originally published in March 2026 and was most recently updated in November 2026.
news.summary: Midterm incumbents like Sen. Susan Collins and Rep. Hakeem Jeffries have spent tens of thousands of dollars on campaign travel.
news.author: Taylor Rains

news.title: The Senate on a razor’s edge: The races that will decide America's midterms
news.text: Polling stations are opening across the United States in a midterm election that, a year ago, Republicans expected to survive with their Senate majority intact. That expectation has been reduced to a hope.Start with the House of Representatives, where the question is no longer whether Democrats win, but by how much. Prediction markets give them a 95% chance of taking control. The Cook Political Report now rates 222 seats as at least leaning Democratic, four more than the 218 needed for a majority, against 195 for Republicans, with 18 pure toss-ups. A good night for Democrats could see them controlling as many as 230 seats. A great night means the Senate and a blue wave.The magic numberRepublicans hold 53 of the Senate's 100 seats. To take control, Democrats need a net gain of four. Three is not enough: in a 50-50 Senate, Vice President JD Vance casts the tie-breaking vote, just as Kamala Harris did a record 33 times as vice president; however, Senator John Fetterman, the Democrat from Pennsylvania, could muddle certain partisan votes in a 50-50 Senate.Prediction markets now give Democrats roughly a three-in-four chance of winning the Senate. Cook rates six races as toss-ups, all of them held by Republicans.The battleground covers 12 seats. Democrats are defending three: Michigan, Minnesota and New Hampshire. Republicans are defending nine: Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Nebraska, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina and Texas.Two of the three Democratic seats look safe. In Minnesota, Peggy Flanagan leads Michele Tafoya by 5.2 points in the RealClearPolitics average. In New Hampshire, Chris Pappas leads former Senator John E. Sununu by eight points in the same average. Michigan is another matter, but we will come back to it.North Carolina: AbandonedNorth Carolina is a swing state, but it leans Republican: it has voted for the Republican presidential candidate in every election since 1980 bar one. With Senator Thom Tillis retiring, it should have been a fair fight.Instead, national Republicans all but walked away. The Senate Leadership Fund, the party's main Senate super PAC, had planned to spend $71 million backing its candidate, Michael Whatley. It cancelled its remaining ads in early October, after spending more than $30 million. Former Governor Roy Cooper now leads Whatley by eight points in polls from both Quantus Insights and Trafalgar Group, two Republican-leaning pollsters.Barring an upset, North Carolina will be the Democrats' first flip. That leaves three more to find.Ohio and Texas: The big prizesDemocrats placed one of their biggest bets in Ohio. Sherrod Brown, who lost his seat two years ago, is running against Republican Jon Husted, who was appointed to JD Vance's old Senate seat in 2025. Brown leads by 2.8 points in the RealClearPolitics average, in a state Trump won by double digits.Texas would be the bigger upset. The state has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1988. Yet Democrat James Talarico leads Republican Ken Paxton 49% to 47% in the latest Texas Southern University poll—in line with other recent surveys. Still, this is within the margin of error and is effectively a tie. Texas probably isn’t turning blue. Republicans lead every other statewide race in the University of Houston's Hobby School poll, from governor down to railroad commissioner. What Talarico could benefit from is ticket-splitting: voters backing a Republican for governor, attorney general or Congress, then crossing over to the Democrat for the Senate. Republican Governor Greg Abbott wins 93% of Republicans in the Hobby poll. Paxton wins 88%.Part of the problem for Paxton is Talarico, a disciplined young candidate who has run a strong campaign. The other part of the problem is Paxton. The embattled attorney general, impeached by his own party in the Texas House in 2023 and acquitted by the state Senate, is viewed unfavourably by 57% of likely voters and favourably by just 42%, according to Texas Southern University. Trump backed him over four-term Senator John Cornyn in the primary. If Paxton loses, it will be a wound Republicans partly inflicted on themselves.The curious case of AlaskaAlaska votes Republican for president, but it has a long independent streak. It sent Democrat Mary Peltola to the House in 2022. This time, Peltola is challenging Senator Dan Sullivan, and she leads 48% to 46% in the latest New York Times/Siena poll. Again, within the margin of error.Then came the other Dan Sullivan. The New York Times reported last week that Democratic operatives, including senior Peltola aides and officials at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, recruited Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired teacher, to run as a spoiler and confuse voters. Ballot-stacking is generally legal, but the optics are terrible. Peltola denies involvement. Governor Mike Dunleavy has ordered a criminal investigation and the Justice Department sued, unsuccessfully, to stop Alaska certifying the result if Sullivan loses.A trick meant to take votes from Sullivan could end up costing Peltola the race, or the legitimacy of her win. Expect President Trump to aggressively attack the result should Peltola win.Kansas: A pastor in the pulpitKansas has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932. This year, the Democrats are running Adam Hamilton, the senior pastor of the largest Methodist congregation in the country, against Senator Roger Marshall. Hamilton leads by 4.1 points in the RealClearPolitics average.Even the Washington Post's pollsters, whose own survey had Hamilton 10 points ahead, caution that Democrats were far more eager to respond than Republicans. But in a state Trump won by double digits, a single-digit race is a warning.The rest of the map In Maine, Troy Jackson leads Senator Susan Collins by 3.6 points in the RealClearPolitics average—but never underestimate Senator Collins, who has a history of pulling off electoral upsets. Iowa is a coin flip, with Josh Turek at 48% and Ashley Hinson at 47% in the New York Times/Siena poll. In South Carolina, Senator Darline Graham, appointed in July after the death of her brother Lindsey, leads Democrat Annie Andrews by 2.6 points in the RealClearPolitics average. Nebraska offers Republicans the most breathing room, with Senator Pete Ricketts leading independent Dan Osborn by six points in the latest Times/Siena poll.Michigan: The Republican lifeline?If Republicans are to hold the Senate, Michigan may be where they do it. It is the only Democratic-held seat in RealClearPolitics' toss-up column, in a state that voted Trump, Biden, Trump. With Senator Gary Peters retiring, a Republican win would force Democrats to find five flips.The Democratic nominee is Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive former public health official backed by Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, whom Republicans tie to the Democratic Socialists of America. A staunch critic of Israel, he has pledged to oppose further US aid to the country. His platform still includes Medicare for All and abolishing ICE, but on the stump, he has traded the left-wing agenda for a populist pitch.Some in his own party have been harsher. On Sunday, Congresswoman Haley Stevens, whom El-Sayed narrowly beat in the Democratic primary, endorsed Mike Rogers, the Republican candidate, after being disinvited from a joint campaign event. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer called it "a despicable betrayal". Senator John Fetterman, a fellow Democrat, took Stevens' side, saying El-Sayed has "the worst case of little man syndrome I've ever seen". El-Sayed still leads by 5.3 points in the RealClearPolitics average, but data from Trafalgar Group has him just one point ahead. A Republican win in Michigan would be a major upset, but the path to it is narrower than El-Sayed's.It comes down to turnoutThis should have been a year in which Republicans kept the Senate. Instead, dissatisfaction with Washington, the economy and Trump has turned it into a close race that could break either way.By most metrics, Democrats hold the enthusiasm advantage. Polls have favoured the Democrats nationally, but we have seen that mistake before. The question is which model holds. In 2022, pollsters underestimated Democrats. In 2024, Republicans exceeded most pollsters' expectations.Both models come down to the same thing: whether that enthusiasm becomes votes. Republicans hope to hold the blue wave at bay. Turnout will turn the tide, one way or the other.
news.summary: Democrats look all but certain to take the US House. The real fight is for the Senate, where a handful of races in states Republicans never expected to defend will decide who controls Washington.

news.title: Desi romance with Trump is fading amid racism and immigration bite
news.text: TOI Correspondent From Washington: Donald Trump made an unlikely political breakthrough in 2024, prising away a slice of Indian-American voters from a community that had reliably backed Democrats for decades. Two years later, the romance appears to have soured.A new survey by the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace finds that the Republican gains have largely evaporated, with Indian-Americans swinging back towards Democrats ahead of the November 2026 midterms. According to the Indian American Attitudes Survey conducted in October, 62 per cent of Ind-Am citizens intend to vote Democratic in their congressional district, against just 19 per cent backing Republicans, whittled down from nearly 30 per cent who voted for Trump in 2024. Another 12 per cent are undecided.
