news.title: Inside the Decision Desk: When will we know Senate and House control?
news.text: In 2024, Donald Trump’s election night wins in the presidential battlegrounds of Georgia, North Carolina, Texas and Florida meant that most Americans went to bed on Tuesday with a good idea of the result of the election — and woke up to the networks having called enough states to declare Trump the president-elect. Two years later, control of Congress is at stake. Republicans are trying to hang on to slim majorities in both chambers as Democrats try to wrest power in Washington for the final two years of Trump’s term. Democrats are heavily favored in public polling in the House and in a number of key Senate contests — and if those numbers prove accurate, it’s possible that NBC News could project control of both chambers on election night. But it’s more likely that determining the winners in important races will take time. Of course, no one, including the Decision Desk, will know what will unfold until election night, but we will have a good sense possibly early in the night of how the contests are trending. The answer of when we could call control in both the House and Senate depends not only on how states count their votes, but on how close the races will be. When we could know Senate control Senate control will likely come down to the eight races that NBC News rates as either toss-ups (Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, Texas) or lean Democratic (Maine, Michigan, New Hampshire). Assuming that Democrats win the states NBC News currently rates as “Likely” Democratic (which includes flipping North Carolina’s Senate seat from red to blue, and keeping Georgia in their column), Democrats still need to win five of these eight contests. Some of these states are quick to count their ballots, and others are perennially slow. If some of these Senate contests are as close as we expect, calling control of the Senate as a whole could take us into the early morning hours of Wednesday, regardless of who wins those individual races. It is also a real possibility that Americans will wake up at a slightly more reasonable hour on Wednesday without a majority decided, even if we have a good sense of who will ultimately win. And if Senate control comes down to the outcome in Alaska, we’ll all be here awhile. In that case, it will take a couple of weeks to know who won the majority thanks to the state’s ranked choice voting system. Past elections offer a useful guide to how quickly we expect to see votes counted in each of these states, even if the timing Tuesday night is not exact. Let’s look more closely at each of these categories — the fast-counting states, the slow-but-steady states, and the ranked choice wild cards. The fast counters Votes in Iowa, Kansas, Ohio and Texas were counted fairly quickly in 2024. We expect over 80% of the vote in those states to be counted by midnight Eastern time. If those historical patterns hold, there is a good chance that those Senate races will be called. And some of these calls may come in before midnight if there is some spread in the races as some recent polls suggest. But Democrats must win five of these battleground Senate races to take a majority, which means that even if they win all four states here, NBC News would still not be able to project control of the Senate. The steady counters In two of the key battleground states, New Hampshire and Michigan, nearly all votes will be counted over the course of election night, but more steadily and slowly than the fast counters. Here, elections are administered by towns and municipalities, not by counties. This results in a more decentralized and variable counting process that lasts until early morning, or even midday Wednesday. How quickly these races are called really depends upon the margin of the race. Earlier in the election cycle, polls suggested both these races would be close. Recent polls favoring the Democratic candidates and what appears to be a Democratic advantage in the early vote in Michigan mean there’s a wide range of timing possibilities there. If the nationwide Democratic momentum translates to results, New Hampshire could possibly be called before midnight. But that seems to be highly unlikely in a place like Michigan, where Wayne County, home to Detroit, often releases large batches of votes between midnight and 3 a.m. ET. This is such a significant source of ballots that statewide races in Michigan often cannot be called without Wayne County’s results. The takeaway here is that if the Senate races in these states are close as the polls have indicated all along, it’s unlikely that calls will come before the early morning hours. But it all depends upon how far apart the two candidates are in the state, and we won’t know that until tonight. The ranked choice states Maine and Alaska are the slowest counters of the group. As in New Hampshire, Maine’s elections are administered by towns, each with their own schedule for tabulating ballots and releasing results. In Alaska, mail ballots from remote corners of the state can arrive up to 15 days after the election. If these historical patterns hold, there will not be enough votes counted on election night to call a close race in either state. In 2024, the presidential race in Maine was called on Wednesday at 4:40 p.m. ET, and in Alaska on Thursday at 10 a.m. ET. Then-Vice President Kamala Harris won Maine by about 7 points, while Trump won Alaska by 13 points. It’s possible the margins in this year’s Senate contests could be much closer. There is a second complication in Maine and Alaska that could cause even more delay in knowing which party will control the Senate. These states both use ranked choice voting for their Senate races, in which voters rank the candidates in order of preference. If no candidate is the first choice of more than 50% of voters, the winner will be determined by ranked choice tabulation, in which the candidate with the fewest votes is eliminated and their votes are reallocated based on voters’ next-most preferred candidates. In Alaska, the ranked choice tabulation occurs 15 days after Election Day. Maine does not provide official guidelines on when its ranked choice tabulation will occur, but in June, the ranked choice results were released 10 days after Maine’s primary election. In either case, if one or both of these seats are needed to win a majority, we may not know until the next day, or even for several weeks, which party will control the Senate. What about the House? Democrats only need a net gain of three seats to flip control of the House, and they’re heavily favored to succeed. But the size of that majority depends on how much voters shift their support toward the Democrats and away from Republicans. A recent NBC News Decision Desk analysis shows evidence that this nationwide shift could be big enough to produce a historically large majority for the Democrats — or it could be sufficiently small that either party could end up with a razor-thin majority. (The House is made up of 435 seats, all up for re-election every two years, and 218 seats are needed for control.) The size of that majority for either party matters significantly to our ability to project control of the chamber. The smaller the final size of the majority, the longer it will take for the Decision Desk to be certain of who will control the House. If current polls are overestimating Democratic support and the size of the House majority for either party is small, the 2022 and 2024 elections provide some idea of timing. During the 2022 midterms, it took the NBC News Decision Desk eight days after Election Day to project that Republicans would win a slim majority. This call came as the Decision Desk projected the Republicans would win California’s 27th District, their 218th win. The ultimate size of their majority was nine seats. In the 2024 election, the Republicans won an even smaller majority — just five seats. This election also took until the second Wednesday after Election Day for the Decision Desk to project the 218th seat for the Republicans. If the size of the Democrats’ or Republicans’ majority this year is a single-digit number of seats, we expect it to take days or weeks for either party to reach 218 seats. Just like the Senate elections, the House elections in Maine and Alaska use ranked choice voting to determine a winner. If control of the House hinges on Maine’s 2nd District or Alaska’s lone district, we may have to wait until ranked choice tabulation occurs 10 to 15 days after Election Day. On the other hand, if current polls end up being close to accurate, Democrats would be poised to win at least 230 seats, according to the recent Decision Desk analysis. This could speed up when we know control. Throughout the night, the NBC News Decision Desk uses a statistical model to estimate the total number of seats that the Democrats and Republicans will end up winning. It is possible that NBC News will report this estimate on election night. The House model relies on past and current vote counts; it does not use any polling, including exit polls, in its estimation. Early House indicators with clues for timing Elections in states with early polling close times or that count their ballots quickly can also provide an indication of where things may end up. Kentucky’s 6th District, which Trump won in 2024 by 15 points, is a good example of an early bellwether district. The Republican-held district has its polls close at 6 p.m. ET, and in 2024 it reported nearly 90% of its votes by 8:40 p.m. While the Democrats do not need their candidate, Zach Dembo, to win this district to earn a majority, a low-single-digit win by the Republican candidate, Ralph Alvarado, is a favorable signal for the Democrats’ chances of winning the House. If Dembo were to win this district, it would likely foretell a Democratic tsunami, as there are 267 districts nationwide where Trump performed more poorly on his way to the White House. And if Alvarado were to win by a margin close to or in the double digits, it may suggest that neither party will end up with a large majority. Florida, which tends to report its votes quickly, also has several congressional districts worth paying attention to early in the night. One of these is Florida’s 25th, where Democrat Jared Moskowitz seeks re-election in a district that Florida Republicans redrew to favor Trump by 9 points. If Moskowitz loses to Republican Scott Singer, it would be a major victory for Republicans and may foreshadow the party holding on to House control. If Moskowitz wins comfortably, it may signal a large Democratic wave. Florida’s 14th District and Florida’s 22nd District are also Democratic-held toss-ups that Republicans redrew to be districts Trump would have won by 10.5 points. Given how quickly Florida counts its ballots, these two districts may be the first toss-ups NBC News can project. If one party were to win both of these districts early in the night, that party could very well end up with the majority.
news.summary: In 2024, Donald Trump’s election night wins in the presidential battlegrounds of Georgia, North Carolina, Texas and Florida meant that most Americans went to bed on Tuesday with a good idea of the result of the election — and woke up to the networks having called enough states to declare Trump the president-elect.
news.author: John Lapinski,Marc Trussler,Stephen Pettigrew

news.title: Abdul El-Sayed, Mike Rogers Face Off in High-Stakes Michigan Senate Race
news.text: Washington: Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers are testing two sharply different theories for winning one of the nation’s premier swing states Tuesday in a white-knuckle contest that may determine control of the Senate. El-Sayed is aiming to prove that an unapologetically progressive agenda centered on universal healthcare can win a general election in a state President Donald Trump carried two years ago. The former Wayne County health director narrowly defeated establishment-backed Rep. Haley Stevens in an expensive and bruising Democratic primary. Michigan’s diverse electorate has created a complicated political battleground, with both nominees seeking statewide support while navigating divisions among the state’s large Jewish, Muslim and Black communities. Bitter disputes over U.S. support for Israel and accusations of antisemitism overshadowed the race, culminating in Stevens' shocking endorsement of Rogers in the final days of the race. For Rogers, the race is a second chance after he lost Michigan’s 2024 Senate election by fewer than 20,000 votes. This time, the former congressman must win without Trump as a galvanizing force at the top of the ballot and as high gas prices and other costs have weighed on Republicans nationally. El-Sayed has sought to expand Michigan’s Democratic coalition with a populist message, hoping to drive up youth turnout after months of campus rallies, while winning over disillusioned Republicans in rural areas. No Republican has won a Senate race in the state since 1994, but the retirement of two-term Democratic Sen. Gary Peters created a rare opening. The race has become a focal point in the national fight for Senate control, drawing well over $100 million in advertising since the Aug. 4 primary. Democrats need to pick up four seats to win the majority, and losing any could put that out of reach. The campaign has also featured some of the year’s most inflammatory rhetoric . Republicans repeatedly have sought to link El-Sayed, who would be the first Muslim senator, to terrorist organizations, despite no evidence of such ties. Trump repeatedly called him a “jihadist.” The nation's most contentious Democratic primary left scars While Stevens' endorsement of Rogers stunned Democrats, it reflected tensions that had simmered since the primary for Stevens and some of her supporters. A four-term representative of parts of metro Detroit, she received significant support in the August contest from Black and Jewish communities in those areas. El-Sayed had to work in the postprimary sprint to win over those voters. In September, Kamala Harris, the first Black vice president, campaigned with El-Sayed and told a gathering of the NAACP that he could be a “stopgap” on Trump. Barack Obama, the nation’s first Black president, joined a rally for El-Sayed and other Democrats in Michigan days before Election Day. He has also been criticized by some in the Jewish community, and Stevens said her defection came after he didn't do enough to address the community's concerns. El-Sayed has been a vocal critic of Israel and was criticized for his response to a March attack on a Michigan synagogue, when he said that “hurt people hurt people.” The attacker had lost family in an Israeli strike in Lebanon. El-Sayed later said that he was “sorry” to “anyone who feels like my comments might have been hurtful.” Republicans have highlighted El-Sayed's ties to Hasan Piker, a popular political streamer who has made inflammatory comments about Israel, Jews and the Sept. 11 attacks. El-Sayed appeared with Piker multiple times during the primary but has since distanced himself from him . El-Sayed faced nearly $60 million in spending from outside groups during the August primary against Stevens. The American Israel Public Affairs Committee, or AIPAC , spent nearly $30 million, its largest investment in a single race. Rogers lost with Trump on the ballot. Can he win without him? Republicans opted to nominate Rogers again after his razor-thin 2024 loss, when then-Rep. Elissa Slotkin prevailed even as Trump won Michigan by more than a percentage point. Once a CNN contributor who criticized Trump, Rogers has aligned himself more closely with the president in recent years. Unlike two years ago, Rogers faced no viable Republican primary challenge this cycle, allowing him to spend months raising money and preparing for the general election while Democrats battled through their costly and divisive primary. But the political environment has presented fresh challenges. The war with Iran continues as everyday costs, particularly at the gas pump, remain high. Trump has also waged a trade war with...

news.title: From Texas To Pennsylvania: 5 House Battles That Could Reshape the US Congress
news.text: Democrats are seeking to overturn the Republicans' narrow majority in the US House of Representatives as voters head to the polls for the 2026 midterm elections, with five closely watched congressional contests expected to offer early indications of the battle for control of the chamber. All 435 House seats are up for election. Republicans currently hold 218 seats against 214 for Democrats, with one independent and two vacancies, leaving the opposition party needing only a small number of gains to secure a majority. The five races highlighted by Newsweek are in Kentucky, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Texas and Virginia. They are being closely monitored because their results could offer clues about the extent of Democratic support across districts previously won by President Donald Trump. Kentucky's 6th Congressional District One of the first contests to attract attention is Kentucky's 6th District, centred on Lexington and its suburbs. Republican Ralph Alvarado is facing Democrat Zach Dembo in the race to succeed Republican Representative Andy Barr, who is running for the Senate. Trump carried the district by 15 percentage points in 2024. The Cook Political Report classifies the contest as a toss-up. A strong Democratic performance could provide an early indication of how competitive other Republican-held districts may become. North Carolina's 1st Congressional District Republican-led redistricting has made the seat held by Democratic Representative Don Davis more conservative. Trump won the district by around 12 percentage points under the new boundaries, compared with approximately three points under the previous map. Davis is facing a challenging re-election contest, with the Cook Political Report rating the race a toss-up. The outcome will also offer an indication of whether Democrats can retain support in rural parts of the South despite the revised congressional boundaries. Pennsylvania's 1st Congressional District Republican Representative Brian Fitzpatrick is defending his seat against Democrat Bob Harvie. Fitzpatrick won re-election by nearly 13 percentage points in 2024, despite Kamala Harris narrowly carrying the district. The Cook Political Report moved the contest from Lean Republican to toss-up shortly before Election Day. A Democratic victory would indicate that even Republican incumbents with established electoral support are facing competitive challenges. Pennsylvania's 7th, 8th and 10th districts are also being watched closely. Texas' 15th Congressional District Republican Representative Monica De La Cruz is facing Democrat Bobby Pulido in a closely contested race in South Texas. Trump won the district by 18 percentage points in 2024, but Republicans are facing questions about whether their gains among Hispanic voters will hold in the midterms. The contest is being treated as a toss-up by the Cook Political Report. A shift in Hispanic voter support towards Democrats could also affect other competitive races in the region. Virginia's 1st Congressional District Republican Representative Rob Wittman is facing Democrat Shannon Taylor in Virginia's 1st District, which includes suburban areas outside Richmond. Trump carried the district by approximately five percentage points in 2024. Democrats are hoping to build on their support in suburban communities, while Wittman is seeking to retain a seat that has remained competitive. The Cook Political Report classifies the contest as a toss-up. Beyond these five races, Democrats are also targeting Republican-held seats in New Jersey, Iowa, Wisconsin, Nebraska, Arizona and Colorado. The Cook Political Report has identified 16 Republican-held districts where Democrats are favoured to win. The results in these contests will be important in determining whether Democrats can secure the gains needed to take control of the House and provide a congressional check on the Trump administration.
news.summary: As the 2026 midterm elections approach, Democrats aim to reclaim the House of Representatives from Republicans, who currently hold a slim majority.
news.author: Samannay Biswas

news.title: Voters will decide control of Congress in major test of Trump's second term
news.text:
Election Day is here. Voters nationwide will decide control of the U.S. House and Senate. Democrats must flip four seats in the Senate and three seats in the House to wrest control of the chambers from Republicans. Control of Congress would give Democrats a way to push back against President Donald Trump's agenda during the final two years of his term. The battle for control is playing out mostly in states and districts Trump previously won by wide margins.

All eyes are on Senate contests in Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio and Texas, while House battlegrounds are scattered across the country.

Democrats have homed in on Trump's poor approval rating, public dissatisfaction with the war in Iran and affordability concerns. Republicans have focused on social issues, while Trump has made himself the central character of the midterms.

The Latest:

The nation's longest Senate winning streak is at stake in Kansas

Sen. Roger Marshall is trying to fend off an unusually strong challenge from Democratic megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton in a race that's generated a Kansas record for spending on advertising.

A Democrat hasn't won a Senate race in the state in 94 years.

But Marshall is seeking a second term at a moment of deep frustration with Trump's handling of the economy, and Hamilton made affordability a key issue while positioning himself as a moderate who could work with Republican colleagues in Washington.

Hamilton is the founder and senior pastor of the Kansas City-area Church of the Resurrection. With 25,000 members, it's the nation's largest United Methodist congregation.

DeSantis urges Trump, Republicans not to 'gaslight' voters

In a Monday interview with commentator Stephen A. Smith, Republican Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said Trump originally promised not to start new wars in the Middle East, but is currently in an "open-ended" conflict in Iran, which has driven up fuel prices.

DeSantis said some Republicans have tried to blame former President Joe Biden for the higher prices, but he urged them to be honest.

"Gas is higher and it hurts people, working-class people," he said. "And it's higher because of this conflict. That's just a fact. If you can't admit that to voters, then you're gaslighting them and they're not going to listen to you on other things."

DeSantis unsuccessfully competed with Trump for the 2024 presidential nomination and could run again in 2028.

Sen. Susan Collins tries to keep her seat while fending off Troy Jackson

Collins is running for her sixth term on a pledge to continue serving Maine as one of the few remaining moderates in the Senate.

The Republican faces a challenge from Democrat Troy Jackson, who entered the race late. Jackson has tried to paint Collins as too close to Trump, while Collins has touted her willingness to break from the rest of the Republican Party on key votes.

Collins is the only Republican senator from New England, and she has triumphed in previous tough elections.

This time, Democrats focused on unseating her from the beginning, but the party's June primary winner, Graham Platner, withdrew from the race after facing sexual assault allegations that he denied.

Jackson became the new nominee after winning a special nominating convention in late July.

Justice Department dispatches 1,000 election monitors to the polls

The Justice Department announced early Tuesday that it is sending roughly 1,000 federal election monitors to all 50 states to observe Election Day voting.

Many are expected in populated areas that tend to vote for Democrats. They include past hot spots for election tensions, like Detroit, Philadelphia and Georgia's Fulton County.

The monitoring program isn't new, but it has faced criticism from voting rights groups concerned about federal interference and voter intimidation.

The NAACP sued after the department said it would include law enforcement officers in the program, but a judge ruled against the group overnight, arguing the government had made it clear that monitors would be in plainclothes, would not carry firearms and wouldn't have the power to make arrests at poll sites.

The Justice Department has said its monitors will observe and will not interfere with voting.

House races playing out deep in Trump country

Republicans are mostly on defense in the battle for control of the U.S. House.

Most of the top battlegrounds are districts Trump won in 2024, sometimes by a lot.

Republicans and allied groups pulled spending from several House races in October, shifting, for example, away from GOP incumbents in Iowa and New Jersey.

At Trump's urging, Republicans in states including Texas and Florida tried to give themselves a boost with early redistricting, but that may turn out to be a flop.

Democrats are defending a handful of seats in Trump country as well, and there are pockets of potential GOP upside around the country.

The AP has a detailed rundown of the House districts in play and the fight for the House majority.

Senate control up for grabs in states Trump carried

Control of the Senate hangs in the balance in a way few could have foreseen.

Originally, Democrats believed they only had a narrow path to the majority, and their plan required flipping seats in Alaska, Ohio, Maine and North Carolina.

However, the map has shifted, and Democrats believe they have a shot at Texas, Kansas and Iowa as well.

Many of these are states Trump won by double-digit margins two years ago.

Democrats need to play defense as well. Although they're expected to hold Georgia, they also need to lock down Michigan and Minnesota.

In Maine, a voter feels 'the weight of the world'

In Falmouth, Maine, 60-year-old Susan Myers said she's optimistic that Senate candidate Troy Jackson can take advantage of anti-Trump sentiment and defeat longtime Republican Sen. Susan Collins. She's also aware of how recent elections have gone for diehard Democrats like herself.

"I'm hopeful. I feel like there's been so much disappointment these last few election cycles that I don't want to get my hopes up," she said.

Myers voted early at Falmouth Town Hall and was picking up an absentee ballot for her daughter.

She said so much national attention on Maine this election has been overwhelming. The Senate race is one of this year's most competitive and could decide which party controls the chamber.

"It feels a little bit like we have the weight of the world on our shoulders," Myers said.

Latinos form a crucial bloc of swing voters

Latinos helped return Trump to the White House in 2024. Now they're poised to play an outsized role in the midterms.

The path to a U.S. House majority runs through heavily Latino districts in states such as Arizona, California, Colorado, Florida and Texas. The front-line Senate race in Texas likewise could hinge on Latinos.

About 6 in 10 Hispanic adults disapprove of Trump's handling of the presidency, according to an Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll from October. About 7 in 10 disapprove of his performance on the economy.

One key factor will be how effective Democrats have been at making the case for themselves. Will disaffected Trump supporters vote for Democrats, or just sit out the midterms?

In Michigan's Senate race, history and control of the chamber are on the line

Democrat Abdul El-Sayed is seeking to become the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate. Republican Mike Rogers wants to be the first member of his party to win a Michigan Senate race in more than three decades.

The contest to replace retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters is among a handful that could determine which party controls the Senate.

Although Michigan Democrats have been successful in recent midterm elections, Trump carried the battleground state in two of his three campaigns. That divided political landscape helped set the stage for one of the most bitter and contentious Senate races of the cycle.

El-Sayed has accused Rogers of being a "puppet" for Trump. Rogers has accused El-Sayed of having ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, while Trump has falsely called the Democrat a "jihadist."

Progressives are hoping an El-Sayed victory will signal their agenda can resonate in a battleground state ahead of the next presidential election.

Millions of Americans will be voting in new congressional districts

Mid-decade redistricting shook up the House map ahead of the midterms, changing the boundaries of around one-third of congressional districts.

The AP analyzed each district's 2024 presidential vote margin before and after redistricting and found that while many individual districts saw dramatic shifts in partisanship and demographic makeup, the national U.S. House map did not shift significantly toward either party.

Learn more about how redistricting shaped the 2026 midterm elections and see how your district boundaries changed in this map.

Midterm results will chart the course of Trump's final two years

Trump is staring down twin threats from Capitol Hill for his last two years as president if his party loses at least one chamber in Tuesday's midterms: investigations and impeachment.

Democratic lawmakers are eager to exercise oversight, with senior officials long telegraphing how they would go after an administration they believe has escaped accountability for policies, personal profits and abuses of power.

The majority party controls gavels on powerful House committees, which come with larger staff budgets and more expansive resources, including subpoena powers.

Less certain are prospects for impeaching Trump, although House Democratic leaders will almost certainly come under pressure from their left flank to do so. Rather than Trump, who was impeached twice during his first term but acquitted by the Senate both times, Democrats may instead try to impeach Cabinet officials.

If Republicans lose the Senate, Trump's ability to push his judicial and executive branch nominees through to confirmation will also be severely weakened.

Races for Senate, governor in Iowa are open for the first time since 1968

Iowa's top of the ticket is up for grabs after Republican Gov. Kim Reynolds and Sen. Joni Ernst opted out of reelection bids.

Republicans control state government and comprise the entirety of Iowa's federal delegation. But the openings have given Democrats opportunities to win over voters who may want a new direction amid high grocery and gas prices, manufacturing job losses, a crippled agricultural economy and growing cancer rates.

In the governor's race, Rob Sand, the state auditor and only Democrat in statewide elected office, faces Republican Zach Lahn, a political newcomer who stunned even members of his own party when he won the primary over a Trump-endorsed congressman.

Democrat Josh Turek and Republican Ashley Hinson are competing for a U.S. Senate seat. Hinson, a congresswoman endorsed by Trump, has tried to assure voters she will push back when his policies are wrong for Iowa. Turek, a state lawmaker, was endorsed by Barack Obama, the last Democrat seeking federal office to win Iowa before Trump won the last three presidential elections.

Judge blocks Trump administration from sending lists of alleged noncitizen voters

A federal judge has ruled that the Trump administration must stop sending voter lists of alleged noncitizens to election officials, as it has done in California and Washington state, while urging the states to set aside those ballots.

U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan in Washington, D.C., said in her decision late Monday that more voter data transmissions would likely confuse voters and election officials at a time when election resources need to be focused on administering the midterms.

States and voting rights groups have pushed back on the administration's claims and said the lists are riddled with errors.

The decision is one in a string of court losses for the administration in its efforts to expand federal authority over elections, which are run by the states.

Southwest flooding forces the Navajo Nation to change some Election Day voting plans

The Navajo Election Administration says it has altered five polling locations — two in Arizona and three in New Mexico.

The tribe's reservation surrounds the Four Corners Monument, where Arizona, New Mexico, Utah and Colorado meet. The area has seen major flooding since October, with rivers overflowing their banks and some residents having to evacuate.

The tribe says it has more than 298,000 members.

GOP loses immigration advantage

Trump roared back to power due to the Biden administration's border troubles. He cut illegal crossings of the border, which were already plummeting, to close to zero.

That's when the trouble started.

The president turned to the trickier task of deporting people in the U.S. illegally from the interior. Soon the main image of illegal immigration wasn't desperate people crossing the border, but mothers screaming as they were torn from their children, or masked federal agents chasing people — sometimes citizens — through streets.

Trump openly bemoaned how the U.S. didn't get enough migrants from Scandinavian countries and only accepted white South Africans into the country as refugees. And then two citizen protesters were shot and killed by immigration agents during the administration's raids on Minneapolis.

Now the GOP fears it will especially lose ground in immigrant-rich areas running from New Jersey to Florida to Texas. And polls show more voters oppose Trump on immigration than support him.

Democrats are hopeful — but not optimistic — in South Carolina

Lindsey Graham's sudden death left South Carolina Republicans scrambling to pick a new nominee in a special primary, which his sister, Darline Graham, ultimately won.

The switch-up left the state's Democrats with renewed hope they could break a 20-year drought on winning a statewide race.

But even some of Democratic nominee Annie Andrews' supporters acknowledge their state might not yet be ready to go blue, despite Democrats' advances in neighboring North Carolina and Georgia.

South Carolina has consistently backed Trump, who endorsed Graham, urged her to run and has stumped twice for her in the state.

Graham and Andrews have portrayed each other as ill-prepared for the role.

Latest views on Trump from AP-NORC polling

Trump might not be on the ballot, but Americans are very unhappy with his performance so far in his second term.

Only about one-third of U.S. adults, 35%, approve of how Trump is handling the presidency, according to AP-NORC polling from October.

Trump's approval tends to stay within a fairly narrow range, but the most recent measure is below where his overall approval stood shortly after he started his second term, when 42% of U.S. adults approved of how he was handling the presidency.

He's seen modest declines in approval among Republicans and independents. About 70% of Republicans approve of how Trump is handling the presidency, down from 82% at the start of his term.

Trump's current approval rating is slightly below where it stood in October 2018.

Voters are frustrated by inflation and appear ready to penalize Republicans

Over the past two elections, voters turned out against Democrats because of high inflation.

But Trump's promise to bring down prices has failed. Inflation is running at 3.7% annually, up from 3% when the president's second term started.

Trump's tariffs pushed up inflation last year, and his decision to start a war with Iran has caused higher oil, gasoline and diesel prices.

As a result, consumer sentiment is lower than it has been during recent recessions. And the unemployment rate is still a healthy 4.2%.

The voter anger over inflation makes it harder for Republicans who campaigned on low prices to defend their House and Senate majorities.

The Georgia governor's race pits a billionaire against a potentially historic figure

Republican nominee Rick Jackson is a billionaire businessman making his first bid for public office.

Democratic nominee Keisha Lance Bottoms is the former Atlanta mayor and would be Georgia's first Black governor. Nationally, no Black woman has been elected governor of any state.

The winner will succeed Republican Brian Kemp, a two-term governor who by law could not run again. Republicans have won every Georgia governor's election since 2002.

Jackson initially pledged to govern "like Trump, but with a Southern tone." He's since loosened that embrace and emphasized his personal biography as a former foster care teenager who became a healthcare magnate.

He's said his childhood struggles make him ideal to represent 11 million Georgians. And he's spent nearly $200 million of his own money trying to prove it.

Bottoms disputes Jackson's self-made everyman narrative, saying he's trying to buy the office to be a Trump lackey.

Polls have opened on the East Coast

In-person Election Day voting has begun. Polls are open in a handful of East Coast states, including Connecticut, Maine, New York, New Jersey, and parts of Kentucky and Indiana.

At 6:30 a.m. ET, polls in Ohio, North Carolina and West Virginia will open. Polls in 14 more states will open at 7 a.m. Polls will be open in every state, plus Washington, D.C., by noon ET.

Trump's economic approval has taken a hit with Republicans

Americans are broadly frustrated with Trump over the economy and other pocketbook issues, according to AP-NORC polling.

About one-quarter of U.S. adults approve of how Trump is handling the economy, down from about 4 in 10 in the months after he started his second term. The decline is particularly notable among Republicans, only about half of whom approve of Trump's economic approach right now. That's down from 78% in March 2025.

Trump has similarly low ratings on his handling of the cost of living. Only about 2 in 10 U.S. adults approve of him on this issue, while about 8 in 10 disapprove. That includes roughly 6 in 10 Republicans who disapprove of Trump on costs.

The poll showed about 8 in 10 voters say the economy or the cost of living are among their top issues for the election.

Democrat Roy Cooper looks to flip a Republican-held Senate seat in North Carolina

Cooper, a former governor, was hailed from the start as Democrats' top Senate recruit.

Republicans countered with Michael Whatley, Trump's handpicked Republican Party chair whom the president urged to run for the seat.

The winner will succeed Republican Sen. Thom Tillis, who announced his retirement and became an outspoken Trump critic.

The race became a testing ground for the two parties' fight over how to frame the economy and Republicans' sweeping tax-and-budget law that Trump called the "one big, beautiful bill."

Cooper avoided personal criticisms of Trump but hammered Whatley and Republicans on inflation. Whatley cheered GOP tax cuts on tips, overtime and Social Security.

Republicans have dominated Senate elections in North Carolina for the last half-century. But Cooper has never lost an election, starting as a state senator before winning four terms as attorney general and two terms as governor.

A handful of House Republicans face headwinds in seats Harris carried in '24

Those congressmembers are trying to hold onto their seats in districts Democrat Kamala Harris carried in 2024.

There were just three such Republicans until redistricting complicated the picture: Don Bacon, who is retiring in Nebraska's 2nd District, and Mike Lawler in New York's 17th and Brian Fitzpatrick in Pennsylvania's 1st District — both of whom are running in contested races this year.

After redistricting battles touched off by Trump, who sought to pick up more seats for his party, the number of Republicans in Democrat-leaning seats climbed.

Four seats in California represented by Republicans became more favorable for Democrats. In one of them, Rep. Kevin Kiley said he was leaving the GOP and would serve as an independent.

And another seat currently represented by a Republican in Utah became Democratic leaning after legal wrangling following redistricting there.

Midterm elections coming to a close as voters pass judgment on Trump's second term

Voters struggling with high prices and angry over an unpopular war with Iran will decide whether to drastically shift power in Washington in midterm elections Tuesday that will serve as a referendum on President Donald Trump 's second term.

Democrats were cautiously optimistic about their prospects as they watched Republicans spend the campaign's final stretch pumping tens of millions of dollars into states and districts that Trump won handily just two years ago. They are betting that discontent over Trump's failure to deliver on his promise to tackle rising costs, and perceptions that he has been more focused on gilding the nation's capital than their pain at the pump, will depress Republican turnout and drive their own voters to the polls.

Republicans held out hope that their overwhelming money advantage would help stem the tide, but they were bracing to lose control of the U.S. House and fighting to hang onto the U.S. Senate — an outcome that seemed unlikely earlier this year, given a map widely seen as favoring the party.

Still, the margins are tight in both chambers and just one or two seats could tip the balance. Democrats need a net gain of four seats in the Senate to win the majority, an uphill climb because many of the most competitive races are in historically red states. In the House, they only need three.
news.summary:
Election Day is here. Voters nationwide will decide control of the U.S. House and Senate. Democrats must flip four seats in the Senate and three seats in the House to wrest control of the chambers from Republicans. Control of Congress would give Democrats a way to push back against President Donald Trump's agenda during the final two years of his term. The battle for control is playing out mostly in states and districts Trump previously won by wide margins.



     All eyes are on Senate contests in Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio and Texas, while House battlegrounds are scattered across the country.

news.title: How Florida Governor Ron DeSantis will shape his state’s 2026 midterm race  - St. Lucia Chronicle – Daily St
news.text:
Few modern governors have left as deep a mark on Florida’s character as Republican Ron DeSantis.

Across his two terms, the 48-year-old politician has overhauled the state’s political landscape, turning what was once a swing state into a Republican stronghold.

The Florida governor has also established himself as a key national figure in United States politics. During the 2024 presidential race, he was considered one of the chief Republican challengers to President Donald Trump.

DeSantis leaves office in January: Due to term limits, he cannot run in a third election for governor.

But experts say his legacy as a hardline Republican will define the race to succeed him in Tuesday’s midterm elections.

US Representative Byron Donalds is campaigning to defend the Republicans’ hold on the governor’s mansion in Florida, but he faces stiffer-than-expected competition from former Congress member David Jolly, a centrist Democrat.

“Was [DeSantis’s position] going to alienate some voters? It definitely has. We’ll find out tomorrow if it’s enough to make a change,” Aubrey Jewett, a political science professor at the University of Central Florida, told Al Jazeera.

Dark horse turned dominant force

A decade ago, DeSantis was hardly the household name he is today in the US.

A former naval officer who served three terms in the US House of Representatives, the Republican was by no means a shoo-in for the governor’s chair when he first ran for office in 2018.

The race was tight. Even with Trump’s endorsement, DeSantis only scraped past his Democratic rival, Andrew Gillum, by less than half a percentage point.

At the time, Florida was a quintessential “purple” state, capable of leaning towards either Republican or Democrat.

Under DeSantis’s leadership, however, the state took a rightward turn. The last Democrat to win statewide office in Florida was Nikki Fried, the former agricultural commissioner – and her victory came eight years ago.

Ever since, Democrats in Florida have endured a dry spell, while the Republican margin of victory has grown.

In 2022, for instance, DeSantis overwhelmingly won re-election by 19 points, the largest gap since 1982. He also became the first Republican gubernatorial candidate in 20 years to win the Democratic stronghold of Miami-Dade County.

By Trump’s re-election in 2024, Florida’s reputation as a reliably red bastion was undeniable.

Trump notched a decisive victory with 13.1 percentage points over former Vice President Kamala Harris in Florida’s presidential vote that year, a far cry from his wafer-thin 1.2-point advantage during the 2016 election.

According to Florida’s Division of Elections, Republicans currently hold an advantage of 1.5 million registered voters over the state’s Democrats.

That is a dramatic reversal from 2020, when Democrats held a registration advantage of at least 100,000 voters.

Many experts credit DeSantis with spearheading this registration surge. Republicans have been attracted to the state by DeSantis’s platform of low taxes and light regulations, as well as his rejection of pandemic-era restrictions.

Trump himself made the Mar-a-Lago resort in Palm Beach, Florida, his permanent residence in 2019, in a move widely speculated to take advantage of Florida’s favourable tax regime.

A model for the right

Though Trump and DeSantis were briefly rivals during the 2024 Republican primaries, Jewett said the Florida governor has helped shape the meaning of “Trumpism”, the president’s political movement.

DeSantis himself has held up Florida as a “blueprint for America’s revival”.

Under his leadership, Florida has participated in Trump’s immigration crackdown and sought to purge public universities of diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) initiatives.

In April 2022, for instance, he signed into law the Stop Woke Act, which limited how race and gender were taught in public schools by barring instruction that portrayed any group as “inherently racist”.

Part of the law was later struck down after advocates argued that it constituted censorship in violation of the First Amendment of the Constitution.

Other DeSantis-era laws, like 2022’s Parental Rights in Education Act, curbed classroom instruction on sexual orientation and gender identity.

“Those things have been cemented in Florida’s K-12 system,” Jewett explained. “There’s not a lot that the school boards could do, given that the governor has removed several people for policy disagreements.”

Those laws, however, had wide-reaching impact across the US.

States like Arkansas, Indiana, Kentucky and Iowa subsequently pursued laws curtailing how public schools addressed sexuality, gender identity and race in the classroom.

Florida’s future after DeSantis

As Floridians head to the polls to choose DeSantis’s successor, Jewett said DeSantis will cast a long shadow over state and national politics for years to come.

“Whether anyone agrees or disagrees with [DeSantis], from a neutral political science perspective, the man has had a huge impact in Florida and across the nation,” he said.

Donalds, the Republican, has pledged to continue DeSantis-style politics, calling the outgoing leader “best governor in the country”. While in the US Congress, Donalds even sponsored legislation to limit how gender and race are taught, echoing DeSantis’s own legislative platform.

His challenger Jolly, a Republican-turned-Democrat, is pitching himself as an alternative to “partisan politics”, with affordability and healthcare at the heart of his campaign.

Jewett expects Donalds to preserve much of DeSantis’s right-wing agenda, though not necessarily replicate his approach to all subjects, including Black history.

The DeSantis administration has previously been accused of attempting to sanitise the teaching of slavery by rejecting an Advanced Placement course on African American history.

“Maybe on the racial issue […], you might see a little bit of softening there,” Jewett said of Donalds.

He cautioned, however, that Donalds was likely “not going to turn into a progressive on those issues either”.

DeSantis, meanwhile, is unlikely to disappear from national politics.

“I don’t think we’ve seen the last of him,” Jewett said. He predicts DeSantis will “certainly try to run for president again” in 2028.

news.title: David Kaufman: A far-left Democratic win today will prime Americans to vote for a Republican in 2028
news.text:
As much as they would love to retain the House and Senate this week, a massive Democratic win in today’s midterms could be the best thing that ever happens to the Republicans. At least when it comes to the race for the White House in 2028. 

And ultimately, isn’t this what the Midterms are really all about? 

Conventional wisdom has it that the 2028 Republican presidential nominee will either be Vice-President JD Vance or Secretary of State Marco Rubio. The two have been battling quietly between themselves for months to see who will carry on the MAGA flame — eager to attain alpha-status while avoiding the crosshairs of their boss, Donald Trump. But the most consequential player in this war will be their eventual Democratic challenger — if not the post-term Democratic party itself.

But who will emerge as that 2028 rival? That is ultimately the highest-stakes outcome of the Midterms. Should the Democrats triumph today — winning history-making contests in Michigan, Florida, Maine and Texas — their extremist tilt will almost certainly shift into hyperdrive. That means mere moderates like California Governor Gavin Newsom, his Pennsylvania counterpart Josh Shapiro and even former VP and twice failed presidential candidate Kamala Harris could easily be deemed too centrist to retain the support of their now left-lurching party. 

The weekend denunciation of Michigan Rep. Haley Stevens for refusing to endorse her former rival Abdul el-Sayed for Senate demonstrates how tiny the Democrats “big-tent” has become. 

So that leaves Alexandia Ocasio-Cortez (AOC), the 37 year Queens congresswoman who could either run for the U.S. Senate or aim for the White House. AOC clearly understands this is her make-or-break moment, noting back in September: “It’s very all or nothing… If I were to run in this cycle and not win, I would be done.” 

Already her potential Republican opponents view a win by the controversial Egyptian-American el-Sayed — along with his equally improbable candidate cohort — today as ensuring an AOC run for the White House. “We’re a divided country,” As Republican Texas Sen. Ted Cruz of the Congresswoman over the weekend. “Look, if she is the nominee, she could win.”

He may be overstating things. 

While there is little doubt AOC could secure her party’s nomination, securing the approval of that divided nation will be an entirely different endeavor. And the elements that make her so appealing to the Democrats — such as her Socialist leanings and far-left ideals — could easily turn off Middle America. 

Just look at el-Sayed for a clue of what AOC’s eventual Republican rival could throw at her down the line. Over the weekend in an appearance on the 60 Minutes news program, el-Sayed suggested he has little problem with biological men changing in female dressing rooms in front of young girls because they will eventually see nude men on social media platforms. 

The Stevens defection managed to drown out much of the scrutiny over el-Sayed’s illogic. But this is just one outlandish notion from one far-left Democrat their eventual presidential nominee will need to manage. And there are just so, so many of them — far-left Democrats and their seemingly endless number of outlandish notions. 

Beyond their extremist views are the actual voter numbers required to get a presidential nominee elected. While there is little doubt the Democratic Socialists have been masterful in getting their candidates across the finish line, their actual voter numbers are woefully meager. How meager? Just look at Darializa Avila Chevalier, the Democratic Socialists of America candidate who won the Democratic primary in June for New York’s 13th District, which includes Upper Manhattan and the South Bronx. 

The sprawling area is home to 750,000 residents, roughly the population of my hometown San Francisco. Barely 35,000 people living in District 13 bothered to vote in the primary leading Chevalier to a win by just 2,000 votes. AOC isn’t performing much better. During her August reelection run, she received just over 31,000 votes — which means that 97 per cent of her constituents did not cast a ballot for her. 

America is a nation with notoriously low voter turnout and smaller-scale elections in non-presidential years always underperform. But these minuscule numbers lay clear just how niche the DSA is when it comes to actual ballots cast. Further, working against the party is their candidates’ relative youth and lack of broad recognition. 

Even a relative party veteran like AOC has only been in politics for barely a decade — compare that to a potential Republican rival like Rubio who’s been part of the government machine since AOC was a child (and showed the world what actual foreign policy chops look like at the Munich Security Conference earlier this year, where AOC could barely geo-locate Venezuela). 

This is why an emboldened DSA faction fronted by the likes of AOC — who sent $1 million to help shore up the el-Sayed campaign last month — could keep the Republicans in the White House for four more years. Though, as Cruz suggested a few days back, there are no guarantees — especially if Vice-President Vance ultimately triumphs over Rubio to be anointed Trump’s successor.

Such a scenario would prove a weaker foil to an emboldened DSA-powered Democrat. Rubio vs. AOC pits two Latinos against each other in an election cycle where the Hispanic vote — leery of the White House’s immigration overreach — has never been more consequential. As Latino support for Trump plummets, Vance, despite his multi-ethnic family, offers far less appeal to minority voters. 

As America prepares to vote in what Politico has described as “the Armageddon of all elections,” the future for both the Democrats and Republicans has never been less clear — and primed for upheaval. Ultimately, the Democrats need a clear sweep tonight in order to reestablish themselves as serious change-makers going into 2028. The Republicans, however, need merely to not crash and burn in order to remain viable. 

Either way, both sides understand an old order is now fading — and no one is entirely sure what to make of its replacement.

David Christopher Kaufman is a New York-based journalist and former New York Post editor and columnist, and founder of The Octagon Project. Sign up for his Substack newsletter, Counterintuitive.

news.title: Why neither MAGA nor Democrats are particularly bothered about Indian-Americans
news.text: That minority groups are often used by progressives as a political football is evident to all, but no one summed it up as sharply as Malcolm X, who observed: “The white liberal differs from the white conservative only in one way: the liberal is more deceitful than the conservative. The liberal is more hypocritical than the conservative. Both want power, but the white liberal is the one who has perfected the art of posing as the Negro's friend and benefactor.”Today, the average Indian-American voter finds herself in a similar conundrum, except that, unlike the African-American voters of yore, neither liberals nor conservatives – with a few honourable exceptions – even care to pay lip service to earn a few brownie points.Consider how little noise the American political machine – on both sides of the aisle – made when a potential massacre was averted because a crazy 19-year-old's rifle jammed in the parking lot of a Hindu temple in suburban Chicago.As the midterms arrives, Indian-Americans find themselves in familiar territory: between a rock and a hard place, staring into the abyss of political irrelevance. Despite being one of the richest immigrant groups in the country, Indian-Americans may feel that America has rarely been more hostile towards them.On one side are MAGA’s open racists, who see Indian-American students enjoying a football game and imagine a great replacement in a strange iteration of the Tebbit Test, where even loyalty to one’s new land cannot overcome skin pigmentation.On the flip side are the Democrats, who, despite claiming to stand for minority rights, can’t even call Indians by their proper name, referring to them as “South Asians”, and are wont to platform people who are usually found at Dismantle Global Hindutva conferences.It’s a delicious twist of Shakespeare’s tongue that, after labelling Native Americans as “Indians”, so much of the American commentariat likes to call Indians “South Asians”. Unfortunately for us, when white folks make a faux pas, it lives on through history as the correct term.As Pushpita Prasad, an Indian-American community leader, pointed out to TOI Digital: “It’s frankly disrespectful to try and roll an India label into something else. India is a massive and historical label. Yet in 2020, Kamala Harris, the daughter of an Indian woman, gets called South Asian, while Jill Biden's Italian American heritage is respectfully used, even though her family immigrated in 1900.”Prasad also made a similar point about Diwali in a 2022 essay for the Coalition of Hindus of North America (CoHNA), co-authored with Smitha Raj, arguing that rebranding the Dharmic religious festival as a generic “South Asian” celebration amounted to cultural appropriation and erased its religious roots.New Jews to New ZionistsThe sobriquet "South Asian" vacillates wildly depending on the context.A dish invented in India becomes Pakistani or South Asian; grooming gangs, on the other hand, earn the South Asian label.Anti-India hatred in Texas is labelled rising hatred of South Asians, while caste is always an Indian problem, as is “Hindu nationalism”, which is always rising and is almost always blamed for every evil in the world when it cannot be explained by Zionism or white supremacy. Twenty-six years after Jagdish Bhagwati named Indian-Americans the “new Jews”, Hindus are now often labelled the “new Zionists”.In fact, the caste bogey has been so prevalent in American discourse that California Democrats tried to push through a specific caste-discrimination bill that was eventually buried by Governor Gavin Newsom – ostensibly after a quiet word from the White House – because common sense prevailed and grown-ups realised that California didn’t have a raging caste issue.The more under-reported irony of that particular kerfuffle was that the campaign was spearheaded by Equality Labs, whose caste-sensitivity material was examined in a 2024 NCRI-Rutgers study. The researchers found that exposure to the material actually increased prejudice rather than reducing it. Participants became more likely to perceive caste discrimination where none was established and to endorse dehumanising descriptions of Brahmins.That’s not to say Indian-Americans cannot move the needle. They can when it exists within the ambit of the culture-war sphere, like getting Apu banned in The Simpsons, but in general, Indian-Americans struggle to counter global Anglosphere narratives about India, and that tends to pass the burden of Indian politics onto the diaspora.Great Power, No VoiceAnd this predicament is rather curious because Indian-Americans have never had greater representation in the US establishment, but with greater power didn’t come a greater voice.We’ve come a long way from the Samosa Caucus.New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, an Indian-American, is one of the most well-known Democratic faces across the country, but while he might shake a leg to the title track of Dhoom, he is still averse to referring to himself as Indian-American and even repeats mendacities about his ancestral state.Kash Patel might say Jai Shree Krishna at his FBI confirmation hearing but seldom speaks about atrocities against his co-religionists. Then again, he has been busy jet-setting across the country with his country-singer fiancée or chugging beer with hockey players.Vivek Ramaswamy, who was co-head of DOGE – before his abrupt exit following an epic diatribe on American laziness – is hoping to become governor of Ohio. While he was vocal about being Hindu during the presidential election debates – albeit presenting his version of Hinduism as crypto-Catholicism – he has been quieter in the run-up to the Ohio governor race. After the temple attack in Chicago, Ramaswamy’s silence was louder than his campaign’s obnoxious video attacking his opponent, Amy Acton.Ro Khanna, Pramila Jayapal, Ami Bera and Suhas Subramanyam are seeking re-election to Congress. In California, Khanna faces fellow Indian-American Ritesh Tandon, while in Washington, Jayapal is being challenged by another Indian-American Republican, Nirav Sheth. Elsewhere, Amish Shah is contesting Arizona's 1st Congressional District, and Pooja Sethi is attempting to become the first Indian-American elected to the Texas Legislature.Yet, while Indian-Americans have become more prominent, none of the issues that affect the Indian community are particularly at the forefront. Racism against Indians is hardly worth discussing in American media outlets, and when it is, it is bundled together as discrimination against South Asians, which is often mentioned alongside Islamophobia.While there are numerous groups that now speak exclusively for the problems faced by Hindu-Americans, some of them, as Voltaire showed with the Holy Roman Empire, barely make a peep for actual Hindu issues – like the atrocities faced by minority Hindus in Bangladesh – but are more willing to hold forth on the Middle East.While MAGA, as Malcolm X famously described white conservatives’ reaction to black people, is fairly open about its animus towards Indians, claiming without proof that they participate in nepotism or H-1B fraud, the other side of the aisle is filled with people who often paint Indian-Americans as oppressors at the top of the caste hierarchy.While MAGA goes bonkers about a Hanuman statue on private land in Texas, its liberal opponents use the BAPS case in France to claim parochialism and misogyny among Hindu groups, even though a probe confirmed that the group had never explicitly asked for women to be removed from the Eiffel Tower.Neither of these issues directly affects the midterm results, but they show how easy it is to make Hindus or Indian-Americans pantomime villains.For a long time, Indian-Americans have been held up as a “model minority”, and perhaps that’s because they were never particularly bothered about political power, thinking that their status and money could protect them from the racism aimed at other minority groups. Or perhaps it was for that reason that Indian-Americans now find themselves at a crossroad. The numbers suggest Indian-Americans aren’t confused about whom they are going to vote for, even if they remain less certain about whom to identify with.Dem Vote, No Dem LoveAccording to the Carnegie Endowment's Indian American Attitudes Survey, released on November 2, 62% of Indian-American citizens intend to vote for Democratic candidates in the House elections, compared with just 19% for Republicans. Another 12% remain undecided. In Senate contests, the Democrats enjoy a similarly commanding lead of 63% to 21%.That's a 43-percentage-point Democratic advantage in House voting intentions, a rather remarkable figure considering the gains Trump appeared to make among Indian-Americans in 2024, when 30% supported him against 62% for Kamala Harris.But look beyond the surface and the numbers get more interesting.Despite the overwhelming preference for Democratic candidates, only 46% of Indian-American adults identify as Democrats, compared with 19% who identify as Republicans and 26% as independents. And those numbers have barely changed since January 2026.The most revealing finding, however, is that 35% of Indian-Americans intending to vote Democratic say they are doing so primarily because they oppose the Republican candidate or party, rather than because they support the Democrats. Among intending Republican voters, just 17% cite opposition to the Democrats as their principal motivation.So, while MAGA appears to have succeeded in alienating Indian-Americans as it has most other groups who flipped in 2024, it hasn't necessarily made them fall in love with the Democrats. A substantial section of the community is voting against the Republicans rather than enthusiastically embracing the alternative.The Democrats can count on their votes, but whether they can count on their affection is an entirely different matter. And perhaps the most peculiar aspect of this entire debate is how little the priorities of ordinary Indian-Americans resemble the ideological arguments conducted on their behalf.Carnegie's earlier 2026 survey found that inflation and prices were the biggest concern for 21% of respondents, followed by jobs and the economy at 17%, healthcare at 13% and immigration at 11%. Just 2% named US-India relations as their most important political issue.For all the American commentariat's fascination with caste, Hindu nationalism and the geopolitical implications of Indian identity, the average Indian-American appears rather more interested in the cost of living, employment and healthcare.Which raises an uncomfortable question for both parties.If a community can produce some of the richest people in America, occupy positions at the highest levels of government, finance political campaigns and remain one of the Democrats' most reliable voting constituencies, why does it still struggle to have its particular concerns heard?Perhaps that is the real political predicament facing Indian-Americans as they head to the polls. They may have acquired enough influence to help decide who governs America, but they still appear to be struggling to influence how America understands them. They know whom they intend to vote against. Who will speak for them after the votes are counted remains a rather more complicated question.About 133 years ago, a man born Narendranath Dutta said he was from India (rather than a princely state or presidency, as was the norm then) and preached tolerance at the World’s Parliament of Religions in a speech that evokes awe even today. It’s sad that, so many years later, Americans of all stripes have become particularly intolerant towards his descendants.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
news.summary: About 133 years ago, a man born Narendranath said he was from India and preached tolerance at the World’s Parliament of Religions in a speech that evokes awe even today. It’s sad that, so many years later, Americans of all stripes have become particularly intolerant towards his descendants.

news.title: 5 things you need to know about 2026 US midterm elections
news.text: Millions of Americans have already voted in early ballots while millions more headed for polling stations on Tuesday as the U.S. elects members of the House of Representatives, Senate and governors in states across the country.Held in the middle of each four-year presidential term, the midterms by definition do not involve the president, however, for anyone who thinks they lack drama ⁠or importance this year, consider these two statistics: More than 57 million people had already ⁠cast their ballots as of Monday, according to the University of Florida Election Lab, well above the 46 million who voted early in the 2022 midterm elections. This election is on track to be the most expensive in U.S. history. The nonpartisan watchdog OpenSecrets estimates a total of $11.9 billion will be spent by candidates and outside political groups. Elon Musk alone ​had spent about $366 million to support Republicans as of three weeks ago, according to campaign finance records.Still, midterms generally attract fewer voters ​than ⁠the higher-profile presidential races. More than 155 million votes were cast in the 2024 presidential election, for instance.#1 Control of Congress at stakePlenty is at stake in this midterm election as Democrats try to win majority control of the U.S. Congress.Currently, Republicans hold a 218-214 majority in the House, where there are two vacancies and one independent who caucuses with Republicans. Democrats must win a net gain of four seats to win control.Democrats also are fighting to win the Senate, where Republicans hold a 53-47 majority. They must net four additional seats to get control. Twelve races, including those in conservative-leaning states like Kansas and Texas, could decide the outcome.Midterm elections generally are dangerous territory for the political party that holds the White House and/or Congress.For 2026, that means that President Donald Trump and his Republicans controlling the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives are in perilous political positions.#2 Verdict on presidencyThe midterms can be an opportunity for voters to, in effect, grade the president's performance and possibly trigger White House course corrections if they receive low marks.Midterm election results also can give aspiring presidential candidates hints on how to tailor their messages to voters in the next presidential campaign, which in this case will be in 2028.Approval of Trump's performance is at a near record low of 32%, according to Reuters/Ipsos polling.Domestic issues like rising ⁠consumer prices ⁠are likely to have an impact on the outcome of many races and could erode support for Republicans.At the same time, there is evidence that Democrats are more enthusiastic about voting this year than Republicans and more of them have already cast their ballots, according to the University of Florida Election Lab.There are also signs that Latino voters who veered to Trump in 2024 might be returning to Democrats because of frustration over the economy and some of Trump's immigration enforcement tactics.However, a landslide for the Democrats is far from assured. Republicans could benefit from continued skepticism towards Democrats, a Republican spending advantage on campaigns, and fears from moderate voters over some primary wins by left-wingers.#3 History of shockwavesRecent history tells the story of the shockwaves a midterm election can produce.In the 2010 midterms, during the Democratic presidency of Barack Obama, Republicans scored major victories, winning 63 additional House seats amid an underperforming U.S. economy and weak support for Obama's landmark health care reform legislation. Democrats lost their majority. In the Senate, they held onto control despite losing six seats.The Republican wave was a "shellacking," Obama lamented at the time. He subsequently faced ⁠Republican demands for significant reductions to non-defense spending.Democrats returned the favor in 2018, with Trump in the White House. They gained a net total of 40 House seats, but lost a net two Senate seats.This year's elections also have races for governors in 36 of the 50 states and voting in nearly every state for seats in state-level legislative bodies.Currently, Republicans control 55% of state legislative seats across the country, while Democrats hold 43.8%, according to Ballotpedia.#4 Speaker's spot up for grabsIf Democrats manage to win the House, the next speaker – second in line for the presidency after the vice president – is likely to be Democratic Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York. He ​is currently the House Democratic leader.Jeffries, who would become the first Black American to hold the powerful office, would be in a position to direct House committees to launch investigations into a range of controversial activities by Trump and his associates. Jeffries repeatedly has said Democrats would look into what he has called "unprecedented levels of corruption" during the ⁠Trump administration.He also would steer Democrats' ‌legislative priorities through the ‌House. He has said Democrats would focus on making healthcare, groceries, housing, energy and other costs more affordable.A Republican win, on the other ⁠hand, would ensure that the speaker's gavel remains in that party's hands, either with current speaker Mike Johnson or whichever ‌Republican prevails if he is challenged for the job.Republican priorities are likely to be focused on additional tax cuts, huge increases in defense spending, and deeper social safety net reductions, building on Trump's 2025 "One Big Beautiful Bill."#5 Marquee racesAmong the most-watched House ​races are Republican Representative Mike Lawler's bid for reelection to a ⁠New York district that Democratic candidate Kamala Harris won in her 2024 presidential campaign and an open seat in a Nebraska swing district where ⁠farmers and truckers face sharply higher fuel prices as a result of the U.S. war against Iran.Also high on Democrats' list of House seats they hope to take from Republicans are two ⁠in Pennsylvania and one in New Jersey.Hovering over ​all of this are questions over whether Trump will try to meddle in the elections, which are administered by the 50 individual states.Since 2020, he has repeatedly insisted, falsely, that there is widespread cheating in U.S. elections. State election officials and Democrats in Congress have been preparing for possible legal challenges to any moves by his administration to try to intervene.
