news.title: Where Is the Other Dan Sullivan? What We Know
news.text: "FAKE ALASKA CANDIDATE DANIAL J. SULLIVAN, JR., IS MISSING IN ACTION! HE HAS TOTALLY DISAPPEARED, GONE! NOBODY HAS BEEN ABLE TO FIND HIM," President Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social early on the morning of November 3. Controversy has swirled around there being two candidates in the Alaska Senate race with the same name. Incumbent Senator Dan Sullivan is seeking reelection against Democratic challenger Mary Peltola. Also on the ballot is the independent candidate Daniel J. Sullivan. And the latter Sullivan, a retired schoolteacher, has been seemingly absent as of late. CBS News reported ahead of election week that Daniel J. Sullivan had left his hometown of Petersburg earlier this week, citing multiple sources. One Petersburg resident who is a former student of Sullivan’s told CBS News that she had seen him on a flight to Anchorage on Monday. That was two days before Alaska’s closely contested Senate race was rocked by a New York Times investigation which reported that Democratic operatives linked to Peltola’s campaign had recruited Daniel J. Sullivan. A Democratic Senatorial Campaign (DSCC) spokesperson previously denied any involvement in a statement to Newsweek. "The DSCC is not involved with Dan J. Sullivan," the spokesperson said. The Peltola campaign also denied involvement, telling Newsweek in a statement, "The Alaskans for Mary campaign has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign. Like Mary, our campaign is focused on lowering costs and fixing the rigged system in DC." Meanwhile, a spokesperson for Senator Sullivan’s campaign told Newsweek that Alaskans "deserve the truth," accusing Peltola and Democrats of trying to "recruit candidates to deliberately deceive and confuse voters." As America heads to the polls for the midterm elections, the question lingers: where exactly is the other Dan Sullivan? This is what we know so far. Newsweek has contacted Sullivan for comment via email outside of regular business hours. On the day of the midterm elections, the whereabouts of Daniel J. Sullivan are unclear. Illinois-born Sullivan is a registered Republican and has lived in Petersburg since 1980. He is running as an independent and said in a campaign statement that he has become "increasingly concerned that our sitting U.S. Senator has lost touch with the people he was elected to represent." "Alaska deserves a senator who puts Alaska first," he said in that statement. Sullivan’s campaign website states that as Alaska’s next senator, Sullivan will "focus on delivering the kind of transformative change needed to get Alaska back on track." His campaign website links out to social media profiles on Instagram and Facebook. The Facebook profile has 760 followers, and the last post, a link to a local news article about Alaska’s Republican Senator Lisa Murkowski, is dated to September 30. The Instagram account has 125 followers and no posts. CBS News’ report dates the reported sighting of Sullivan by a local resident to Monday 26th. It is unclear if there have been any further sightings of the former teacher. Nick Sortor, a conservative influencer who has ties to the Trump administration, has posted about the independent Senate candidate’s absence on X. In a post on X on November 1, Sortor said that he had staked out Sullivan’s house for more than two days, and that he "couldn’t detect even the slightest movements in the house." Sortor’s post said that Sullivan had gotten on a flight, similar to what CBS News had reported, and alleged that this came after Sullivan caught "wind of the BOMBSHELL story about his recruitment to run for Senate to confuse voters—despite being holed up in his house for the ENTIRE rest of the election." Responding to speculation around his candidacy being fake, Sullivan told HuffPost in October, "How could I be a fake Dan Sullivan? That is my real name!" And sentiment surrounding Sullivan is mixed. In a separate post, Sortor spoke to local residents who he identified as "direct neighbors," of Sullivan’s. The neighbor said that Sullivan was a Democrat and had previously supported Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders and former Vice President Kamala Harris. And it has been widely reported that there have not been traditional campaign materials like mailers or signs circulated by the candidate, which is consistent with his lack of social media postings. Andrew Worhatch, a Petersburg fisherman, told CBS News that "I don’t think it’s a serious candidacy." However, this doesn’t mean that Sullivan is entirely without his supporters. Local resident Keely Hankins told CBS News, "I’ve known Dan for a long time. I know his family. I know he’s raised good children," and said that Sullivan was the only candidate capable of representing southeast Alaska. 'I might be having a brain freeze' Some support, though, may be unintentional. Both names of the incumbent Senator Dan Sullivan and the independent candidate, Daniel J. Sullivan, will appear on the ballot, differentiated by their middle initial and by the word "incumbent" next to the senator’s name. But this already appears to be confusing voters. In live footage captured by News Nation at the polls, Greg Martone, an Alaskan voter realized that he may have voted for the wrong Dan Sullivan. "I don’t remember seeing the other Dan Sullivan; I totally forgot to look for two Dan Sullivans," he said. "I might just be having a brain freeze, but I don’t remember the second Dan Sullivan." It was not immediately clear who Martone, who intended to vote for the incumbent senator, voted for. Senate race tightens Alaska is now heading to the polls for election today, as the closely watched Senate campaign comes to a close. The final polls showed Peltola leading the incumbent Sullivan, but by a narrower margin than earlier in the month, by 48 percent to 46 percent in a New York Times/Siena poll of 610 likely voters released on Sunday and conducted between October 23 and October 30. A previous New York Times/Siena poll, released on October 3, had given Peltola a wider margin, with 50 percent of the vote to Sullivan's 43. Early voting had surged ahead of the elections, with more than 58,000 ballots cast as of October 28, according to data from the state's Division of Elections. That figure already surpassed the amount seen during the state’s 2022 midterm and is set to meet or exceed the record early turnout seen in the 2024 presidential election. The midterm elections could go on to reshape the balance of power in Washington. But it could be hours, days, or perhaps even weeks before the result is projected after the polls close. Contact Newsweek editors for this story: Robert Greenall and Ben Kelly
news.summary: The midterm elections are here. But the whereabouts of independent Alaska Senate candidate Daniel J. Sullivan are unclear.

news.title: Republicans feel the blues as US midterms begin: Key races and faces to watch
news.text: The battle for control of the US Congress is under way, and Republicans have reason to be nervous.As millions of Americans head to polling stations on November 3, the latest surveys point to a difficult electoral environment for President Donald Trump's Republican Party, with Democrats building a substantial lead in the national congressional preference polls and gaining ground in several traditionally Republican states.The elections are shaping up as a referendum on Trump's second presidency, with voters weighing the administration's handling of the economy, the cost of living, immigration, tariffs and the war involving Iran.For Democrats, the midterms offer an opportunity to turn dissatisfaction with the White House into control of Congress. For Republicans, the challenge is to prevent a midterm backlash from becoming a decisive repudiation of Trump's political agenda.All 435 seats in the House of Representatives, 35 Senate seats and 36 governorships are being contested.The outcome will determine not only who controls the legislative agenda for the remaining two years of Trump's presidency but also how much political leverage the president retains heading into the 2028 presidential election.The numbersThe national polling picture has shifted considerably in the Democrats' favour in the final stretch of the campaign. A polling aggregation updated on November 3 puts the Democratic advantage on the generic congressional ballot at approximately 8.4 percentage points.The figures represent national preferences for congressional elections, rather than predictions of individual seat outcomes. Nevertheless, a Democratic lead of this magnitude is significant, particularly given how narrow the Republican majority in the House is.(function(){function e(){window.addEventListener(`message`,function(e){if(e.data[`datawrapper-height`]!==void 0){var t=document.querySelectorAll(`iframe`);for(var n in e.data[`datawrapper-height`])for(var r=0,i;i=t[r];r++)if(i.contentWindow===e.source){var a=e.data[`datawrapper-height`][n]+`px`;i.style.height=a}}})}e()})();An earlier RealClearPolling average, cited by Al Jazeera on October 31, had Democrats ahead 51.4% to 43.2%, an 8.2-point advantage. An Economist/YouGov survey also found that 44% of registered voters expected Democrats to control the House after the election, against 31% who expected Republicans to retain it.The Senate picture was less settled in that survey: 39% expected Democrats to win control, while 36% anticipated a Republican majority.Perhaps the most consequential development is the latest forecast from election analyst Nate Silver's Silver Bulletin. Its final November 3 forecast says a Democratic House majority now looks almost certain and that Democrats have also moved into a strong position to capture the Senate.The model's polling averages show Democrats ahead in practically every major Senate battleground, including Texas, Ohio, Michigan, Maine and Iowa. Even states that Republicans would ordinarily expect to defend comfortably have become competitive.The figures are especially striking in Texas, Ohio and Kansas, where Democrats are attempting to break through in states that have traditionally leaned Republican in federal elections.However, polls are not predictions. A lead of three or four percentage points can disappear within the margin of error, and turnout, undecided voters and differences between likely-voter and registered-voter samples could still change the outcome.Why the Democrats believe a blue wave is possibleHistorically, the party occupying the White House tends to lose ground in midterm elections. The president's party has lost House seats in 18 of the last 20 midterm elections over the past 80 years, making the November vote particularly uncomfortable for Trump.But this election is also being shaped by a combination of issues that Democrats believe have created an unusually difficult environment for Republicans.The economy and cost of living: Affordability has emerged as a central campaign issue. Voters are concerned about everyday expenses, energy prices, healthcare costs and the pressure on household budgets. Republicans are facing questions about whether Trump's economic policies have delivered the relief promised during the 2024 presidential campaign. Democrats have sought to connect tariffs and the Iran war to higher costs for consumers, farmers and businesses. In Iowa, for instance, the impact of tariffs and the rising cost of diesel and fertiliser have become central to the campaign. Rural voters, traditionally an important Republican constituency, are being targeted by Democrats with an affordability message.The Iran war: The war involving Iran has become another major political vulnerability for the administration. Republicans are facing criticism over its economic consequences, particularly energy prices and the wider uncertainty surrounding American military involvement. The issue has also created a difficult balancing act for GOP candidates who must defend the president's foreign policy while attempting to keep the focus on domestic concerns.Trump's approval ratings: Trump's popularity is another major concern for Republicans. The New York Times polling average put his approval rating at approximately 37% ahead of Election Day. Democrats have sought to turn dissatisfaction with the president into votes against Republican candidates, even in constituencies that Trump won comfortably in 2024.Early voting and turnout: More than 43 million Americans had already voted early, either in person or through returned mail ballots, five days before Election Day, according to an Associated Press analysis. That was nearly 10 million more than at the equivalent stage before the 2022 midterms. Texas had recorded more than 6.3 million early ballots by October 28, against 4.2 million at the corresponding stage in 2022 — an increase of around 50%. Georgia had also crossed 2.5 million early ballots by October 30, surpassing its 2022 early-voting figure of 2.3 million. The numbers indicate heightened electoral engagement, although early voting figures alone cannot establish which party will benefit.The House: Republicans' biggest vulnerabilityThe party entered the election with 219 seats against the Democrats' 214, with two vacancies. Democrats therefore need a net gain of just four seats to secure a majority.That relatively small hurdle has made dozens of districts competitive, including several that Trump carried in 2024.The challenge for Republicans is compounded by the fact that the president's party generally faces a midterm disadvantage. Democrats, meanwhile, have been encouraged by the national polling advantage and their performance in a number of special elections.The Cook Political Report and other election forecasters have identified a broad collection of Republican-held seats that could become vulnerable.Among the most important House contests are:NEW YORK Republican Congressman Mike Lawler faces Democrat Cait Conley in New York's 17th Congressional District. The constituency is particularly important because it is among the few Republican-held districts that Kamala Harris carried in the 2024 presidential election. Lawler has built his political identity around appealing to moderate voters, but the national political environment could make his re-election considerably more difficult. Conley is attempting to capitalise on dissatisfaction with Trump and turn the district's Democratic lean in the presidential election into a congressional victory. The latest polling aggregation puts Conley approximately two percentage points ahead, making this one of the most closely watched Republican-held seats.IOWA Iowa's first congressional district is another important test of whether Democrats can win back voters in traditionally Republican territory. Republican Congresswoman Mariannette Miller-Meeks faces Democrat Christina Bohannan, who has unsuccessfully challenged her in previous elections. The contest has become more competitive amid concerns about tariffs, farm costs and the wider economic outlook. Democrats have also invested heavily in the district. Reuters reported that they had spent approximately $11 million compared with $7 million by Republicans. The latest polling aggregation showed Bohannan with a substantial lead, although the district's Republican lean and the history of Miller-Meeks' victories make this a race worth watching closely.TEXAS Texas has become a particularly important battleground because of the Republican effort to redraw congressional boundaries to improve the party's chances of retaining its House majority. Republicans hoped the redistricting exercise would create additional favourable seats. But Democrats are attempting to turn the backlash against the process into an electoral advantage. Several Texas districts are now being closely monitored, including the 9th District, where the polling aggregation shows Democrat Alex Mealer narrowly ahead of the Republican incumbent. The 15th District is another contest to watch, with Republican Monica De La Cruz facing a challenge from Democrat Bobby Pulido. The outcome will help establish whether Republican efforts to reshape congressional boundaries have delivered the expected advantage.Other House races to watchArizona's 1st District: Democrat Amish Shah is challenging Republican Jay Feely in a competitive open-seat contest. Shah's campaign has attracted significant outside spending, and the latest polling aggregation gives him a four-point advantage.Florida's 22nd District: Democrat Pia Dandiya is challenging Republican Casey Askar in a seat that has been rated a toss-up by major election forecasters.Pennsylvania's 7th District: Republican Ryan Mackenzie faces Democrat Ryan Crosswell in another closely watched contest.Michigan's 10th District: Democrat Christina Hines and Republican Michael Bouchard are competing for an open seat after John James entered the gubernatorial race.Montana's 1st District: Democrat Sam Forstag is attempting to unseat Republican Aaron Flint in a district Trump won comfortably in 2024.New Jersey's 7th District: Democrat Rebecca Bennett is challenging Republican Tom Kean Jr., who has faced criticism over his absence from congressional votes.These contests are part of a much larger battle. CBS News identified 42 House races that could determine which party controls the chamber.Senate: Could Democrats pull off an even bigger upset?The Senate battle is more complicated.Republicans currently hold 53 seats against the Democrats' 47. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to reach a majority, assuming the existing chamber alignment.This is a considerably more difficult proposition than winning the House because Republicans are defending seats in a number of states Trump carried by comfortable margins in 2024. But the latest surveys have given Democrats fresh hope.Five Senate contests deserve particular attention.1. Texas: James Talarico's opportunity to make historyTexas is emerging as one of the biggest potential Democratic breakthroughs of the election.Democrat James Talarico is challenging Republican Ken Paxton, the state's attorney general, for a Senate seat.Paxton defeated incumbent Republican Senator John Cornyn in the GOP primary, but his nomination has raised questions about whether Republicans have selected the strongest possible candidate for a general election contest.His history of personal and political controversies has given Democrats an opening.Talarico, a state representative and former teacher, has sought to build a campaign around economic issues, healthcare and a broader appeal to voters dissatisfied with the political establishment.The November 1 New York Times/Siena poll put Talarico ahead 50% to 43%.A polling average also showed him leading by approximately three points. A Democratic victory would be particularly significant: the party has not won a Texas Senate election since 1988.2. Michigan: Abdul El-Sayed takes on Mike RogersMichigan is another state where Democrats are hoping to make a significant gain.Democrat Abdul El-Sayed is challenging Republican Mike Rogers for an open Senate seat following the retirement of Senator Gary Peters.El-Sayed, a progressive former Michigan health official, won a divisive Democratic primary against a more moderate opponent.Rogers, a former congressman, is attempting to return to the Senate after losing his previous election battle against Elissa Slotkin.The latest New York Times/Siena survey gave El-Sayed a commanding 53%-42% lead.This is particularly important because Michigan is a major battleground state where the Democratic candidate's performance could help establish whether the party's national polling advantage is translating into votes.3. Ohio: Sherrod Brown attempts a comebackFormer Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown is attempting to reclaim his seat after losing his re-election bid in 2024.He faces Republican Senator Jon Husted, who was appointed to the seat vacated by JD Vance after Vance became vice-president.Brown has sought to position himself as a champion of working-class voters, an important constituency in a state that has moved increasingly towards Republicans in recent elections.His campaign is attempting to make the election about manufacturing jobs, economic insecurity and the cost of living.The New York Times/Siena poll put Brown ahead 49%-44%, suggesting that Ohio could become one of the biggest Democratic surprises of the night.4. Maine: Susan Collins faces a serious challengeRepublican Senator Susan Collins is fighting to retain her seat against Democrat Troy Jackson.Collins has survived several difficult election campaigns and has often benefited from her ability to attract support beyond the Republican base.But the political environment is different this time. Maine voted for Kamala Harris in 2024, and Democrats believe the state's electorate could turn against Republicans in the midterms.The November 1 Siena poll showed Jackson leading Collins 51%-45%.A Democratic victory here would be particularly consequential because Collins has been a prominent Republican figure in the Senate for decades.5. Alaska: Mary Peltola threatens another Republican seatFormer Democratic Congresswoman Mary Peltola is challenging Republican Senator Dan Sullivan in Alaska.Alaska is not an obvious Democratic pickup opportunity. The state has a strong Republican voting history and has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 2008.But Peltola has demonstrated an ability to appeal to voters beyond the traditional Democratic base.The latest Siena poll showed her leading Sullivan 48%-46%.Even a narrow victory would be a major breakthrough for Democrats and could prove decisive in the battle for Senate control.Other Senate contests that could decide controlStateDemocratic candidateRepublican candidateLatest polling pictureKansasAdam HamiltonRoger MarshallHamilton +5IowaJosh TurekAshley HinsonTurek +1GeorgiaJon OssoffMike CollinsOssoff +9.2North CarolinaRoy CooperMichael WhatleyCooper +10.9New HampshireChris PappasJohn SununuPappas +7.3NebraskaIndependent/Democratic-aligned candidatePete RickettsRicketts +0.9Kansas is especially interesting. Democrat Adam Hamilton is attempting to become the first Democrat to win a Senate election in the state since 1932.The race against Republican Senator Roger Marshall has become competitive because of concerns over affordability, energy costs and the Iran war.Georgia, meanwhile, is a test of whether Republicans can unseat Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff. Republican Mike Collins is challenging him, but the latest polling averages suggest Ossoff has a substantial advantage.North Carolina is another important opportunity for Democrats. Former governor Roy Cooper is running against Republican Michael Whatley in an open-seat contest. Cooper's popularity and statewide political experience have made him a formidable challenger.Together, these races could determine whether Democrats can overcome the unfavourable Senate map and take control of the chamber.Governor races: Democrats eye a historic breakthroughWhile congressional control is the biggest national prize, the gubernatorial contests could produce a political realignment of their own.A total of 36 states are electing governors, representing approximately 80% of the US population. Nineteen of those contests involve open seats.Democrats are hoping to win control of a majority of governors' offices for the first time in two decades. Their last such breakthrough came in 2006, when they flipped six governorships during the midterm elections of George W Bush's presidency.The most closely watched races include:1. Ohio: Vivek Ramaswamy vs Amy ActonThis is arguably the most closely watched gubernatorial contest from an Indian-American perspective.Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, backed by Trump, is running against Democrat Amy Acton, the former Ohio health director.Ramaswamy entered the campaign with considerable national visibility, having previously contested the 2024 Republican presidential nomination and later worked with the Trump administration's Department of Government Efficiency initiative.Acton, meanwhile, is seeking to make the race a referendum on Republican leadership in the state.The latest New York Times/Siena survey put Acton ahead 49%-43%. Another November 1 survey by Survey 160 showed her leading 51%-44%.The polling average on November 2 gave Acton a lead of approximately 3.8 points.The campaign has also been marred by controversy over a political advertisement involving Acton's family, which attracted criticism from both Democrats and some prominent Republicans.A Democratic victory would be a significant setback for Trump, who has publicly backed Ramaswamy.2. Texas: Gina Hinojosa vs Greg AbbottDemocrat Gina Hinojosa is mounting a challenge to Republican Governor Greg Abbott, who is seeking another term.No Democrat has won a statewide election in Texas since 1994, making the contest particularly significant.Hinojosa has sought to make affordability, healthcare and economic opportunity central to her campaign.The New York Times/Siena survey showed her narrowly ahead 48%-47%, putting Abbott under unusual pressure in a state where Republicans have dominated statewide politics for decades.3. Georgia: An opening for DemocratsGeorgia has not elected a Democratic governor since 1998.The open-seat contest has therefore attracted considerable national attention, with Democrats believing that the wider political climate could help them overcome the state's Republican lean.4. Iowa and Alaska: Testing Republican strongholdsBoth states have competitive open-seat gubernatorial contests.In Iowa, Democrat Rob Sand is challenging Republican Zach Lahn, while in Alaska Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins is facing Republican Bernadette Wilson.The Siena survey gave the Democratic candidates leads of 51%-43% and 54%-46%, respectively.5. Florida: Can Democrats make another breakthrough?Republican Byron Donalds, a prominent Trump ally, is challenging Democrat David Jolly.Florida has become increasingly Republican in recent elections, but Democrats believe the economic environment could make the contest more competitive than expected.Indian-Americans in the fray: A growing political footprintThe 2026 elections are also important for the Indian-American community, with candidates of Indian origin contesting positions ranging from the US House of Representatives to governorships, attorney-general offices and local government.Read also | Indian-American candidates in 2026 US midterms: Key races, profiles, latest polling & what's at stakeThe growing presence of Indian-Americans in American politics reflects a broader shift in the country's political landscape. Their participation is no longer confined to a handful of congressional constituencies. Candidates are competing in states across the country, representing both major political parties.Among the prominent candidates are Democratic lawmakers Ro Khanna, Pramila Jayapal, Ami Bera and Suhas Subramanyam, all seeking another term in Congress.Republican Vivek Ramaswamy is the most high-profile Indian-origin candidate contesting a gubernatorial election.Other Indian-origin candidates to watchThe election also features several Indian-American candidates seeking to expand their political representation beyond the traditional congressional contests.Amish Shah — Arizona: The Democrat and former Arizona state legislator is challenging Republican Jay Feely in the 1st Congressional District. The race has attracted significant outside spending and could become an important Democratic pickup.Pia Dandiya — Florida: Dandiya is contesting Florida's 22nd Congressional District against Republican Casey Askar. The race has been rated a toss-up by several election forecasters.Saritha Komatireddy — New York: The Republican candidate is challenging Democratic Attorney General Letitia James. A former federal prosecutor, Komatireddy has worked on national security and organised-crime cases. Polls have shown James with a lead.Nithya Raman — Los Angeles: The Indian-origin Los Angeles City Council member is challenging incumbent Mayor Karen Bass. Her campaign adds another prominent South Asian face to the American political contest.Pooja Sethi — Texas: A Democrat contesting Texas House District 47, Sethi is a lawyer who previously served as chief of staff in the Texas Legislature.Sandeep Srivastava — Texas: Srivastava is challenging Republican Matt Shaheen in Texas House District 66. He previously contested a congressional election in 2024.There are also Indian-origin candidates contesting other state-level positions and legislative seats, reflecting the expanding reach of the community in American politics.Why the outcome mattersThe midterms are not just about which party controls Congress. They could determine the political trajectory of Trump's remaining two years in office.A Democratic takeover of the House would give the opposition control over committees, investigations, legislative priorities and congressional oversight.It could also complicate the administration's ability to pass major legislation, particularly on immigration, taxation, federal spending and foreign policy.A Democratic Senate majority would have even greater consequences. It could influence confirmations of senior administration officials and federal judges, while giving Democrats control over a chamber that has been central to Trump's legislative agenda.A Republican victory, on the other hand, would allow the president to continue governing with support from both chambers and would weaken the argument that voters have rejected his second-term agenda.There is also a longer-term political calculation.Read also | US midterm elections 2026: Why it's a do-or-die fight for Trump & the Democracts - explained in 10 chartsPotential Democratic presidential contenders, including governors and senators, will be closely watched. Strong performances could establish them as credible candidates for 2028, while Republican candidates will be judged on their ability to maintain Trump's coalition.The gubernatorial elections are particularly important because state governors exercise considerable authority over election administration, a matter likely to become increasingly significant as the country approaches the next presidential election.What happens next?Polling stations are opening across the country on November 3 (from 3.30pm IST) with voting hours varying by state and local jurisdiction.The first results will emerge after polling closes in individual states. However, the Senate and House contests are likely to produce different timelines for a clear picture, particularly where margins are narrow and mail ballots take longer to process.For Indian audiences, the first substantial results are expected to emerge during the morning and afternoon of November 4, India time.The biggest immediate indicators will be the early returns from competitive House districts, followed by the Senate battlegrounds in states such as Texas, Ohio, Michigan, Maine and Iowa.A Democratic victory in the House is increasingly anticipated by polling models. The real question is whether the party can go further and capture the Senate as well.For Trump, the stakes are considerable. A midterm defeat would not remove him from office, but it could transform the remainder of his presidency into a prolonged battle with an opposition-controlled Congress. For Democrats, the election offers an opportunity to turn public dissatisfaction into institutional power. And for Indian-Americans, it offers another chance to establish that their political presence in the United States is becoming increasingly difficult to overlook.You use AI every day. news.summary: Current polling trends show that Republicans might encounter difficulties during the midterm elections on November 3, largely due to dissatisfaction among voters. This election is being viewed as a crucial test of the government's performance on vital topics including the economy and immigration. As both House and Senate races remain hotly contested, the results are far from certain, with Democrats aspiring to take advantage of this discontent.

news.title: A Strategist Knocked on Doors in Fla. and Georgia. Here’s What Black Voters Want Democrats to Know
news.text:
This election cycle, organizers have knocked on the doors of millions of Americans to hear their concerns and persuade them to vote for their party’s candidates. I laced up my shoes and hit the streets in my home state of Georgia, as well as in Florida, Ohio, and Indiana, to support Democrats in tight races. I rarely canvassed alone. In Port St. Lucie, Florida, I met local organizers like Deb and Lauren, who have been doing the Lord’s work with an ounce of the Lord’s resources. And in Indiana and Georgia, my mom stepped out of her comfort zone and into the arena, setting aside her fear of poorly restrained dogs, because she knows just how high the stakes are for this election.

 Black voters overwhelmingly acknowledge this reality, and talking to Black voters this cycle reminded me of just how seriously we take our vote, that we approach voting as a form of communion, and that a knock on the door can catalyze the next great campaign for office.

I love talking to all voters, but I love talking to my people most of all. Black voters have historically been the backbone of the party, but we’re often overlooked in polls and focus groups. The national media creates narratives about “Black voters” without always appreciating the nuances that exist within our community. Far from being a monolith, the Black voting bloc must be dissected along a multitude of dimensions. Young Black voters, older Black voters, Southern Black voters, church-going Black voters, and Black immigrant voters all have different concerns, and I got to hear about those concerns while canvassing this cycle.

In Florida, I met a Black man around my age, whose number-one issue was education. As Deb and I spoke with him, he admitted he knew very little about candidates like Angie Nixon, a Black woman who secured the Democratic nomination for US Senate. He consumed our information voraciously but said that he had to do his research before casting his ballot. While those conversations in the moment can be frustrating (What do you mean you have to do your research?! Do you see what the other side is doing?!), they demonstrate a level of democratic discipline among younger Black voters in particular, who no longer feel blindly loyal to the Democratic Party. These folks recognize that their vote gives them power, and of course, with great power comes great responsibility – responsibility to do your research and to ultimately cast your ballot for the candidate who’ll best advance your interests. It’s on insiders like me to make the case for why, in most instances, those candidates have a D next to their name.

A few streets over from that voter, we pulled up to another home, and upon opening the car doors, were immediately drawn up the driveway by the sweet sounds of Latin music. There was no mistaking I was in Florida! After walking up the driveway, we came across three middle-aged men – two Hispanic, one Black/Afro-Latino – sitting by the entrance of the garage, sipping beers and having a good time. Of all the things they could have been doing – watching football, or talking about their families – imagine my surprise when I discovered they were discussing…their sample ballots! Fifteen minutes, twenty questions, and three politely declined beers later, we left them to do the work of democracy. I wish everyone could see that it’s not just college students or white liberals who host ballot parties. Black and brown men also come together, crack open some cold ones, and bust out their ballots. Like so many Black voters, these men understand the right to vote is sacred – so sacred that they gather in communion to exercise it. So sacred that pastors at churches all across the country, including mine back home in Georgia, are coordinating rides to make sure all of God’s souls make it to the polls.

One of our final stops was at the home of a Black woman, who for years has educated the children of Port St. Lucie. We quickly learned that she did not need us to tell her about the stakes of the upcoming election. Not only had she been driving around to put up yard signs for local school board candidates, but she had been kicking around the possibility of running for office herself one day. When we knocked on her door, she was literally in the other room researching how to do it! We held our first campaign strategy meeting standing right there in the foyer of her house, and I promised her I’d fly back to Port St. Lucie to knock on doors for her when she decides to take the plunge. Our interaction reminded me of how much untapped political potential is lying dormant within so many Black folks, especially teachers, who pour their all into helping the next generation realize their academic potential. Sometimes, all they need is a knock at the door.

This Election Day, I feel inspired by the Black folks I met over the past few weeks in so many different corners of the country. Even after the midterms are over, I encourage my fellow Democrats to keep knocking on the doors of their neighbors. Let’s make sure “fired up, ready to go” becomes our everyday reality, not just a state of being we aspire to every other year.

Gevin Reynolds is a Democratic strategist. He served as associate director of speechwriting to Vice President Kamala Harris.
news.summary:
A Strategist knocked on 1000 doors and now reveals what Black Americans want from Democrats.

news.title: Inflation, Iran, Epstein: Why Trump Could Lose Congress Today
news.text: After several comprehensive victories by the West Indies’ Test cricketers in England, the cricketing world celebrated the “Blackwash”. Now, the United States of America could wake up to a “Bluewash” in a day or two. The opinion polls, almost unanimously, predict a Democratic Party victory in the mid-term elections. There’s a caveat, though: in the past, Trump or his people have often done a percentage point or two better than the opinion polls suggested. Long before he was elected President, Barack Obama pointed out that it wasn’t about red states and blue states; it was all about the United States. Nevertheless, with the United States such a 50:50 country, a wipeout becomes an eye-watering moment for the party shredded by the electorate, and an unprecedented moment of celebration for the winners. Which is why the nail-biting Senate contests in key red states like Texas, Alaska and, good lord, Kansas, are so significant. In all the battleground states, including Georgia, Iowa, Ohio, North Carolina, New Hampshire, Maine and Michigan, the Democrats are at least competitive. But Texas and Kansas are interesting, with both Democratic candidates, James Talarico in Texas and Adam Hamilton in Kansas, ahead, even if by five per cent or less. Kansas last elected a Democratic senator in 1932, as part of Franklin Roosevelt’s New Deal victory. Hamilton is a priest in his sixties, a centrist who refers to himself as a “liberal-conservative” or a “conservative-liberal”. He has held on to his lead in a state of three million people for months. Talarico is only 37 and a divinity student. He has a razor-thin lead in a state that hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate since Lloyd Bentsen, Michael Dukakis’s running mate in 1988, an election in which the Democrats frittered away a 17-point lead. Bentsen, a Tory Democrat, won 38 years ago. Donald Trump won Texas, a state with 40 electoral votes, by 1.5 million votes in the last presidential election. And yes, Ken Paxton, the Republican candidate, is controversial. But if Talarico, on the verge of victory, actually wins, it will be quite a feat. Maine and Michigan have often gone blue, but Trump won Michigan in the last presidential election with nearly 50 per cent of the vote. This time, Abdul El-Sayed, the Democrat, has a handsome lead. And El-Sayed is still, even in the era of Mamdani, an unfamiliar-sounding name for the average American. Susan Collins, the acclaimed senator from Maine, is trailing her Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson. Sure, then Vice President Kamala Harris won Maine in the 2024 presidential election, but Collins, one of the last Rockefeller Republicans, is a doughty candidate with a well-funded campaign. Currently, the US Senate has 53 Republicans and 45 Democrats, who are usually supported by two independents. If the Democrats can hold the three seats in Georgia, New Hampshire and Michigan, where they lead, and win any four of the Republican-held seats in Texas, Kansas, Alaska, Iowa, Maine and Ohio, they will take over the Senate. The House of Representatives, for all the gerrymandering in one or two states, looks set to go to the Democrats. It is entirely possible that the House will turn blue, with the Democrats increasing their tally from 214 to about 235. Some estimates are even higher. Of course, the ruling party usually loses seats in the mid-terms, and since the Second World War there have been only two exceptions. Trump himself lost 42 House seats during his first term, and Obama, in 2010, lost a staggering 64, along with nine Senate seats. A 20-seat gain and a Democratic Senate will pose serious challenges to Trump. Why Are Democrats Ahead?President Trump’s popularity levels are low, very low. There are five reasons for his political difficulties. Inflation is always a no-no, and there is a belief that if gas prices cross $4 a gallon, there will be unhappiness. That is exactly what has happened.Then there is the Iran war, which barely a third of Americans consider acceptable. It has been a long war, dragging on since February 28, and a hugely expensive one. This, naturally, has sent fuel prices shooting up.His decisions on tariffs may have fed inflation as well.Trump’s immigration policies, once popular, may no longer be as acceptable, particularly in states like Texas.Besides, the Epstein scandal is a dark cloud. The British government has taken action, and while there is no evidence of Trump’s involvement as yet, it has created considerable ill-feeling. What Can A Democratic-Controlled Congress Do?If the Democrats control both Houses, a logjam will be inevitable. The Senate can delay or block the appointment of Cabinet members, judges and other officials. The Democrats will be responsible for legislation and, worryingly for Trump, could begin investigations into him and his family. Then there is the war against Iran. Can the Democrats stop the war? It will not be easy at all. Yes, Congress can try to restrict funding, but there is also the presidential veto. It can hold hearings and launch investigations to make things difficult for the White House. Trump remains unpopular, and a section of the Democrats may even think of impeachment. Either way, whether Trump becomes a lame duck remains to be seen, but he will certainly face a hostile, uncooperative and difficult Congress.
news.summary: The upcoming mid-term elections in the United States are anticipated to favour the Democratic Party, with polls suggesting potential victories in several key states, including Texas and Kansas.
news.author: Srinjoy Chowdhury

news.title: Black voters could sway the midterms in surprising places
news.text:
Loss aversion is a phenomenon in psychology and behavioral economics. Defined simply, it means that the pain experienced from a loss is felt twice as much as winning. In politics, that intensity manifests itself in motivation. If you take something away from people, they are going to feel it more acutely than promising them something, and the theft produces a backlash. 

That’s what appears to be happening right now with Black voters. Across the country, they have been lining up to vote early, presumably against Donald Trump and the Republican Party’s MAGA agenda, in astonishing numbers, particularly in the South. That this comes only six months after the Supreme Court gutted the Voting Rights Act in Louisiana v. Callais should not come as a surprise.

In the Trump era, Republicans have become experienced at taking rights away from the American people. For women, it was the roll back of their constitutional rights when the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022, sparking a backlash in that year’s midterm elections. Since Trump returned to office in January 2025, immigrants have come under assault from a xenophobic administration intent on carrying out mass deportations via masked, secret police rampaging through neighborhoods. The LGBTQ+ community, and trans people in particular, have seen their rights stripped away. 

These policies have come as a shock to some Americans who never thought Trump would go there, and they have also opened the eyes of others to the cruelty at the heart of MAGA, overseen by the highest court of the land. But to many Black Americans, the GOP’s agenda and behavior will not have come as a surprise. After all, it’s been at the core of their history going back to before the country’s founding.

Black Americans know what it means to have their civil rights taken away from them. They understand fully the fear of being targeted by brutal, marauding gangs of armed men. In the decade following the Civil War and the passage of the 14th and 15th Amendments, Black people began to participate fully in civil society. Mississippi elected two Black U.S. senators and a lieutenant governor, and former slaves and their offspring enjoyed freedom of speech, movement and opportunity. But the white members of Southern society would not let that stand, and as soon as the federal government withdrew its troops, they stepped in with legal and social barriers to deny Black Americans their rights, this time backed by vigilante and state violence that became Jim and Jane Crow. 

Almost a century had passed by the time Lyndon Johnson signed the Civil Rights Act in 1964 and the Voting Rights Act in 1965, a period characterized by subjugation and violence by the white majority. But Black America kept fighting, against all odds, until they won. 

This year, we have seen yet another attempt by reactionary politicians and judges to turn back the clock. After the Callais decision, several Southern states reverted immediately to form and radically redrew their congressional districts to favor the white majority, making it much more difficult for voters to elect a Black federal and state representatives.

They may come to regret that decision. This isn’t 1955 (or 1855) anymore, as much as Donald Trump would like to make it so, and the Black community is once again mobilizing. According to experts, early voting data is showing something unexpected: The vote is being driven by young voters rather than just those who went through the earlier battles. It’s muscle memory for the Black community.

After 2024, when Trump won a surprising 15% of the Black vote — nearly doubling his share of 8% in the 2020 election — Republicans thought they were defying history to make great inroads within the community. Then, incredibly, the administration began attacking Black America. The result is what some politicos are calling a “Blacklash,” and it could very well be decisive in some places where nobody expected the Democrats to do well. And even if it doesn’t result in flipping seats, it’s a shot across the bow. 

Want more sharp takes on politics? Sign up for our free newsletter, Standing Room Only, written by Amanda Marcotte, now also a weekly show on YouTube or wherever you get your podcasts.

In Mississippi, prosecutor and former judge Scott Colom, who is Black, is running an excellent race against Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, the GOP incumbent. Colom has made some very clever advertisements which have garnered a lot of national attention, but Republicans and Democrats alike had largely ignored the race until just a couple of months ago. Polling has tightened, and the GOP has dispatched an influx of luminaries, including Trump himself. For the first time in years, Democrats from Bill Clinton to Kamala Harris, along with a long line of senators, have descended on the state to support Colom. Former President Barack Obama even cut an ad for him. Mississippi has the largest population of Black voters of any state in the country. If Colum gets a big Black turnout with just enough disaffected whites, he could win. 

Louisiana, after giving birth to the case that saw the Supreme Court’s conservative majority gut the Voting Rights Act, has been winnowed down to one majority Black district in a state that is one-third African-American. But there has been a surge in Black participation akin to what is seen in presidential years, which could prove decisive in a race for Louisiana’s open Senate seat that has been a sleeper until the last couple of weeks. According to a recent poll, Republican Julia Letlow and Democrat Jamie Davis are tied. Among voters who have already cast their ballot, Davis — who is Black — holds a six-point advantage, and 34% of early votes have been cast by Black Louisianans.

Then there’s South Carolina, which has seen Trump make three desperate appearances to shore up Darline Graham’s torpid campaign. The endangered incumbent, foisted upon South Carolina Republicans by the president himself following the sudden death of her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, is not getting the job done. As numbers cruncher Nate Silver pointed out, a recent New York Times poll showing the race essentially tied is not an outlier; she is in deep trouble. As of late October, the Times reports, “Black voters accounted for around 28 percent of early votes, while making up around 20 percent of the overall electorate in recent cycles. The trend is not unlike what we’re seeing in Georgia and North Carolina thus far.” If that holds true through Election Day, we could see the biggest upset of the whole campaign, largely due to Black South Carolinians saying “Enough is enough.”

In a few short hours, all the ads, mailers, signs and rallies will mercifully come to an end. I am cautiously optimistic, but like many, I’ll never celebrate prematurely again. There is good reason, though, to feel more positive than we have in a long time. Trump and his acolytes have overreached. Opting for the big tech credo of “move fast and break things,” they vastly overestimated their abilities — and the American people’s tolerance. 

They have also aroused a group of Americans who know what it is to lose their rights and privileges. With all that history and so many battles, Black Americans have shown what it takes to never give up.
news.summary: SCOTUS gutted the Voting Rights Act. Early voting numbers indicate that Black Americans are fighting back

news.title: Can Bernie Sanders Ensure Enough Left Representation In New Congress?
news.text:
By Satyaki Chakraborty

As the Americans are going to the polls on Tuesday, November 3, there is a new focus in the intensely contested elections between the ruling Republicans and the Democrats which concern both the President Donald Trump and the Democratic national leadership led by its Chair Ken Martin. Both are interested in seeing how many candidates with socialist leanings endorsed by Bernie Sanders get elected in the midterm polls.

84 year old Senator Bernie sanders, the leader of the Democratic Socialist Association(DSA) had endorsed more than 70 candidates in the primaries for the midterm, many of them, were elected in primaries and are now contesting. Apart, the DSA has its own candidates for the simultaneous elections for governors, Mayors and other senior government positions. So, for the first time, there is a possibility that the U.S. Congress will have a good chunk of Leftwing members after the November 3 elections.

The Democratic Party national leadership has a comfortable relationship with Bernie sanders though Sanders openly differs with the leadership on some issues including relating to more benefits for the working class. But at the same time, Sanders has taken a pragmatic position that Trump can be defeated only through the joint actions by the Democratic Party including both centrists and the Left. In fact, he has strong views against some sections of Ultra Left in U.S. politics who argue that the DSA led by Sanders should come out of the Democratic Party and build a real Left alternative to both Republicans and the present Democratic Party.

Bernie Sanders has crisscrossed the states for election campaign in the last two months. He was instrumental in bringing former President Barack Obama to the campaign in the last stage. He built up a formidable group of young socialists including New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani. He is highly popular among the students and youth. Further, Sanders maintains a super organized social media team which effectively intervenes in the digital media in favour of the socialist programme among the voters.

That so-called insurgency within the party that pushes a progressive agenda, rejects corporate funding, criticizes Israel and is determined to pull Democrats to the left has created some worries in the Democratic leadership. The DNC chair Ken Martin wants to make use of the youth power of Sanders but at the same time, he does not want the full blast criticism of this Left group against the right within Democratic Party and the Wall Street tycoons many of whom are fundraisers for the Democratic Party. Former President Bill Clinton as also Barack Obama are in favour of keeping the DNC united and against any activities from DSA which may alienate the common American voters. Sanders also understands the need of unity in the Democratic Party to defeat Trump, but he can’t ignore the views of the insurgents within his DSA.

According to the U.S. media reports, Abdul El-Sayed, the Democrat running for the Senate from Michigan, rejects the socialist label and instead calls himself a “progressive capitalist,” and has gladly accepted Sanders’ endorsement as well as a $1 million donation from proud DSA member, Ocasio-Cortez. Angie Nixon, who’s running for the Senate from Florida, joined the DSA in June and has accepted its fundraising and organizational support but has said she is not a socialist. Other Sanders-backed contenders — Senate candidates Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota, Troy Jackson in Maine and Rebecca Cooke in Wisconsin — are not socialists and never have been.

But these contestants who have got endorsement from Bernie Sanders, are expected to act as per Sanders suggestion and if a significant number of Sander endorsed candidates win, that will make the group as a dominant pressure group in the Democratic Party and the Congress. Sanders supporters say that they are hopeful of the win of minimum 40 candidates endorsed by DSA for the Congress. The DNC leadership has to listen to them and certainly this group will play a big role in determining the future policies and direction of the Democratic Party.

However, this possible win by the Sanders endorsed candidates may lead Trump and the Republicans to spread a big propaganda in the coming period that the country has to be saved from the communists to protect the American way of life. Trump has been campaigning all through that the Democratic Party is a captive of the Democratic Left and the DNC has no other alternative but to surrender to them if they win in many seats. This propaganda will be intensified before the 2028 presidential elections if Alexander Ocasio Cortez decides to contest in the 2028 presidential elections from the DSA as against the establishment candidates like Kamala Harris or Gavin Newsom.

Whatever they call themselves, all of the candidates Sanders has endorsed support the basic tenets of his progressive agenda: addressing economic inequality, providing healthcare for all, fighting corporate greed and rejecting a political system that rewards the rich while short-changing the working class. Sanders argues that those messages resonate with voters everywhere, not just in blue-leaning districts, and he and Ocasio-Cortez, his frequent road companion, are testing that theory by taking their Fighting Oligarchy Tour and their prodigious campaign war chest to GOP strongholds to court the very voters establishment Democrats worry about alienating

U.S. media reports say that Sanders has created a new playbook in which endorsements come with an infrastructure that includes money, a system for identifying and motivating voters, an expansive and effective get-out-the-vote network, and the “Fighting Oligarchy” road show that began in early 2025. The tour draws massive crowds in a festival-like atmosphere that can generate enthusiasm and encourage voter registration. For 2026 midterm, Sanders and his socialist candidates fighting in November 3 polls bring a new hopes to the young generation of America. That is the main factor which the Democratic national leadership can’t ignore. They need Sanders and his Left for winning the midterm polls.

The outcome of elections on Tuesday night/Wednesday will be assessed by all sections of political opinion in U.S. as this will determine the course of the polity in the United States in the next two years till the presidential elections in November 2028. (IPA Service)

news.title: Elon Musk, angry voters, and the AI backlash: What's at stake in the 2026 midterms
news.text: Americans are angry about affordability. The 2026 midterms will show who else will join President Donald Trump in paying the price. Trump has become so unpopular that the map of competitive races extends to Texas, Ohio, and even Kansas. Once considered unlikely, Democrats could sweep Republicans out of Congress. With even one house, Democrats can create headaches that stretch far beyond the White House. The very tech and business elite that cozied up to Trump ahead of his return to power may soon find themselves in the thick of congressional investigations. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has already made it clear that he's ready for a fight. Here are the storylines we'll be watching as the midterm elections unfold. Most registered voters in an October Gallup survey said the economy would be either very or extremely important to their vote. Forty-two percent said gas prices would be extremely important to their decision. Americans are shelling out more at the gas pump than they were a year ago, as the Iran war has pushed up prices. Other polls suggest the cost of living is a crucial issue. Consumer spending is still strong in the US, but that's partly because higher prices are driving up nominal totals. Plus, inflation is eating away at raises. Prices have risen faster year over year than average hourly earnings for six consecutive months. Trump may be unpopular, but building data centers is becoming an even harder sell. Polls show AI is not the top issue in the midterms, but ask a voter about building a data center in their community, and you're liable to get an earful. Across the country, candidates from both parties are racing to portray their opponents as too supportive of data center construction. This may just be the beginning. Some in tech are worried that the backlash brewing now will boil over once the 2028 presidential primaries get underway. Everything is bigger in Texas, including Elon Musk's checks. The SpaceX CEO has donated at least $448 million, a historic sum. Of that total, more than $215 million has gone to America PAC, his allied super PAC. Musk's donations have been rerouted to help Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton's Senate campaign. Polls show Paxton in danger of losing, a potential result that would make it extremely difficult for Republicans to hold their majority. When he's not cutting checks, Musk is using his megaphone on X to repeatedly blast Democrats and boost Paxton at all hours of the day. "It would be game over for America," Musk wrote on X on October 30, warning what could happen if Republicans lose ground during the midterms ahead of the 2028 presidential election. Some of the other major donors Richard and Elizabeth Uihlein, the billionaire founders of Uline, have donated $150 million, mostly to Restoration of America, a pro-Republican super PAC. Jeff Yass, the cofounder of the global trading and technology firm Susquehanna International Group, has donated $110 million, including $30 million to a group supporting Vivek Ramaswamy's Ohio gubernatorial campaign. Rounding out the $100 million + club is George Soros, for years one of the biggest Democratic megadonors, who has given $102 million, mostly to Democracy PAC, a Soros-linked super PAC that supports Democratic candidates. Google cofounder Sergey Brin has given $102 million — not in support of federal candidates but rather in hopes of stopping California's proposed one-time 5% tax on billionaires. Brin is part of a handful of tech elites who have cut large checks ahead of the midterms. Ben Horowitz & Marc Andreessen, two legendary venture capitalists, have donated over $92 million combined, mostly to a super PAC that supports candidates friendly to the AI industry. OpenAI President Greg Brockman and his wife, Anna, have donated $50 million, half of which went to the same pro-AI super PAC. Ohio Senate: Former Sen. Sherrod Brown, an Ohio Democrat, has zeroed in on Sen. Jon Husted's previous support for data center development in one of the closest-watched Senate races. Husted has said the issue should be left to communities and no longer supports offering tax incentives for new data center construction. If Democrats want to flip the US Senate, they'll need to win in places like Ohio. The Cook Political Report rates the race as a "Toss-Up." Texas Senate: Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, a Republican, is trying to avoid losing a Senate seat that could decide control of the chamber. Musk has donated $158 million to the Senate Republicans' allied super PAC, which in turn was donated to a pro-Paxton super PAC. Thanks in large part to Musk's donations, the Texas Senate race is now the most expensive non-presidential campaign in US history. Democratic State Rep. James Talarico has blasted Musk, saying the world's richest man "is trying to buy this Senate seat." The Cook Political Report rates the race as a "Toss-Up." Michigan Senate: The focus of the Michigan Senate race is on just about everything else, but don't overlook AI. Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed, a former Wayne County health official, has echoed Sen. Bernie Sanders throughout the campaign. El-Sayed's AI platform is not different. Like Sanders (and Trump), he wants the US government to have equity in frontier labs. El-Sayed also wants to force big companies like Microsoft to divest from AI giants like OpenAI. While that policy is unlikely to pass, El-Sayed has made it clear that if he wins, he intends to play a king-making role in the 2028 Democratic presidential primaries, where Michigan will loom large. Former Congressman Mike Rogers, the Republican hopeful, has called for a pause on data center development in the state. If Republicans want to hold the majority, Rogers will almost certainly need to flip the seat. The Cook Political Report rates the race as a "Toss-Up." California wealth tax: California may make some history of its own. Despite Gov. Gavin Newsom's opposition, advocates were able to get a one-time 5% wealth tax on those with assets over $1 billion on the ballot. If it passes, California, home to the most billionaires, would be the first state in the country to impose such a tax. The proposal has divided the tech community. Google cofounder Sergey Brin has spent over $100 million to try to stop it. Given California's size and its history of counting votes, it could be days before news organizations can project whether the initiative passed. Complicating matters, Brin and other opponents are supporting competing initiatives that would eventually neuter the wealth tax, provided they received more votes. Michigan 7th: Rep. Tom Barrett, a Michigan Republican, is seeking reelection in a southern Michigan district centered around Lansing. William Lawrence, a cofounder of the progressive climate-focused organization Sunrise Movement, has tried to tie Barrett to a proposed $1 billion hyperscale data center near Mason, Michigan. Barrett has said that local officials should be able to make decisions about data centers, contrasting his views with Lawrence's support of a data center moratorium. Cook Political Report rates the race as a "Toss-Up." Ohio 9th: Republicans' hopes to defy history and retain their majority run squarely through Rep. Marcy Kaptur, a 22-term Ohio Democrat, and her northwestern Ohio district that stretches from the Indiana border to just west of Cleveland. Kaptur has criticized state Rep. Derek Merrin for voting in favor of tax incentives for data center development. (Merrin has said Kaptur is "lying" about his record, but as part of a sweeping 2017 budget law, Ohio lawmakers voted to extend the deadline for certain data centers to qualify for tax incentives.) Cook Political Report rates the district as "Lean Democrat." Pennsylvania 1st: Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, a five-term Pennsylvania Republican, romped to reelection two years ago but is now fighting to hang onto his seat. Bucks County commissioner Bob Harvie, the Democratic challenger, focused his first ad of the general election on his call for a data center moratorium. He also blasted Fitzpatrick over the Republican's previous support for a massive Amazon data center in Falls County. The southeastern Pennsylvania district, which includes all of Bucks County, was one of just three districts that are held by a GOP congressman despite also voting for Vice President Kamala Harris. Cook Political Report pegs the race as "Toss-Up." Wisconsin 3rd: Rep. Derrick Van Orden, a two-term Wisconsin Republican, is trying to hold on to his western Wisconsin district, which includes Eau Claire and La Crosse. Democratic nominee Rebecca Cooke, a former political consultant who now works as a waitress, has echoed Sen. Bernie Sanders' call for a federal moratorium on data center development. She has also hammered Van Orden over data centers, who has responded in turn by accusing Cooke of working too closely with tech groups. Democrats have a good chance to flip the seat, which the Cook Political Report rates as just slightly Republican (R+3). In its latest projections, the organization says Van Orden's seat is now "Lean Democrat."
news.summary: From inflation and AI backlash to Elon Musk's record spending on Republicans, here's what's at stake in the 2026 midterm elections.
news.author: Brent D. Griffiths,Madison Hoff

news.title: Trump’s midterm campaign has distilled his vile message | Sidney Blumenthal
news.text:
Far from veering off his track, Trump in his ceaselessly vile midterm campaign statements has attained an optimal level of Trumpism. He has distilled the raw elements of misogyny, racism and nativism to the purified essence of his political philosophy.

The Republican candidates and his vice-president have followed him down the trail of “defining deviancy down”, as explained by Daniel Patrick Moynihan, in his essay in The American Scholar in 1993, about lowering the bar to make abnormal criminal behavior seem normal, coping through denial of its obvious presence, and through that process trivializing “the manifest decline of American civic life”.

Moynihan wrote:“Here is a theory that clearly implies that there are circumstances in which society will choose not to notice behavior that would be otherwise controlled, or disapproved, or even punished.”

Trump’s disinhibition has been on neon display. In nearly every public speech he has delivered in the last month, he has spewed profane or vulgar language. He has directed his obscenities at Democrats, “dumb sons of bitches”, to whom he is going to “shove it up their ass”, but also called Norway a “shithouse country” for not awarding him the Nobel peace prize.

Trump used to hold up Norway as a model Nordic country as opposed to the “shithole countries” of Africa and Haiti. He has lately been confusing his racial disparagement with his personal peeves and forgetting that his trademark denigrating word is “shithole”, not “shithouse”.

Wielding his vulgarity, Trump has refined Maga without excuses. His animus springs from a deep well of resentment, in the beginning considered enticing forbidden fruit by TV talkshow hosts who gave him $2bn in free airtime in 2016. His rants are little different in substance, even if they now are rancid. In escalating his hyperbole, he fails to realize that such excesses have now become self-discrediting.

Alienating Latinos with his ICE roundups, the young men of his now tattered manosophere and working-class swing voters who believed he would benefit them economically, his supposed 2024 coalition is long gone with the wind. He’s down to his last resort.

At his Republican mini convention in September – for a minimum $25,000 attendance fee; $89,000 for a picture with Trump – he demanded that the paying customers raise their right hands to recite after him: “I pledge, to the greatest president in the history of the United States, that loves us so much he can’t even breathe, that I will go out with my family, my friends, I’ll do it any way, I don’t care if I’m registered or not, I’m going try and cheat like hell …”

The bounder from Queens who frenziedly sought the approval of the Manhattan elites, but whose own clownishness and bankruptcies curdled his dearest desire, has risen on inciting his Maga minions against these specters of elitism.

Yet now, the more he gets his Maga followers to dance to YMCA, and show ever greater devotion in the face of self-evident failure, the more his condescension for them leaks out. “I could say the stupidest things, and you’d clap me,” he said on 11 October in Tennessee to a Maga crowd that immediately burst into applause.

Trump’s routine and flagrant lies about his Iran war, as if he attacked out of necessity because Iran was on the verge of developing a deliverable nuclear weapon, are now accompanied by his proposal to rename the strait of Hormuz “the Trump strait”, which he has frequently been calling the “Hormone strait”, perhaps in the recesses of his mind a conflation.

He hails the “greatest” economy, and promises $5,000 to everyone “if the Republicans win”, his unfulfillable lies a series of false incentives.

Trump tosses out the allure of his ridiculous bribes almost as an aside to get to the red meat. On 27 October, after deriding the Democratic candidate for the Senate from Texas falsely as a vegan, Trump yelled: “I love the meat! Ahhh, I love it! Look!” while he rapidly jerked his hand back and forth from his mouth and grunted, closely resembling either clumsily eating a sausage or an act of fellatio.

This disturbing act followed his weeks-long obsession with men’s “asses”, repeated more than a half-dozen times across four states beginning when he leeringly declared about the Republican candidate for the Senate from Ohio Jon Husted on 12 October: “I don’t do this with men very often. I started examining his body … And I looked, and I watched up and down, and I looked at his ass … ”

His hankering for the aesthetics of men’s asses was matched with his expressions of contempt for women’s professional status whether they were Democratic candidates or members of the press. He told female journalists they were “fake”, “dumb”, should “be quiet” and to one: “Your whole outfit is fake, and so are you.”

He referred to the Democratic candidate for the Senate from South Carolina, Annie Andrews, a pediatrician and public health expert, as “Annie Trannie”, and to the Democratic candidate for the Senate from Florida, Angie Nixon, a state representative, as a “very low IQ person” and someone “who can’t speak or think properly”. She is in fine company as the ninth prominent Black official, from Kamala Harris to the supreme court associate justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, whom Trump has called “low IQ”.

These insults are for Trump simply commonplaces. He has reached new territory, however, with his defense of the ad produced by Vivek Ramaswamy, the Ohio Republican candidate, that charged his opponent Amy Acton, a physician and former director of the Ohio department of health, with lying about being raped repeatedly as a 12-year-old girl by her stepfather. In fact, the records show that she was a victim.

In effect, the ad was a cloaked defense of pedophilia. Trump called it “hitting pay dirt”, while JD Vance slammed the ad’s Republican critics for “whining”.

Trump neatly recapped his nostalgic Roy Cohn-era Red Scare, nativism and bigotry in his attacks on Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate for the Senate from Michigan, labeling him a “jihadist lunatic”, a communist and “on the side of the terrorists”. Trump told a Maga crowd to “send him back to where he came from”.

El-Sayed, born in Michigan, was already back where he came from. JD Vance came to Michigan to prove his superiority as a man of the people and an intellectual at the same time to falsely assert that El-Sayed “says not only should we have sharia law, but if you criticize it you’re a white supremacist”.

Mike Rogers, the Republican candidate in Michigan, insistently and falsely claimed that El-Sayed had “pledged his support to the Muslim Brotherhood” and adhered to “this radical Islamic agenda”.

In Kansas, the Republican senator, Roger Marshall, facing a tough challenge from Adam Hamilton, the Democratic candidate and pastor of the largest United Methodist congregation in the country, accused Hamilton of pedophilia: “He pushes drag shows for kids … is that grooming? Yeah, he probably is grooming.”

Perhaps the most pathetic descent of the Republican candidates to validate their credentials in Trump’s cult of personality through imitation was the wan effort of Darline Graham Nordone, whom Trump had induced into the Senate seat in South Carolina left vacant by the death of her brother, Lindsey Graham.

Utterly unprepared for the position, floundering like a broken-winged sparrow, she introduced Trump at a rally on her behalf, by calling her opponent Annie Andrews “batshit crazy”. She had managed to eke out “batshit” to please Trump.

On 27 October, Trump stumped at a rally in Texas for Ken Paxton, the scandal-ridden Republican candidate for the Senate, dangling his $5,000 promise if Republicans win.

“You’ll be my guest at Mar-a-Lago,” Trump said. “The problem is that for $5,000, the most you’ll be able to buy is a hamburger and maybe a small dessert. I’m not even sure you could buy that. No, don’t go there. That’s not a good place if you’re price-conscious.”

And so, Trump mocked his followers and their economic plight, for which they cheered and laughed.

Four days later, Trump staged a lavish jungle-themed Halloween costume and drag party at Mar-a-Lago, with tables spread with caviar and king crab as the “trick-or-treat”, flashing green strobe lights, performers hanging from the ceiling, dancers in full-body spandex animal print leotards, face-painted guests in drag style, some with reptilian headdresses, a live miniature pony and a caged zebra. The House speaker, Mike Johnson, and attorney general, Todd Blanche, were among the revelers.

On 20 April 1945, on the night of Hitler’s last birthday, as the Red Army closed in on Berlin, Hitler held a staid little party with Heinrich Himmler and Hermann Goering after which they fled the capital. Above the Führerbunker, in the Old Reich Chancellery, the staff and officers remaining broke into stores of champagne, played jazz records and held a wild hedonistic party.

An annoyed Hitler trying to sleep below sent an aide up to order them to shut off the phonograph and stop the party. But the Führer’s command was disobeyed. The end was near.

As the Mar-a-Lago Halloween drag party reached a fever pitch, Donald Trump burst in wearing his blue suit and red tie, and flapping open his jacket.

“I came as Donald Trump,” he announced. “I had 10 minutes … rich people spend nine hours getting ready.” He raved with pride: “Look at all my rich members. They spent all day getting ready. Look at these guys.” And he danced to YMCA.

 Sidney Blumenthal, former senior adviser to Bill Clinton and Hillary Clinton, has published three books of a projected five-volume political life of Abraham Lincoln: A Self-Made Man, Wrestling With His Angel and All the Powers of Earth. He is a Guardian US columnist and co-host of the Court of History podcast

The president has spewed vulgar and hateful rhetoric even as he reveals his disdain for his followers

Far from veering off his track, Trump in his ceaselessly vile midterm campaign statements has attained an optimal level of Trumpism. He has distilled the raw elements of misogyny, racism and nativism to the purified essence of his political philosophy.

The Republican candidates and his vice-president have followed him down the trail of “defining deviancy down”, as explained by Daniel Patrick Moynihan, in his essay in The American Scholar in 1993, about lowering the bar to make abnormal criminal behavior seem normal, coping through denial of its obvious presence, and through that process trivializing “the manifest decline of American civic life”.
