news.title: House Of Reps: Democrats Are Trying To Bench-Press Their Way Into Young Men’s Hearts
news.text:
WASHINGTON ― Democrats in the 2024 presidential election lost young men by major margins: 55% of men aged 18-29 backed President Donald Trump, while just 41% backed then-Vice President Kamala Harris. It was a massive shift to the right compared to the 2020 presidential election.

That loss set off waves of teeth-gnashing and introspection in the party, which likes to think of itself as having a youthful, forward-looking sheen. Answers to the problem were proposed: Democrats needed to find a liberal answer to the popular podcaster Joe Rogan, who had endorsed Trump. They needed to moderate on social issues, especially those tied to gender. They needed $20 million to study the problem.

Two years later, polls indicate the party has a massive lead among young men, and even has a shot at winning the votes of men of all ages. No liberal Rogan equivalent has emerged ― even if Rogan and his podcast cohort are significantly less Trump-enthusiastic than they were in 2024. The party has moderated somewhat on immigration and gun control.

How did they do it? There are two possibilities: either Trump’s broken promises on combatting inflation, releasing the Epstein files and ending foreign wars alienated young men. Or Democrats’ seemingly newfound dedication to making gains at the gym is translating into gains at the polls. 

Polling released Sunday showed Michigan U.S. candidate Abdul El-Sayed running almost even among men with his Republican opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers, who had a 10-percentage-point lead among men in the same poll two months ago.

El-Sayed campaigns with a combative rhetorical style, likes to wear tight T-shirts and has made multiple videos of himself working out ― while also insisting he’s not showing off in the same way as Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth or Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., two men who are also fond of filming themselves exercising.

“Being a man is not about how you show up at the gym. It’s like how you show up for your family. It’s about how you show up in your community,” El-Sayed said in one recent video in which he’s standing next to a rack of barbells. 

Other Democratic candidates who’ve posted videos of themselves lifting weights include Colin Allred, Beau Bayh, Jason Crow and Cait Conley.

“Most politicians are weak, bought-and-paid-for by special interests,” Bayh, who is leading in the polls for Indiana secretary of state, says in an ad showing him on a bench press. (He’s the son of Evan Bayh and the grandson of Birch Bayh, both of them former U.S. senators.) 

Trump, meanwhile, has taken to rhapsodizing about Ohio Republican Sen. Jon Husted’s buttocks, which he has described as “a pile of muscle.”

For Democrats, the reps could be paying off. At the very least, they’re not hurting a realignment of younger male voters that would maybe be happening anyway because of widespread dissatisfaction with inflation and Trump’s handling of foreign and domestic policy. 

A nationwide survey of men ages 18 to 30 released in September found Democrats had a 17-point advantage among the young men most motivated to vote. 

“Young men have definitely swung back away from Trump more fervently than just about any other demographic in the electorate. Part of it is just pure thermostatic politics, but most of it, I think, is Trump’s own doing,” Charlie Sabgir, director of Young Men Research Project, told HuffPost, adding that voters linked Trump’s war in Iran to the higher cost of gas. 

Sabgir also pointed to a recent analysis finding male podcasters talking much less about the president lately. 

“Trump himself has definitely lost a lot of his kind of masculine appeal, however you want to call it, his kind of cultural cachet,” Sabgir said. 

As for El-Sayed, the Michigan Democrat made a concerted effort to appeal to younger male voters since launching his campaign last year. One of his videos showed him getting a spot on the bench press from Hasan Piker, a socialist Twitch streamer and fitness enthusiast who lamented there are more millionaires in America than men who can bench 225 pounds. (That’s the amount Bayh benches in his ad; in this video El-Sayed put up 315 for one rep.) Maybe the macho habits have helped El-Sa win over voters. 

“There’s no evidence that it has not helped him,” Sabgir said. 

But El-Sayed has caught a ton of flak for his association with Piker. His former opponent in the Democratic primary, Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.), cited Piker as a reason for her shock endorsement of Republican Mike Rogers, even after El-Sayed distanced himself from the streamer. Is it possible Piker has helped El-Sayed’s numbers?

“I’m not everybody’s cup of tea, right? I know what my role is,” Piker told HuffPost in August. “My role is to get people who are under the age of 45, who are disillusioned with politics, who are just not usually invested in politics, to be primed and activated for the right kinds of candidates and for the right kinds of policies.”

Billy Begala, executive director of the Speaking with American Men project, a Democrat-backed initiative that researches political shifts among men ages 18 to 29, said young men’s opinions of Trump have “completely inverted” since the start of 2025. At the time of Trump’s inauguration, young men believed his presidency would make a positive difference in their lives by a 33-point margin, he said. Today, that number has plummeted to a negative 35-point margin.

In other words, “a devastating −68-point swing,” Begala told HuffPost. “The fling young men had with the right — which helped Trump win young men by 14 points in 2024 — is resoundingly over.”

The reasons why? Trump didn’t follow through on his promises to make their wages stretch further, make homeownership more accessible, bring down the cost of living and end foreign wars.

“On each point, Republicans have betrayed these young men,” Begala added, “and they have taken notice.”

news.title: Surging ICE raids shadow final weeks of California congressional race  - St. Vincent Tribune – Daily St
news.text:
Bakersfield, California – In a nondescript car park, a memorial with orange marigolds and prayer candles has been erected in honour of recently deceased labour organiser and civil rights leader Dolores Huerta.

Huerta was a well-known figure in California’s Central Valley, where she helped found the United Farm Workers union (UFW) and win better wages and working conditions for migrant and Latino labourers, who were vital to the state’s huge agricultural sector in the 1960s and 1970s.

The term “si, se puede”, coined by Huerta and translating to “yes, it can be done”, has also been placed on the display of a local theatre in her honour.

If Huerta represents a tradition of social and economic justice and labour organising that continues to resonate, an uptick in immigration raids across the valley over the last month has underscored the degree to which insecurity, both economic and political, remains a stubborn reality for many of the region’s agricultural workers.

Since early October, federal immigration agents, often masked and in unmarked vehicles, have fanned out across the Central Valley as part of a 45-day effort titled “Operation Save California” by the Trump administration.

Those raids, part of the administration’s mass deportation campaign, have become a flashpoint in the race for California’s 22nd congressional district, one of several contests in the state that Democrats hope will help deliver them a majority in the United States House of Representatives in the midterm elections on November 3.

While Republican incumbent David Valadao has been a fixture of the Central Valley for years, winning six of his last seven races, progressive challenger Randy Villegas is seeking to capitalise on popular frustration over the rising cost of living, healthcare cuts and immigration raids.

In a small building down the road from the Huerta memorial in Bakersfield, one day before the election, a room full of volunteers chant her slogan, encouraged by labour leaders and Democratic representatives such as California Senators Adam Schiff and Alex Padilla, before they knock on doors.

“I’ve spoken to local business owners who have told me how their businesses are now struggling as a result of these ICE raids, and many of them have now pivoted to delivering things like groceries,” Villegas told Al Jazeera, noting that some residents are afraid of leaving their homes amid the increase in raids.

“It’s having an impact on people who just want to go to work, want to go to school,” he added.

‘Unlawfully targeted’

Immigration authorities say the raids have targeted criminals and deny that they are racially discriminatory.

“Allegations that DHS law enforcement engages in ‘racial profiling’ are disgusting, reckless, and categorically FALSE,” the Department of Homeland Security said in an email. “What makes someone a target for immigration enforcement is if they are illegally in the US – NOT their skin colour, race, or ethnicity.”

But the administration’s depiction of targeted operations focused on people with serious criminal backgrounds is at odds with accounts from farmworkers, labour organisations, local officials, and advocacy groups, who describe aggressive methods and a dragnet approach.

“These are not criminals. These are hard-working, long-term members of our communities being unlawfully targeted simply for looking Latino and working class,” Teresa Romero, president of the UFW, whose members have campaigned for Villegas, said in a statement on October 10.

“We are seeing car windows being smashed and farm workers dragged from vehicles in the middle of the road while on their way to work.”

A woman who spoke with Al Jazeera over the phone on condition of anonymity said her husband, a farmworker in Fresno County, had been detained by immigration agents while returning home from work during the first week of October.

“I understand that if they [those arrested] are criminals or have done bad things, they have brought it on themselves,” the woman said of immigration arrests over a phone call. “But my husband has not done anything. The only thing he has done is work.”

She adds that her four children, all of whom are citizens born in the US, became anxious after the incident, and that some now begin to cry when they hear a knock at the door and fear that their mother will be taken away as well.

‘Word spreads’

Local officials say such stories have reverberated through their communities.

“When you have a small community like ours, and folks are actually detained, word spreads,” said Olivia Calderon, mayor of the city of Arvin.

“I had pastors ask me whether ICE takes a day off on Sunday because people don’t want to go to church,” she added.

Villegas has drawn a link between the raids and Valadao’s vote in favour of a bill that is set to transform ICE, often accused of excessive force and disregard for civil liberties in its operations, into the most well-funded law enforcement agency in the country.

Asked about the impact of the raids in a debate with Villegas in early October, Valadao responded by mirroring the government’s claims that many of those targeted have criminal backgrounds and that “it is what it is.”

As Republicans and Democrats jostle for control of the House, the race has also received national attention.

Prominent figures such as leftist Senator Bernie Sanders, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and Republican House Speaker Mike Johnson have visited in recent months to rally in support of their respective candidates.

Labour organisations, such as UFW, have also mobilised members to knock doors for Villegas.

But polls suggest a tight race between Valadao and Villegas, even after a partisan redistricting measure passed by California voters in 2025 resulted in a series of newly drawn maps, including parts of the 22nd district, meant to favour Democrats.

Valadao has proven himself to be a resilient candidate. His upbringing in the Central Valley, where his Portuguese parents settled and worked as dairy farmers, has helped him build close ties with ranchers, growers, and conservative voters who play an influential role in the region. While California in general is a bastion of support for the Democratic Party, rural areas are often favourable terrain for Republicans.

While Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris defeated Donald Trump in California by nearly 20 points in 2024, Trump carried Kern County, where Bakersfield is located, by a similar margin.

Still, Villegas and his supporters are hoping that concerns over the rising cost of living, driven in part by the Trump administration’s decision to launch a war on Iran that has sent energy prices soaring, will help him dislodge the resilient Republican incumbent.

Priscilla Ortega, a 23-year-old in the city of Lamont, said she is “annoyed and very angry” about rising prices and the impact of immigration raids.

“It was really unnecessary,” she said of the war on Iran, adding that rising fuel costs have made her commute to her job as a warehouse worker in the region much more expensive.

“That could have gone to food for my household or bills that need to be paid,” she added. “People are sick of the prices increasing.”

news.title: House Election Tracker: 5 Key Races to Watch on Midterm Election Night
news.text: Democrats are hoping to erase Republicans' narrow majority in the House of Representatives in the 2026 midterm elections on Tuesday, when all 435 House races are up for grabs. Republicans currently hold 218 House seats to Democrats' 214, with one independent and two vacancies, so Democrats only need to flip a few seats to win control of the chamber. Democrats enter Election Day optimistic about their chances of flipping control of the House, as the party outside of the White House historically has picked up seats in the midterms when the president is unpopular. That is the case for Presisdent Donald Trump, whose approval has suffered amid voter frustration with the state of the economy and cost of living. Only a fraction of the 435 contests are expected to determine the outcome. Roughly 50 House races were expected to be competitive, stretching from battleground districts in Arizona and California to Colorado, Michigan and Pennsylvania. A Democratic takeover would establish a major check on the Trump administration. It would give Democrats the ability to block legislation passed without bipartisan support, while opening the door to congressional investigations of the Trump administration. Meanwhile, a continued Republican majority would preserve the GOP's control of the lower chamber and strengthen Trump's ability to pursue his legislative agenda. On the eve of the election, the Cook Political Report classified 18 races as being pure toss-ups, with an additional 18 in each category for Lean Democratic and Lean Republican. An additional 18 races were classified as being Likely Democratic, with 17 landing in the Likely Republican column. The forecaster gives Democrats an overall edge to take the House, favoring them in 222 races. But those toss-ups will have major implications for the size of the potential Democratic majority. A larger one would give the party more of a mandate to block the administration's actions as well as more cushioning on major votes where some Democrats may defect. A handful of races in states that are called early could signal how deep Democrats are able to penetrate Trump-won districts. Here is a look at the dynamics at play in five of the races to watch early in the night. Kentucky's 6th District One of the earliest tests of the night will be in Kentucky's 6th District, which Trump carried by 15 points in 2024. It's based around Lexington and it suburbs and is seen as a toss-up by the Cook Political Report. Democrat Zach Dembo and Republican Ralph Alvarado are running to succeed Representative Andy Barr, who is running for Senate. Democrats don't need to flip this district to win a majority, and victory in such a conservative district would be seen as a significant upset even in a strong year for them. But the margins here could be an early signal. If Democrats outright win the race or even come within a few points of the seat, it would be a major red flag for Republicans about how the rest of the night may go. But if Alvarado wins more comfortably, it could be seen as an early sign that Democrats may not get as large of a majority as they would hope. The district is notably important because Kentucky, along with Indiana, is the first state where polls close at 6 p.m. ET. Of course, no single district is going to completely tell the story of the midterms, as local factors and candidate quality could also sway any given race. But this contest has emerged as a major bellwether that will be closely watched by analysts early in the night. North Carolina's 1st District Republicans redrew the district held by Democratic Representative Don Davis as part of mid-decade redistricting. Under current lines, Trump won the seat by about 3 points. But in the new district used for this year's elections, Trump won by about 12 points, a more conservative seat based around eastern North Carolina. Democrats are primed to have a good night in the Tar Heel State. Former Governor Roy Cooper, a Democrat, has emerged as a clear favorite in the Senate race, despite the state backing Trump by about 3 points two years earlier. This seat will test whether Democrats are able to win back voters in rural Southern states, a question facing Democrats in Senate contests in places like Mississippi and South Carolina. It also tests the power of an established incumbent whose district was changed significantly in redistricting. A key question the GOP faces this year is whether its redistricting arms race was really worth any gains, and this seat, a top target, could prove crucial to that test. The Cook Political Report classifies it as a toss-up. In addition, North Carolina's 11th District in the western part of the state, held by GOP Representative Chuck Edwards, is also competitive. The Asheville-based district is seen as Leans Democratic by the Cook Political Report, with Democrat Jamie Ager being seen as the favorite over Republican Jennifer Balkcom, who became the nominee after Edwards announced his withdrawal earlier in the year. Pennsylvania's 1st District There are four Pennsylvania House races that are competitive and could be seen as important bellwethers, but Pennsylvania's 1st District is an important gauge into how far the blue wave could sweep. Republican Representative Brian Fitzpatrick won reelection by nearly 13 points in 2024, even as former Vice President Kamala Harris narrowly edged out Trump in the district. Fitzpatrick, a moderate, is among the GOP's top overperformers, who year after year has defeated Democratic challengers despite the seat's blue tinge. If Fitzpatrick loses to Democratic challenger Bob Harvie, it would be a sign that even entrenched Republican incumbents are at risk across the country. The race is seen as a toss-up by the Cook Political Report, which shifted the race out of the Lean Republican column last week, in the final stretch of the campaign. Pennsylvania's 7th and 10th Districts are both seen as particularly important races for Democrats. In the 7th District, based around Allentown, Republican Representative Ryan Mackenzie, who flipped the seat in 2024, is facing a challenge from Democrat Bob Brooks. In the 10th District, Republican Representative Scott Perry faces a rematch against Democrat Janelle Stelson, who nearly unseated Perry in 2024 despite Trump winning the seat by 5 points. If those two seats don't flip, Democrats may be facing a more difficult night, as they're both Lean Democratic in the Cook report. In Pennsylvania's 8th District race, GOP Representative Rob Bresnahan—who also flipped the seat in 2024—faces a challenge from Scranton Mayor Paige Cognetti, marking another toss-up to watch. Texas' 15th District South Texas was one of the Republican Party's greatest triumphs in the 2024 election. But two years later, those gains are now threatened to be wiped out. The region, with a large Hispanic population, has long voted for Democrats but flipped to Trump in the most recent election. But polling suggests the president's support among Hispanic voters has waned. Texas' 15th District is one race to watch to gauge whether Republicans' inroads with these voters will hold, or if there will be a significant reversion to Democrats. Trump carried the seat by 18 points. Republican Representative Monica De La Cruz is facing a challenge from Democrat Bobby Pulido in what has emerged as a toss-up in the Cook Political Report. Democrats will need a strong Hispanic reversion to flip this seat. There are several other races in Texas and other states where a Hispanic reversion would spell trouble for Republicans. In Texas, a shift back to Democrats would all leave Republicans facing tougher odds in the 23rd, 28th, 34th and 35th Districts. All backed Trump in 2024 but were once seen as more competitive. Strong margins in South Texas could also bode well for Democrats James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa in the Senate and governor's race, respectively, which will be among the most closely watched contests. Virginia's 1st District Virginia's 1st District was one that barely shifted from 2020 to 2024, even as the national trends shifted significantly toward the GOP. Suburban areas outside of Richmond did not see significant rightward movement, with Chesterfield County actually shifting leftward, defying national trends. Democrats hope that could leave GOP Representative Rob Wittman vulnerable against Henrico County Prosecutor Shannon Taylor in the suburban seat that backed Trump by only about 5 points in 2024. This seat will test the durability of Democrats' gains in wealthy suburbs over the past decade against another Republican who has historically overperformed. The race is a toss-up, according to the Cook Political Report. It borders two other important districts as well. In Virginia's 2nd District, Republican Representative Jen Kiggans faces former Democratic Representative Elaine Luria, who lost reelection in 2022. Trump carried the seat by less than half a percentage point in 2024, and the race is seen as Lean Democratic by Cook. Meanwhile, forecasters have also seen a more competitive-than-expected race in Virginia's 5th District, where GOP Representative John McGuire faces former Democratic Representative Tom Perriello. Cook considers it Lean Republican, but Sabato's Crystal Ball recently shifted it to the Leans Democratic column, despite early expectations that McGuire may face an easy race. Democrats' Must-Win Pickups There are 16 seats held by Republicans where Democrats are favored to win in the midterms, according to the Cook Political Report. These races are true must-wins for Democrats to have a chance of winning a House majority, especially because not every seat Democrats currently hold are guaranteed to stay in their hands. In fact, Democrats are expected to lose at least a handful of seats due to redistricting in states like Florida, Louisiana, Tennessee and Texas. Democrats losing any of these seats would be a red flag that they may not enjoy as much of a blue wave as they would have hoped. These top-tier pickups include NC-11, PA-07, PA-10 and VA-02. On the East Coast, this includes New Jersey's 7th District, where GOP Representative Tom Kean Jr., whose monthslong absence from the House garnered national attention, faces Democrat Rebecca Bennett. There are four seats in the Midwest where Democrats are seen as favorites to flip. Those include Iowa's 1st District, where Representative Mariannette Miller-Meeks faces a rematch against Democrat Christina Bohannan in what was among the closest races of 2024, and Iowa's 3rd District, where Democrat Sarah Trone Garriott is challenging GOP Representative Zach Nunn. Both are Leans Democratic in the Cook report. Cook also classifies Wisconsin's 3rd District—where Democrat Rebecca Cooke is locked in a rematch against Republican Representative Derrick Van Orden—as Leans Democratic. Cooke lost by fewer than 3 points in 2024, even as Trump carried the district by 7 points. Nebraska's 2nd District, where Democrat Denise Powell and Republican Brinker Harding are competing to succeed GOP Representative Don Bacon, is seen as Likely Democratic. There are also a number of these seats in the West, where results may be posted later Tuesday night ET. Democrats are favored to flip two seats in Arizona, which are rated Leans Democratic. Democrat Amish Shah is favored over Republican Jay Feely in Arizona's 1st District, an open seat, while Democrat JoAnna Mendoza is seen as having an edge over Republican Representative Juan Ciscomani in Arizona's 6th District. Colorado's 8th District, based around northern Denver suburbs, is another must-win. Democrat Manny Rutinel is challenging first-term Republican Representative Gabe Evans in the swing seat. Meanwhile, in California, Democrats are expected to easily win the 1st, 6th and 41st Districts due to redistricting. California's 48th District is seen as Lean Democratic. Democrat Marni Von Wilpert and Republican Jim Desmond are vying for the Southern California seat that became more Democratic in redistricting, backing Harris by about 3 points. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Samantha Beech, Gray R. Thomas, Edward T. Cummins
news.summary: Republicans enter the final stretch holding 218 House seats to Democrats’ 214.

news.title: Sharp Left Turn: Democrats Have a Shot to Take Congress on Socialist Momentum
news.text:
Democrats are on the verge of reversing their political fortunes. The party is heading into the midterm elections Tuesday under the kind of conditions campaign consultants dream of, after two years wielding hardly more power than a strongly worded letter.

Donald Trump has spent the erratic waning years of his presidency leading his party into a political wilderness by waging a deeply unpopular war on Iran and driving the cost of living ever higher. Republicans who enjoy a governing trifecta have tried to distance themselves from the party’s decision-making and its leader, a once-animating force who has turned himself into a liability. Poll after poll says the same: Democrats are poised to take control of one or both houses of Congress — and spend the next two years thwarting Trump’s agenda.

But after a primary season dominated by an ascendant left wing and a broader rejection of centrist politics, the question isn’t just whether Democrats win on Tuesday. It’s what kind of Democratic Party emerges on Wednesday morning. 

“I really like the socialism aspects,” said Gibrel Said, a supporter of Abdul El-Sayed at his closing rally in Detroit Monday night. In the marquee contest serving as a referendum on the Democratic Party’s future, the Michigan Democratic Senate nominee espouses progressive politics and has often been associated with the the left’s agenda-setting socialists, though he doesn’t identify as one. His race has been rocked by the kind of left-versus-right identity crisis that presents a perennial challenge for Democrats. 

“One, Medicare for All; two, how do we fund things that help us as constituents,” Said told The Intercept, ticking off things he appreciates about the candidate. Said, who lives in the Arab enclave of Dearborn, Michigan, especially praised El-Sayed’s willingness to buck party leadership and speak out on U.S.–Israel policy. “Instead of tiptoeing around the subject, he very adamantly says, hey there’s a genocide happening here, we shouldn’t send our money.”

Cycle after cycle, in state after state, an insurgent band of Democrats critical of the political establishment’s ties to corporate interests and its unflinching commitment to Israel has had to overcome the barriers erected by its own party’s centrist leadership. Both sides present themselves as the true representatives of working people: the centrists by arguing that more transformative ideas will scare off lower-information voters, the left by saying they represent the masses.

How much of this trickles down to actual voters? On Monday, The Intercept followed canvassers and spoke to voters in Michigan, Maine, and Texas, asking about which issues had permeated and taking the temperature of voter enthusiasm. Some rolled their eyes at the spats that have dominated the headlines, dismissing the idea that eleventh-hour backstabbing would make a difference. Others regurgitated right-wing misinformation. Many complained of too many campaign mailers.

“They’re wicked mean,” said Sharon McDonnell, a supporter of Troy Jackson, the Democratic Senate nominee in Maine. Speaking to The Intercept in the town of Yarmouth, she described one mailer that included a photo of Jackson chomping a cigar and describing him as “evil.” “It’s just nasty.”

In Maine, the party’s left flank seized power in the nominating process for the Democratic Senate candidate — then fought to hang onto it after onetime rising star Graham Platner flamed out after a sexual assault allegation (which he denies). With Jackson, a former state Senate leader, Maine now offers progressives one of two opportunities to test their message at the Senate level, where a candidate has to secure appeal statewide, not just in deep-blue House districts.

The other is Michigan, where the intraparty battle is still raging. Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., demolished her past attempts at fence-mending when she endorsed Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers on Sunday and abandoned El-Sayed, who beat Stevens in a Michigan primary that saw $30 million in outside spending from the super PAC for the American Israel Public Affairs Committee. 

The dustup has had Democrats biting their nails and moderate party leaders making the cable news circuit to demand party discipline — this time, to scold a centrist. The party leads in the polls for 218 of the 435 seats up for grabs in the House of Representatives, but they need to perform well in seven key states — Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, and Texas, in addition to Maine and Michigan — if they want to win the Senate. 

“I think she’s counterintuitively, perhaps, given people a reason to rally some more,” said Kathleen Britton, an El-Sayed supporter at the Detroit rally on Monday, of Stevens. “I really don’t think it’s gonna help Mike Rogers.”

Earlier that day, in a predominantly Black neighborhood of Detroit, a prominent Black supporter of El-Sayed preparing to knock on voters’ doors described Stevens’s endorsement as an “ego-driven statement.”

Mike Bland, the executive director of the Black Men Vote PAC, highlighted that Stevens made her public endorsement of Rogers in a Black church in Detroit. He doubted that Stevens, whose criticism of El-Sayed centers primarily on his skepticism of the U.S. relationship with the state of Israel, would be able to pull Black voters to Rogers, a conservative former House representative whose campaign has repeatedly peddled anti-Muslim tropes against El-Sayed.

“How can I say this without cursing? She used a Black church as a prop, and we have seen that time and time again,” Bland said. “Black folks aren’t stupid.”

Over the past month, El-Sayed has rallied with Barack Obama and Kamala Harris, the two most prominent Black politicians in America — and hardly radicals estranged from the establishment power center. At the same time that Stevens was making her endorsement of Rogers public, El-Sayed was attending a get-out-the-vote event at another church in Detroit. The two primary foes were supposed to appear together that day with Rep. Jim Clyburn, D-S.C.

One of the Democrats’ most coveted Senate pickups didn’t present much of an opportunity for the left in the primary, but it has still been characterized by intraparty animosity.

In Texas, where both Democratic Senate primary contenders espoused relatively moderate politics, outgoing Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D-Texas, has declined to campaign with state Rep. James Talarico, though she endorsed him after he beat her in the state’s March Democratic primary.

Talarico has been performing well with Latino voters, a massive voting bloc that helped fuel his primary victory. But Crockett — who, unlike Stevens, is Black — has suggested that Talarico has not done enough to excite Black voters, a demographic she carried in the primary. On a canvassing operation targeting Black voters in the Dallas–Fort Worth area on Monday, few Black Texans who spoke to The Intercept expressed excitement for Talarico. But most had already voted for him, saying they were motivated to do their civic duty. 

Black voters frequently discussed concerns over affordability, gas prices, and homelessness. Canvassers told The Intercept they had heard some of those voters express concerns over their perception of Talarico’s policies toward transgender children, at times espousing blatant misinformation, such as the idea that Talarico supported arresting parents who refused to give their children gender-affirming surgeries. 

“ I don’t stand for that,” said voter Jermiah Robinson, referring to her belief that Talarico pushed “sex-change” surgery for minors. Like many voters, she cited the cost of living as her most pressing issue. Robinson said she would “want to vote for him if he stands by his words, and he’s actually like ‘Yeah, I’ll help out as far as prices and everything.’” 

Talarico appears to have improved his margins with Black voters in the final stretch. According to the Texas Politics Project at the University of Texas, Talarico is leading with 79 percent of the Black vote, signaling a significant increase in support from Black voters from just last month. The conventional wisdom suggests that he could barely ask for a better opponent than the scandal-plagued Republican candidate, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. 

In 2015, Paxton was indicted on felony securities fraud charges in Texas, in a case that dragged on for roughly nine years, and ended with Paxton being required to do community service and pay restitution. And in 2023, the Texas House of Representatives voted across party lines to impeach him as attorney general for alleged corruption and retaliation against whistleblowers.

Scandal kept rocking the race for Senate in Maine, where longtime Republican incumbent Sen. Susan Collins faces her toughest reelection challenge yet from Jackson. Before Jackson, who lost a race this cycle for the state’s Democratic nomination for governor, there was Platner, hailed early as a working-class champion who faced a series of personal scandals in his successful primary campaign. There was the revelation of a Nazi tattoo that he claimed not to understand until last October. There were crudely worded Reddit posts and stories of cruelty from women he’d dated. One former girlfriend’s allegations of sexual assault ultimately ended his campaign — and set off a scramble to find a replacement that progressives ultimately won by elevating Jackson. 

By Monday, Mainers who spoke to The Intercept appeared exhausted by the lengthy, contentious, and expensive Senate race that has dominated the state.

“There’s a lot of fatigue. People are tired of it,“ said Charlie Dingman, who chairs the state Democratic Party. “I have had some conversations at doors with people that have led me to think that the extremely negative and extremely untruthful ads may be backfiring.”

Tyler Echard, in Norway, said he’d already cast an absentee ballot for Democrats down the ticket. He was disgusted with a deluge of political mailers and eager to stop seeing them pile up on his doorstep.

“The amount of mailers we get — just mailers, not just handed at the door but in the mail — especially from the Republican side, the amount of money is probably more than I will make in my lifetime, spent in this election,” Echard said. “At some point, we gotta get legislation because money’s just gonna run everything into the ground. I ain’t got it, so I can’t influence it.”

Frustration with the status quo in Congress could spell the end for Collins’s 30-year career in the Senate. On Monday, a University of New Hampshire poll found Jackson leading Collins by 4 percentage points. And in September, Collins found herself thrust into a scandal of her own, when ProPublica revealed that the FBI anti-corruption squad was investigating an alleged pay-to-play scheme between Collins and a donor eager to secure government contracts.

The Intercept later exposed that, alongside a series of campaign donations, defense contractors cozy with Collins had received lucrative carveouts in defense spending. (Collins has denied wrongdoing in all cases.)

But the incumbent senator has faced controversy and come out victorious before. And some Mainers doubt they’ll see change either way.

“I can’t vote for either side,” said a man, who declined to share his name with The Intercept, walking down a rural road in Norway with a hunting rifle slung over his shoulder. “You can’t trust neither of them.”

news.title: Fateful moment is at hand for Trump presidency
news.text:
Midterm elections are always a verdict on a sitting president. But the 2026 edition could become something rarer and more significant — a catalyst that points the way to a new political era.

Tuesday’s election is critical for Trump’s presidency and legacy. It could either sustain the MAGA movement’s decadelong grip on national life or initiate its decline. It could result in redemption for Democrats two years after their crushing defeat in the last presidential election. And in both parties, it will demarcate the opening chapters of the 2028 presidential race.

The midterms are the first chance for voters to place some constitutional restraints on a freewheeling president who has the most aggressive view of executive power in modern times.

If Democrats win back the House of Representatives or the Senate on Tuesday, Trump will face a seismic tide of investigations: into his conduct; his Cabinet; alleged government corruption; his legacy construction spree; turmoil at the Pentagon; and his own fortune, which has swelled since he returned to the White House.

More broadly, the election is also a referendum on nearly two divisive years in which Trump has sought to dismantle swaths of the federal government and used the power of his office to target political enemies. Abroad, he’s replaced traditional global leadership with America First nationalism while starting a new Middle East war; fraternizing with Russian and Chinese dictators; and carrying out extrajudicial killings of alleged traffickers in the Pacific and Caribbean.

But Democrats also have a lot at stake as they tried to repair a brand tarnished by high inflation and lax border security under President Joe Biden’s administration and the chaos of his aborted reelection bid.

For voters to trust them again, they must prove they’re more than just anti-Trump; they must deliver results at a frantic political moment and despite a president who will put up ferocious resistance. Failure would invite voters’ wrath in 2028.

Election Day could also turn into a crucible for US democracy itself. Trump has already challenged the conduct of elections in Alaska and California and drawn comparisons to his effort to overturn the 2020 election by signaling last week that he’d accept the results of the midterms only if he deems them fair.

But most importantly, the elections are a chance for politicians to listen to the people whom they often seem to forget they serve. Millions of Americans are desperate for relief from the costs of food, housing and healthcare and feel rising anxiety about the possible impact of AI on their job security.

Trump’s strange campaign

Trump is the most unorthodox president of modern times. But his decision to make the election about his performance amid a deeply unpopular war and boiling public dissatisfaction with his decisions was iconoclastic even for him.

His erratic final pitch, delivered on a journey through wobbling GOP districts in red states, touched on almost everything but the economic issue voters care about most. He boasted about the new ballroom he’s building at the White House; bizarrely lauded the backside of Ohio Sen. John Husted; and lashed out with some of the most explicit anti-Muslim and bigoted rhetoric of any US election campaign.

On Sunday, the president shrugged off polls showing Democrats heavily favored to recapture the House and threatening multiple Republican senators in states he won by wide margins, instead promising a triumph for the GOP on Tuesday night.

“A vote for any Democrat anywhere in the country is a vote to put a deranged group of extremists into power and it could really hurt us, and we are not going to let anything hurt us, because we have the greatest country right now,” Trump said in Iowa. House Speaker Mike Johnson, at Trump’s side, vowed, “We are going to win and shock the world on Tuesday night. I believe it.”

But if voters react badly to Trump’s depiction of a new economic “golden age” and evident indifference to their struggles, he will be consigned to a lonely political plight — shocking even for a man once subject to multiple criminal cases. His self-themed campaign would make it an unusually personal blow, especially if his handpicked Senate candidates lose in states like Texas and Georgia. The idea that Trumpism has permanently changed politics would be called into question, and the GOP would be plunged into soul-searching over its future direction.

And next year, the isolation would become more acute under the relentless pressure of Democratic investigations after the end of a rubber-stamp Republican Congress.

A Democratic victory would turn into a fateful test

A good night for Democrats would count as a political earthquake only two years after Trump staged one of history’s greatest comebacks by beating Democratic nominee Kamala Harris to win a nonconsecutive second term.

Yet even if the party were to win both chambers, Trump will still enjoy considerable clout, including with expansive constitutional authority to conduct foreign policy. The president’s history of spurning checks and balances means he’d fight any attempt by Democrats in Congress to rein in his powers, with showdowns likely over the war, budgets and policy-making.

But if Democrats rack up the net gain of four seats needed to win the Senate, they will acquire the ability to block Trump’s campaign to complete his conservative transformation of the judiciary and potentially to fill any new Supreme Court vacancy.

And any potential Democratic majorities could also challenge Trump on his conduct of the war with Iran — which he is waging without congressional authorization — and funding for military operations if he has failed to end the conflict by the time new lawmakers are seated on January 3.

“Right now, (it) is about stabilizing the country itself and providing some check against not just an out-of-control presidency and a corrupt presidency but everyone’s costs,” Democratic Sen. Brian Schatz told CNN’s Kasie Hunt last month. “Diesel, gasoline agricultural products, consumer products … everything is up, and I think people want to see us do not everything but a few things that will take the pain out of what they’re experiencing.”

But while the loss of Congress could turn Trump into a lame duck, he’s unlikely to act like one. The history of his first term suggests pitched legal battles over congressional subpoenas and attempts by Democratic investigators to penetrate deep into the administration and trawl for evidence in his family finances.

The president’s veto power, and the requirement for 60 votes to pass major legislation in the Senate, means Trump will be able to temper Democratic hopes for sweeping change.

Lessons for 2028 are already being drawn

The midterm results will also shape the 2028 presidential race likely to explode into life as soon as the votes are counted.

A huge GOP defeat could raise doubts about whether Trumpism will outlast Trump’s political career. Potential presidential candidates such as Vice President JD Vance would confront the delicate task of separating themselves politically from a president who remains a hero to the grassroots but who, according to polls, has lost the rest of the country’s confidence on almost every issue.

Democrats lining up for a tilt at their party’s presidential nomination will parse midterm results for winning messages. Key figures such as Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro could enhance credentials with thumping reelection wins.

The election aftermath is sure to reignite the party’s debate over ideology. If progressive candidates like Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed win their races, movement leaders such as New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez will argue the country is ready to embrace more left-wing policies on healthcare and the economy.

The schism between progressives and moderates burst into the open on Sunday when defeated Michigan Democratic primary candidate Haley Stevens sensationally endorsed Republican nominee Mike Rogers over El-Sayed, ostensibly amid a clash over Israel.

Midterms polls also show limited public confidence that Democrats can meaningfully reorient the nation. A 2026 victory would therefore turn into a 2028 audition.

“The Democrats have to prove in 2027 they have won,” former White House chief of staff Rahm Emanuel told CNN’s Brianna Keilar last week. “I’m for comprehensive hearings, follow the money, everything. Venezuela … the Russian money, the oil, all these deals,” said Emanuel, a possible 2028 Democratic presidential primary candidate.

“But if you don’t do ethics reform, you haven’t delivered change. … If you don’t deliver a rise in the minimum wage, you haven’t addressed affordability.”

This is the risk for Democratic leaders: Trump’s intractability and veto power could reduce them to passing endless affordability bills that go nowhere. That won’t impress angry voters.

But that’s for next year, if Democrats win.

The last rites of the midterms must first play out. And Trump still doesn’t seem to get the message. In a telling symbol of obliviousness, he’ll deliver his closing argument in Washington on Monday at the National Mall’s Reflecting Pool, which was just repaired at great expense and which showcases his legacy fixation.

With millions of Americans in need of tangible economic relief, the event may deliver an eloquent explanation of why Trump and the GOP risk a painful reckoning on Election Day.

news.title: Democrats poised for midterm gains, but how big?
news.text:
Democrats are expected to make gains in Congress, governors' mansions, and statehouses nationwide on Nov. 3, but how far and wide the so-called "blue wave" will reach remains uncertain.

In addition to expected wins in traditional battlegrounds such as North Carolina, Democrats hope a so-called "blue wave'' will wash over states President Donald Trump won by double digits in 2024, such as Texas, Kansas and Ohio. The Trump administration and its allies shifted resources to shore up historically conservative strongholds, while giving up on keeping the tide from wiping out vulnerable suburban Republicans, such as Rep. Tom Kean Jr., R-New Jersey.

In anticipation of the midterm elections, which typically benefit the party out of the White House, many Republican-led state legislatures redrew congressional districts to bolster their party's odds. Even so, every nonpartisan projection shows Democrats heavily favored to win a majority in the House of Representatives.

More: Cook Political Report shifts 14 races toward Dems ahead of midterms

Whether Democrats will also win a majority in the Senate, despite needing to flip seats in at least three states Trump carried in 2024, remains less certain but increasingly likely.

An unpopular incumbent president

A big reason for Republicans' grim outlook is related to Trump's popularity, whose job approval poll numbers have sunk to historic lows. A Fox News survey released Oct. 14 found Trump's approval rating at 36%, while 64% of registered voters said they disapproved of his job performance. That marks the lowest approval rating he has received in the network's polling during either of his two terms.

Typically, when a president's job numbers are below 50%, their party loses an average of 36 seats, according to Gallup, a leading pollster.

More: What if polls are wrong? Projected Dem wins depend on their accuracy

Other critical measures of voter confidence about the country's direction have also plummeted amid skyrocketing fuel costs spurred by a war with Iran, which infuriated voters who trusted Trump's campaign promises to halve energy costs in his first year in office, "end" inflation, make groceries cheaper and “stop wars” instead of starting them overseas.

The University of Michigan's consumer sentiment index, which has tracked how Americans feel about the economy for nearly 80 years, recorded its second-lowest score in history in October.

Democrats have pounced on affordability in campaign speeches, political advertisements and debates.

"So many broken promises," Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Georgia, said during an Oct. 7 rally in Savannah. "More people are unemployed; the wars are still raging; the debt is exploding; (and) prices are going up."

Ossoff is the only Democratic senator seeking reelection in a state Trump won in 2024. Polls show him running away with what was once considered Republicans' best opportunity to pick up a Senate seat.

Tatishe Nteta, a political science professor at the University of Massachusetts Amherst and director of UMass Poll, said Trump has become the central figure across multiple demographics and areas ahead of what could be the worst midterm debacle since the 2006 elections amid President George W. Bush's second term.

"If we're correctly capturing the sentiment of Americans, then what we're seeing is a repudiation of President Trump and his agenda, his policies and his vision for the future of the country," Nteta said. "And this is affecting Americans in red states and blue states."

Trump losing independents, MAGA faithful at critical juncture

Through much of the final stretch, Trump has been visiting areas that are normally reliably Republican, including holding rallies in Alaska, Ohio, and Texas.

Despite Trump's preferred candidates performing well in Republican primaries, divisions over the Iran war and disillusionment over rising costs have diminished the "Make America Great Again" movement's popularity. A national University of Massachusetts Amherst Poll released Sept. 10 backs found a 9 percentage point drop among GOP voters who identify with MAGA compared to March.

Even more troubling for the administration and its supporters are surveys showing just 13% of U.S. adults saying they "strongly approve" of the job Trump is doing, according to a Focaldata-Financial Times poll, released Oct. 11. That is a noticeable collapse when compared to previous metrics that showed roughly 26% of Americans saying the same in a Quinnipiac University poll released in May.

As a result, Republicans are in such a defensive crouch that Senate Leadership Fund, a GOP-aligned super PAC, canceled ads in North Carolina, where holding retiring Republican Sen. Thom Tillis' seat appears increasingly out of reach. Meanwhile, GOP money has been pumped into Kansas, where Democrats haven't won a Senate race since 1932.

The Congressional Leadership Fund, a super PAC aligned with Republican House leadership, made a similar choice when it redirected $10 million from various races in October, including Iowa's 10th Congressional District, where Republican Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks' race was moved from "toss-up" to "lean" Democratic by the Cook Report.

John Opdycke, founder and president of Open Primaries, a group that advocates for nonpartisan primaries, said Republicans are suffering from alienating independents. According to Gallup, 45% of voting-age Americans identified as independents in the third quarter of 2026, up from 38% at the end of 2020. 

The AP-NORC survey shows Trump's job approval among independents dropped by roughly 17% compared to where it was before he took office in January 2025. Trump lost the most ground among those without a college degree, going from about 48% during the 2024 presidential election to roughly 27% when the Iran war first started.

"I'm not saying that independent voters have flipped a switch, but they're supporting and amplifying dozens of alternative candidates at the congressional and gubernatorial level," Opdycke said.

GOP questions polling accuracy

For optimistic conservatives, the best argument blossoming from Republican leaders is that the surveys forecasting a Democratic takeover of Congress are just plain wrong.

House Speaker Mike Johnson said as much during an Oct. 13 Fox News interview, arguing GOP voters "don't want to respond to polls anymore."

Leaders of certain polling firms have admitted that their models are much better at measuring political views than predicting election results. In an Oct. 14 op-ed for The Hill, Pew Research Center President Michael Dimock said those concerns are magnified during midterm elections that are known to "have lower turnout, localized dynamics and low information."

Going into the 2022 midterms, for instance, GOP leaders boasted about flipping up to 60 House seats given former President Joe Biden's low approval numbers at the time, but Republicans only eked out a net gain of nine seats in the House and lost a Senate seat to Democrats.

Some polls showed former Vice President Kamala Harris winning in 2024, including in most of the seven swing states that Trump ultimately swept on Election Day. Nteta said there are certain populations that have always been a challenge for pollsters to capture historically, including people living in rural areas where Republicans often dominate.

"It's a reflection of... the declining trust in institutions that we're seeing across our political landscape and social landscape," he said.

Trump has used sharp attacks to energize the GOP base in red states and districts, such as using an anti-trans slur to describe Annie Andrews, the Democratic nominee for Senate in South Carolina, and falsely claiming Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico, of Texas, is a vegan.

He is even offering up cash incentives if his party wins and warning of economic calamity if his opponents do.

"If the Democrats win, you will have a 1929-style economic depression," Trump said during an Oct. 6 rally in Nebraska, where surveys show independent Senate candidate Dan Osborn within striking distance of Republican Sen. Dan Ricketts.

"You're going to go into a depression if they get in," the president added, referring to Democrats. "If the Republicans win, you will each have $5,000 in your pocket, an economic success for our country like we have never seen before."

Democrats cautiously optimistic due to past disappointments

Liberal activists say their chief concern going into Election Day after millions have already cast early ballots is that the Trump administration will use its executive powers to deploy federal agents or seize ballots in more closely contested races.

Trump used a prime-time address in July to sow distrust in U.S. elections, alleging without evidence that China interfered in the 2020 election.

"We are up against a desperate president who's throwing the kitchen sink of lies and tactics and propaganda to try to scare voters," Lauren Groh-Wargo, CEO ofFair Fight Action, a national voting rights group, told USA TODAY in an interview.

"We are in an unprecedented time, so I don't take anything for granted. I think we've got to we've got to fight hard. We got to turn voters out."

As the elections approach, Democrats' hopes have grown to include winning even the Senate race in Kansas, which hasn't elected a Democrat since 1932. Other states they have considered a long shot for decades, such as Texas, are ranked as a "toss-up" by forecasters, in part thanks to strong Democratic nominees like mega-church pastor Adam Hamilton in Kansas and Talarico, a state legislator in Texas.

But Democrats have been surprised and disappointed in some recent election years, most notably 2016 and 2024.

In Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive dogged by persistent skepticism from more moderate voters, holds only a very slim lead in polls against Republican Mike Rogers.

Former President Barack Obama, who campaigned with El-Sayed on Oct. 24, has often commented on the persistence of Trump's coalition. He reportedly warned donors the party "could end up losing all" of the toss-up races.

Some experts prefer to look at fundamental factors such as economic performance, rather than polling. Using one such model, historian Allan Lichtman — often referred to as the "Nostradamus" of U.S. elections — has forecast that Democrats will win at least 52 Senate seats, though conservatives are quick to point out that Lichtman wrongly predicted Harris would win the presidency in 2024.

MAGA megabucks

Another variable is campaign spending, in which Republicans hold a major advantage. Elon Musk, the world's richest person, who came to the rescue by pouring in more than a quarter billion dollars toward congressional races.

Coupled with the roughly $400 million of MAGA Inc., the president's super PAC, Republicans could outspend Democrats in key races such as Texas, where Musk funneled about $158 million to groups backing Paxton, according to the Federal Election Commission.

Texas is the epitome of a state in which there are potentially enough Republicans to flood any swing towards the Democrats − but only if they are persuaded to come to the polls.

"Obviously, we saw in 2016 and 2024 that Trump was able to achieve such massive majorities on the backs of voters that have been considered sort of non-regular voters," Doug Blair, a spokesman for Heritage Action, the lobbying arm for the conservative-leaning Heritage Foundation, told USA TODAY. "So there is a hope that people will come out and vote."

Some polls showed former Vice President Kamala Harris winning in 2024, including in most of the seven swing states that Trump ultimately swept on Election Day. Nteta said there are certain populations that have always been a challenge for pollsters to capture historically, including people living in rural areas where Republicans often dominate.

"It's a reflection of... the declining trust in institutions that we're seeing across our political landscape and social landscape," he said.

Trump has used sharp attacks to energize the GOP base in red states and districts, such as using an anti-trans slur to describe Annie Andrews, the Democratic nominee for Senate in South Carolina, and falsely claiming Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico, of Texas, is a vegan.

He is even offering up cash incentives if his party wins and warning of economic calamity if his opponents do.

"If the Democrats win, you will have a 1929-style economic depression," Trump said during an Oct. 6 rally in Nebraska, where surveys show independent Senate candidate Dan Osborn within striking distance of Republican Sen. Dan Ricketts.

"You're going to go into a depression if they get in," the president added, referring to Democrats. "If the Republicans win, you will each have $5,000 in your pocket, an economic success for our country like we have never seen before."

Democrats cautiously optimistic due to past disappointments

Liberal activists say their chief concern going into Election Day after millions have already cast early ballots is that the Trump administration will use its executive powers to deploy federal agents or seize ballots in more closely contested races.

Trump used a prime-time address in July to sow distrust in U.S. elections, alleging without evidence that China interfered in the 2020 election.

"We are up against a desperate president who's throwing the kitchen sink of lies and tactics and propaganda to try to scare voters," Lauren Groh-Wargo, CEO ofFair Fight Action, a national voting rights group, told USA TODAY in an interview.

"We are in an unprecedented time, so I don't take anything for granted. I think we've got to we've got to fight hard. We got to turn voters out."

As the elections approach, Democrats' hopes have grown to include winning even the Senate race in Kansas, which hasn't elected a Democrat since 1932. Other states they have considered a long shot for decades, such as Texas, are ranked as a "toss-up" by forecasters, in part thanks to strong Democratic nominees like mega-church pastor Adam Hamilton in Kansas and Talarico, a state legislator in Texas.

But Democrats have been surprised and disappointed in some recent election years, most notably 2016 and 2024.

In Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive dogged by persistent skepticism from more moderate voters, holds only a very slim lead in polls against Republican Mike Rogers.

Former President Barack Obama, who campaigned with El-Sayed on Oct. 24, has often commented on the persistence of Trump's coalition. He reportedly warned donors the party "could end up losing all" of the toss-up races.

Some experts prefer to look at fundamental factors such as economic performance, rather than polling. Using one such model, historian Allan Lichtman — often referred to as the "Nostradamus" of U.S. elections — has forecast that Democrats will win at least 52 Senate seats, though conservatives are quick to point out that Lichtman wrongly predicted Harris would win the presidency in 2024.

MAGA megabucks

Another variable is campaign spending, in which Republicans hold a major advantage. Elon Musk, the world's richest person, who came to the rescue by pouring in more than a quarter billion dollars toward congressional races.

Coupled with the roughly $400 million of MAGA Inc., the president's super PAC, Republicans could outspend Democrats in key races such as Texas, where Musk funneled about $158 million to groups backing Paxton, according to the Federal Election Commission.

Texas is the epitome of a state in which there are potentially enough Republicans to flood any swing towards the Democrats − but only if they are persuaded to come to the polls.

"Obviously, we saw in 2016 and 2024 that Trump was able to achieve such massive majorities on the backs of voters that have been considered sort of non-regular voters," Doug Blair, a spokesman for Heritage Action, the lobbying arm for the conservative-leaning Heritage Foundation, told USA TODAY. "So there is a hope that people will come out and vote."

news.title: Trump's midterm reckoning: A repudiation or triumph awaits
news.text:
WASHINGTON — In a bitterly fought midterm election, President Donald Trump and his detractors have found at least one piece of common ground – it's all about Trump.

And as voters head to the polls on Nov. 3, the president faces a reckoning.

After dominating American politics for the last decade, Trump is the animating force in an election that will decide control of Congress and whether his presidency is hemmed in or given more running room. Polling shows most voters view their congressional ballot as primarily a vote for or against the president.

"He’s casting a long shadow over the midterm elections," said Lee Miringoff, director of the Marist Institute for Public Opinion.

Democrats are eager to win majorities in the House and Senate and deliver Trump the type of lasting repudiation they hoped for in 2020, when he lost his reelection bid before staging a comeback. They have an opportunity to significantly weaken his grip on power over his final two years in office. Democrats also hope that possible wins in states and congressional districts that haven't voted blue in decades can help end the Trump era.

On the Republican side, Trump aims to prove his doubters wrong once again with an unexpected triumph despite his low approval ratings, show one more time that polling is a fool's errand, and end his second term with a flourish, while maintaining his iron grip over the GOP.

Recent rallies spotlight both efforts.

Criticizing Trump during an Oct. 28 event in Atlanta, former President Barack Obama told a crowd that the midterms are "our last, best chance of at least reining him in, reining in some of the foolishness of this administration."

In Chillicothe, Ohio, on the same night, Trump again appealed to his base to "pretend" he’s on the ballot.

"I really am on the ballot, if you think, because all of those tax cuts, all of the things that we’ve gotten, all of the victories that we’ve had," he added.

Trump makes big promises with a catch. Republicans must win midterms

Democrats are widely favored to win control of the House, and polling indicates they also have a strong chance of flipping the Senate. States that haven't elected a Democrat to the Senate in decades and went for Trump by double digits are now highly competitive, offering Democrats a historic opportunity to make inroads in traditionally Republican areas.

For the past three weeks, Trump has barnstormed the country to try and hold back a blue wave as Republicans leverage a massive financial advantage in the final stretch. Despite shifting the electoral map to historically red states such as Kansas, Nebraska, Alaska, and South Carolina, most Senate races are close, polling suggests.

"I think you're going to be pleasantly surprised on Tuesday," Trump told a crowd in Lubbock, Texas, on Oct. 27. "People are coming home. They're coming home. They're not going to let our country be destroyed."

Red state woes

Despite his public optimism, Trump has also openly acknowledged that a Democratic sweep is possible, telling reporters he would use his veto pen often under such a scenario and find a way to work out deals with the opposing party.

"I hope that won't be the case, but if it is, that's happened before with many presidents," Trump said last week.

Trump's Oct. 27 trip was his third visit to Texas in October. The state's emergence as a key battleground shows the depths of the president's midterm woes.

Texas last elected a Democratic senator in 1988, and Trump carried the state by 14 percentage points, but the Real Clear Politics average of recent polls shows Democrat James Talarico leading GOP candidate Ken Paxton in the final days of the race. Trump’s endorsement helped Paxton defeat four-term Republican Sen. John Cornyn in the primary, but the scandal-plagued GOP nominee has struggled to gain traction.

When the MAGA's over: Nostalgia sets in for Trump fans at final rallies

Trump allies in deep red states such as Kansas, Ohio, Iowa, and Alaska also are trailing or tied in the average of recent polls. Kansas hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932.

"The fact that Republicans are having to spend time and money in some of these ruby red states shows how bad the political environment is for them, and there’s really no one to blame other than Donald Trump," said Sarah Matthews, who served as a deputy press secretary during Trump’s first administration.

Trump rallied in South Carolina Oct. 29 for the second time in a month, stumping for GOP Senate candidate Darline Graham, sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham. The president endorsed Graham to succeed her brother, helping her win a hotly contested primary.

A recent New York Times/Siena survey showed her tied in the general contest against Democrat Annie Andrews, despite Trump carrying the state by 18 percentage points in 2024.

"These are Trump's handpicked candidates - Ken Paxton, Darline Graham - and I don't think they would be having to play in those states if there were any other Republican on the ballot," Matthews said.

Losing in states that previously have been strong Trump territory would be a massive blow for the president and his party. But Trump has faced big setbacks in the past.

During his first term in 2018, Democrats won control of the House and went on to impeach him over allegations he abused his power in an attempt to have a foreign government investigate a political rival. He was acquitted by the Senate, which remained in Republican control.

Midterm elections: President Trump keeps talking about Sen. Jon Husted's backside

The president went on to lose his reelection bid in 2020 and challenged the results, culminating in a mob of his supporters storming the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021. He was again impeached and acquitted. Trump later was indicted over his role in Jan. 6, and in another case involving hush money payment to an adult film actress.

Trump was convicted on 34 counts in the hush money case, but won reelection anyway.

Now he faces another test. And it comes as Republicans already are starting to position themselves for the 2028 presidential race and what comes after the lame duck president.

Trump could benefit from the low midterm expectations for the GOP.

With many forecasts now predicting a Democratic takeover of both chambers of Congress, Trump and the White House are positioned to claim victory if Republicans lose the House yet hold on to the Senate — even though a Democratic majority in the Senate, which Republicans control 53-47, seemed like a long shot a year ago.

"If Republicans hold on to the Senate and they win a bunch of races where Trump campaigned, he can say, 'I'm still the most important, popular person in the Republican Party,'" said Anthony Fowler, a political scientist at the University of Chicago. "And you won't see a lot of people trying to buck him within the party."

Conversely, losing both chambers would be a bitter pill for Republicans, especially if Democrats flip states where they haven't won a Senate seat in decades, and would prompt questions about the viability of a Trump-centric party going forward.

"It’s going to be a battle for the soul of the Republican Party in many respects," said John Bolton, who served as national security adviser in Trump’s first administration and has become a vocal critic of the president.

'It's called mutilization': Trump hammers culture wars on campaign trail as economic pitch fizzles

A barnstorm to the finish after rallies briefly canceled

With Democrats needing to flip four seats to win control of the Senate, Trump has traveled the country to try to bolster Republican candidates in tight races.

"I think we have a shot at doing well, maybe very well, but you know, pretty well," Trump told reporters Oct. 30.

While polling indicates his party is facing strong headwinds, Republicans are fighting on favorable ground in many states and most of the key Senate races are tight. Democrats are leading by 3 percentage points or less in the Real Clear Politics average of recent polls in Alaska, Texas, Michigan, and Ohio. Kansas and Iowa are tied. Graham is up by 3 points in the average of South Carolina polls.

"Statistically, I see a lot of margin-of-error states," Miringoff said.

Drilling down into the data shows signs of a potential blue wave, though. Miringoff pointed to polling indicating independents are breaking strongly toward Democratic candidates in red states and districts.

Trump's approval rating has sunk to record lows in recent surveys amid concerns about his handling of the economy, the Iran war and other issues. That has raised questions about his decision to play such a central role the midterms, with rallies across the country in the closing stretch.

Trump last week abruptly halted plans to close his midterm blitz with weekend rallies in Kansas and Iowa, two Senate battlegrounds, only to reschedule the events amid speculation that he was giving up in the traditionally Republican states.

Trump on the campaign trail: Trump rallies in Kansas, Iowa are back on after being canceled

Bolton, who served in Republican administrations going back to President Ronald Reagan, said presidents usually keep a lower profile during the midterms, helping with fundraising and sticking to public events in states "where the president's standing is still high."

Trump, meanwhile, has visited nearly every battleground state despite his approval rating being underwater in all of them.

"You don’t go into states where you’re poking the hornet’s nest," Bolton said.

In defying conventional wisdom and campaigning aggressively, Trump is hoping to boost GOP turnout.

"President Trump is the greatest force for turnout in American politics, and that's why he is barnstorming the country and driving voters to the polls in the final stretch," Republican National Committee spokesperson Natalie Baldassarre said. "The momentum is on our side, and Republicans are ready to fight, defy history, and protect our majorities."

Ralph Reed, founder and chairman of the Faith & Freedom Coalition and a close Trump ally, said his group urged the White House to put the president on the campaign trail to help "juice" GOP turnout.

"If we’re able to do better than people expect Tuesday, Trump will deserve a lot of credit," Reed said.

But after thrusting himself into the center of the midterm elections, Trump could be an easy target if Republicans have a bad election night.

"This is, when it comes down to it, undoubtedly a referendum on Trump, and he asked for it. He's the one who said: 'pretend my name is on the ballot'... he played right into it," Bolton said.

Reed said Trump has worked to put the focus on Democrats "by making it clear that many, if not all, of the Democratic candidates hold positions that are out of the mainstream."

"I think the president and his political team have done a very good job of reframing the narrative of this campaign from a referendum on Trump's job performance into a contrast election and a choice," Reed said.

The stakes are high not just for the president, but for his party going forward. Democratic victories in red states would give the party a toehold that could help in future elections, boosting fundraising and grassroots organizing.

"It makes a real difference when you have a statewide officeholder for that respective political party," said former Michigan GOP Rep. Fred Upton, who voted to impeach Trump and later endorsed Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris. "All of a sudden they’re a real leader. They’ve got a network. They’ve got relationships in every one of the counties. There’s a voice that gets equal time.”

Trump says he will accept results if they're 'honest elections'

After Trump worked unsuccessfully to overturn his 2020 election loss, many Democrats and Trump critics fear how he might react to a sweeping midterm loss.

Trump has said he would only accept the midterm results "if they're honest elections."

More: Trump says he'll respect midterm results 'if they're honest elections'

The president has also continued to raise unfounded concerns about widespread voter fraud, and the Department of Justice has taken aggressive steps in the final weeks of the election, suing California over allegations of noncitizens on the voter rolls and seeking to preemptively block certification of Alaska's Senate results.

Trump last week called for the criminal prosecution of Mary Peltola, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Alaska, after a report from the New York Times detailed how aides from her campaign recruited a candidate with the same name as her Republican opponent, Sen. Dan Sullivan, to enter the race as a spoiler.

More: Trump calls for Mary Peltola to be prosecuted after report on Sullivan spoiler

Matthews, who was in the White House on Jan. 6, 2021 and has since spoken out against the president, said she worries Trump is "cooking up some scheme to cast out the results of these midterm elections as well." Democrats and election advocates have been gearing up for a potential showdown with the Trump administration over certifying the results if they go against Republicans.

Whatever happens, Trump could continue to wield considerable power.

Even with a hostile Congress, Trump's critics note he still has immense authority and say the final two years of his administration could see plenty of aggressive moves.

Where his party goes next if it goes down in defeat is an open question. Matthews predicts Trump would still be influential, if less so, as Republicans look to the party's future and the president increasingly becomes part of its past.

"It doesn't mean that Trump is going to become obsolete within the party, he's just not going to have the same power that he wants to," she said.
