news.title: 5 states' election results could be early indicator of blue wave
news.text:
It's Election Day, and voters in all 50 states are headed to the polls for the final chance to weigh in on everything from which party will control Congress to state ballot initiatives to local leaders in a slew of races across the country. 

Democrats are hoping to win majorities in both chambers of Congress, which have been controlled by Republicans for the past two years, and political experts say the party is poised to flip at least one: The House of Representatives.

The factors which point to a Democratic win in the House include historical trends that the party in control of the White House loses seats in midterm elections, President Donald Trump's low approval rating and the fact that Republican's current majority only sits at a thin 218-214 seats. But it's not guaranteed.

Voter ID, guns and culture: These issues are on the ballot Nov. 3

Ballot counting in some states is likely to go well into the night, but elections experts are eyeing a number of districts as early signals of whether there will be a blue wave and, if so, how big it might get.

The early results to these questions could Americans an understanding of where the night is headed, according to Kyle Kondik, a political analyst and the managing editor of Sabato's Crystal Ball at the University of Virginia's Center for Politics:

Florida: Will Republican redistricting in Florida help the party pick up four House seats? Virginia: Virginia Democrats failed to redistrict, but can they still flip two red seats blue? Pennsylvania: Can Republicans hold onto four swing districts in this state that Trump flipped red in 2024? Indiana: Will the Indianapolis suburbs oust their Republican representative in a "blue wave?"Kentucky: A 13-year Republican representative is leaving his seat. Can Democrats pick it up? New York, Ohio and New Jersey: These three Republicans made headlines. Will the blue wave oust them too?

"These are kind of the frontline races, that are, at this point, Democrats are expected to pick up," David Wasserman from the nonpartisan Cook Political Report told USA TODAY. "I think they're kind of the prerequisite districts for Democrats to be able to win the House majority, whereas there are other races in these states that would be signs of like a really big wave."

Midterm elections: One key race in all 50 states and why they matter

Will Republican redistricting in Florida help the party pick up four House seats?

Florida polls close at 7 p.m. ET, and the state is known to report quickly, so its results will be an early insight as to how Republican redistricting efforts hold up, according to Kondik.

In April, lawmakers in the Sunshine State passed redrawn maps that could add four Republican House seats in the state. If Republicans prevail in picking up four Democratic-held seats in Florida's Orlando-area 9th District, Tampa-area 14th District, South Florida/Palm Beach-area 22ndDistrict and Miami-area 25th District, that could indicate good news coming the rest of the evening for Republicans.

5 takeaways: Dem socialists' mixed results in Florida primaries

Kondik, though, says he doubts the party will pick up all four.

Rep. Jared Moskowitz, D-Florida, from the state's 23rd Congressional District is running in the state's new 25th District, and Rep. Debbie Wasserman-Schultz, currently serving the 25th District, is running in the new 20th District after the redistricting shuffle. Those two winning in their new districts would spell good news for the Democrats, experts said.

"Democrats should be able to hold onto the 25th District, which is Jared Moskowitz," Wasserman said. He added that the real toss-up districts are the 14th and 22nd, both of which are represented by Democrats.

Wasserman's Cook Political Report rates Florida's 7th, 9th, 13th and 27th Districts as leaning Republican, and he said if Democrats claim any of those four, it would indicate a huge evening of wins ahead.

Virginia Democrats failed to redistrict, but can they still flip two red seats blue?

Democrats are hoping for two pickups in the state's 1st and 2nd Districts, which are currently held by Republican Reps. Rob Wittman and Jen Kiggans, respectively.

Kiggans is running against the district's former Democratic Rep. Elaine Luria, in a rematch after Kiggans ousted Luria from office in 2022. A Christopher Newport University poll on Oct. 14 said that Luria led slightly.

"Democrats should be able to win in an environment like this," Kondik told USA TODAY of the state's 2nd District. "If they don't, there's probably some sort of problem" for the party.

The state's 1st District is "certainly not a must win seat" for the Democrats to reclaim the majority, Kondik said, but a local prosecutor in the state, Democrat Shannon Taylor, hopes to flip her opponent Wittman's seat.

Wasserman said he expects Luria to win the 2nd District. He called the first district a "bubble race" that Democrats could prevail in, and said that if Democrats can additionally pick up a win in the state's 5th District, that would be a "tsunami race," indicating big wins ahead for Democrats.

Pennsylvania

Can Republicans hold onto four swing districts in this state that Trump flipped red in 2024?

Four eastern Pennsylvania seats are up for grabs, and the results could also be an early indication of whether the blue wave is crashing down on Republicans.

Five-term Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick is considered one of the most moderate Republicans in Congress — he voted against the final version of Trump's signature "big, beautiful bill" — and has long been a target for Democrats. His Bucks County-area 1st District was ranked as leaning Republican until Oct. 30, when the Cook Political Report shifted it to toss-up. In 2024, Fitzpatrick won his fifth term after outperforming Trump in the district by double digit margins, but now, a Democratic county commissioner has the chance to flip it blue.

More: What's at stake in Pennsylvania's midterm elections

Republican Rep. Ryan Mackenzie, meanwhile, hopes to keep his seat representing the eastern Pennsylvania 7th District that includes Allentown. Mackenzie flipped the district red in 2024 by a tight margin of around 4,000 votes.

Eighth District Republican Rep. Rob Bresnahan and 10th District Republican Rep. Scott Perry in the northeast and south-central parts of the state, respectively, face Democratic challenges that experts are watching closely.

"If Fitzpatrick loses, it probably means Democrats are flipping all four, I would think," Kondik said. "But they don't need to win all four. I think they need at least one or two."

Will the Indianapolis suburbs oust their Republican representative in a "blue wave?"

It doesn't seem very likely, as Republican Rep. Victoria Spartz's 5th District is ranked as leaning in the Republican's favor, according to the Cook Political Report.

A Democrat has not represented the district since 1993, but Kondik recalled quick vote reporting in recent elections from Hamilton County, which sits in the district.

"If Democrats flip either of those, that's probably a signal that they're getting more than 20-35 House seats," Kondik said of the Indiana district and one in Kentucky.

A 13-year Republican representative is leaving his seat. Can Democrats pick it up?

In Kentucky's 6th District in the central part of the state, including the city of Lexington, an open race for a seat held by Republican Rep. Andy Barr could provide a sign of a "mega wave" if Democrats flip it, according to Kondik.

"I would watch Kentucky," Wasserman also stressed as a major indicator of whether a blue wave pulls through.

Barr is running for U.S. Senate, leaving his district open. He assumed office in 2013 after winning the seat from a Democrat.

A former Republican state senator, Ralph Alvarado hopes to keep the seat in Republicans' hands, but the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee said in an Oct. 14 poll that Democratic candidate Zach Dembo led by six points.

"I don't quite think Democrats will get there," Kondik said.

Other Republican holds in New York, Ohio and New Jersey

These three Republicans made headlines. Will a blue wave oust them too?

Other eastern time zone tossup races to watch sit in New York, New Jersey and Ohio.

Rep. Tom Kean, R-New Jersey, is defending his suburban swing district after a four-month hiatus from Congress in the spring. While he announced upon his return that he had been hospitalized for depression, the months-long lack of an explanation drew criticism.

Rep. Mike Lawler, R-New York, hopes to keep his Hudson Valley seat in one of the least-red Republican-held districts in the country. He is one of just three Republicans representing a district former Vice President Kamala Harris carried in 2024.

Rep. Max Miller, R-Ohio, is running for reelection in what was once considered a solidly GOP district, until the race was upended by domestic violence allegations leveled by Miller’s ex-wife, Emily Moreno, the daughter of Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio. Miller has repeatedly and vehemently denied the allegations.

news.title: The candidates who will decide the US midterm elections
news.text:
Abdul El-Sayed

Democratic candidate for US Senate in Michigan

Abdul El-Sayed, a former public health official on the left of the Democratic party, beat a moderate member of Congress to win the party’s nomination for US Senate in Michigan, in a race clouded by tens of millions in outside spending. He is facing Republican former congressman Mike Rogers in one of the country’s most-watched races. Michigan is a swing state: while the Senate seat they are fighting for has been held by a Democrat for 12 years, the state narrowly backed Donald Trump in the 2024 presidential election. El-Sayed’s brand of tough talk and the simplicity of his campaign slogan (money out of politics, money in your pocket, Medicare for All) have made him a progressive star – and a frequent punching bag on the right, where prominent figures led by the president have leaned into Islamophobia to criticize him.

Susan Collins

Republican US Senator from Maine

Susan Collins isn’t new to the US Senate. She has been serving since 1997, and is now seeking a sixth term. A moderate Republican, she is a dying breed in the current Maga-tinged Washington during Trump’s second presidency. Maine is a battleground state: Kamala Harris won the state by a clear margin over Trump in 2024. Now Collins, 73, is trying to hang on to her seat in a race that Democrats have targeted as a key to winning back control of the Senate. She initially faced Graham Platner, a Democrat who dropped out of the race after facing rape allegations. Now, Troy Jackson – a former logger who served in the state legislature – is trying to topple the longtime senator.

Adam Hamilton

Democratic nominee for US Senate in Kansas

Kansas’ US Senate election wasn’t on the national radar as competitive at the start of the year. Why would it be? Kansans have not sent a Democrat to the US Senate since 1932. But Adam Hamilton, a megachurch pastor, won a crowded primary and has made the race one to watch this year. While Kansas typically leans right, voters in the state have shown frustration with Republican senator Roger Marshall over inaccessibility and his alignment with Trump, as they struggle to afford fuel and groceries, and grapple with sustained economic instability. Plus, Marshall, who practiced medicine for 25 years, was revealed to have sued hundreds of his patients for unpaid bills, resulting in the arrests of dozens of them. Enter Hamilton, who frequently calls for bipartisan politics that put Kansans first, even if that means standing up to Trump.

Democratic US senator from Georgia

Ossoff, the youngest US senator at 39, is seeking a second term in what should have been a tight race in Georgia, the southern swing state. Polls are suggesting it will not be a close-run thing. The Democrat’s political glow-up and savvy speaking skills, captured in video clips meant to grab voter attention online, have made his reelection seem all but inevitable – and given rise to near-constant murmurs that he’ll run for president in 2028, with regular comparisons to Barack Obama, in tone and in youthfulness. The pair rallied together in Georgia last week. He has accused his opponent, Mike Collins, a Republican congressman, of being aligned with white supremacists – which Collins has vehemently denied.

James Talarico

Democratic nominee for US Senate in Texas

Could Texas finally flip – and could it be a theological Democrat – who does it? James Talarico, a 37-year-old state lawmaker, has been generating buzz – and raising record-breaking sums – in his run for the US Senate. Having fended off the firebrand Democratic congresswoman Jasmine Crockett in the Democratic primary, he now faces the state’s beleaguered Republican attorney general, Ken Paxton, in the general election. With Trump’s backing, Paxton beat incumbent US senator John Cornyn in the Republican primary. The nomination of Paxton – who has faced a host of fraud and misconduct scandals during his time in office – has prompted Republicans to drop tens of millions of dollars to defend a seat they typically win with a clear margin. Talarico, dubbed “Talafreako” by Trump and his allies, has sought to win over independents and Republicans in the red state by appealing to their faith and speaking against corruption in politics.

Republican representative in Ohio

Ohio’s seventh congressional district wouldn’t ordinarily be competitive; Trump won the district by 11 points in 2024. But damaging allegations surrounding Max Miller, the embattled Republican incumbent, have given Democrats hope that they might flip the red seat. The 37-year-old Republican, who worked on Trump’s first presidential campaign, was elected to the seat in 2022. His ex-wife, Emily Moreno, who is the daughter of Republican US senator Bernie Moreno, has alleged Miller physically abused her and their daughter, which he denied. Another of Miller’s ex-partners, former Trump press secretary Stephanie Grisham, has also accused Miller of physical abuse. He denied that allegation, too. The claims have featured heavily in ads against Miller in the district. Brian Poindexter, the Democratic challenger, is a union ironworker focused on addressing the cost of living.

Mary Peltola

Democratic nominee for US Senate in Alaska

Mary Peltola is one of the few prominent Democrats who were deemed to pose a potential threat to incumbent Republican Dan S Sullivan. She entered the race hoping to capitalize on Alaska’s recent independent streak and broad anti-Trump feelings. But in the final stretch, she faced allegations of mistreating staff by using slurs and shoving one aide – which her campaign downplayed, attributing Peltola’s behavior to stress. Her campaign also faced accusations of ballot stacking by recruiting another candidate named Dan J Sullivan to run in the state’s open primary. The New York Times reported that Peltola’s staff worked with the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee to add another Dan Sullivan to the ballot, thereby drawing votes away from the Republican senator. Peltola has said she knew nothing of the plan. Her campaign also denied recruiting candidates into the race.

Angie Nixon

Democratic nominee for US Senate in Florida

Marco Rubio’s elevation from the Senate to Trump’s secretary of state in 2025 left an open seat in Florida, which was filled by Republican Ashley Moody. Now, in the race for a full term, Moody faces Angie Nixon – a progressive and democratic socialist – who staged a surprise victory in the Democratic primary. While the Florida race isn’t seen as super competitive, or a likely win for Democrats, the small business owner and state lawmaker has grabbed attention and seen prominent figures on the left, including congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Senator Bernie Sanders, campaigning for her. Progressives hope that Nixon can make the case that their candidates – and not just moderates – can have broad appeal in red states like Florida. Moody was the state’s attorney general before her appointment to the US Senate.

Darline Graham

Republican US senator in South Carolina

Darline Graham had minimal involvement in politics and had never run for or held public office until this year, when she was appointed to the US Senate seat in South Carolina after her brother’s death. Lindsey Graham served the state in Washington, first in the House and then in the Senate, for decades. She decided – after encouragement from Trump – to seek a full term, and won the Republican primary. But Darline Graham’s inexperience, both in office and with policy itself, has come into sharp focus. Voter frustration with political dynasties have also made the race in this typically red state a toss-up, according to polls. Dr Annie Andrews, a pediatrician, is running against Graham after previously making a run for the US House of Representatives in 2022.

Juan Ciscomani

Republican US representative in Arizona

Juan Ciscomani, a 44-year-old Latino Republican congressman and former gubernatorial adviser, has faced close races for his US House seat in each election, narrowly beating out his Democrat opponent in 2022 and 2024 in the toss-up sixth congressional district in southern Arizona. Ciscomani, who was born in Sonora, Mexico and raised in Tucson, has sought to distance himself from Trump. His reelection campaign is a test of whether Latinos – some of whom swung toward Trump in 2024 and helped deliver his second term – will stick with the president, or side with Democrats, especially after Trump’s aggressive deportation scheme. JoAnna Mendoza, a US Marine Corps veteran and the Democratic challenger, has emphasized her local roots and called out Ciscomani for largely voting with Trump’s agenda.

Rebecca Bennett

Democratic nominee for US House in New Jersey

Rebecca Bennett’s odds of winning this toss-up seat increased when her opponent, the incumbent Republican Tom Kean Jr, disappeared for months from his public office. Kean, 58, was gone for more than three months from his job representing the seventh congressional district. He and his office declined to explain why until he returned, when he told people he had been hospitalized for depression. Before his prolonged absence, Bennett had flown under the radar. As New York Magazine put it: “Tom Kean Jr. needed to vanish to become interesting.” Bennett, a 39-year-old moderate Democrat and former navy helicopter pilot and aircraft commander, hopes to win over voters who are frustrated with Kean’s absence and Trump’s agenda. The district is known for split-ticket voting, whereby voters back candidates from different parties when electing figures to multiple offices in the same election. Bennett, a mother of two, has talked about how affordability concerns affect her household as well, including the cost of childcare.
news.summary:
The 2026 US midterm elections feature firebrand progressives trying to stake out new territory, moderate Republicans struggling in the shadow of Donald Trump, and a host of scandals that have made races closer than they should be.

These candidates could shape not only power in Washington, but public and political understanding of what works – and wins votes – in different places across the country. Can a Democrat win in red Kansas? Could Texas finally flip away from Republicans? Will abuse allegations or absenteeism tank incumbents? How important is capturing online attention?

And how can Republicans run away from Trump, their party’s leader, and modern architect, as his popularity wanes?

The lessons learned – and the candidates who teach them – will play into the 2028 presidential election and alter the makeup of Congress at a critical time for both parties

news.title: Peggy Flanagan vs. Michele Tafoya—What Final Minnesota Polls Show
news.text: The final polls in Minnesota's U.S. Senate race show Democrat Peggy Flanagan ahead of Republican Michele Tafoya, heading into Election Day. Flanagan is Minnesota's lieutenant governor, while Tafoya is a former NFL sideline reporter. They are competing for the open U.S. Senate seat being vacated by retiring Democratic Senator Tina Smith. Three of the latest surveys put Flanagan's lead between three and seven percentage points. InsiderAdvantage has her ahead 49 percent to 46 percent, KSTP/SurveyUSA gives her a 48-41 lead, and Research Co. puts her ahead 52-47 among decided voters. Minnesota has not elected a Republican to the U.S. Senate since 2002, when Norm Coleman defeated former Vice President Walter Mondale. Coleman subsequently lost his 2008 reelection bid to Democrat Al Franken following one of the closest and most protracted recounts in Senate election history. The state has since remained in Democratic hands in every Senate election. It makes this year's contest between Flanagan and Tafoya another test of whether Republicans can break a decades-long losing streak in statewide races. Minnesota has retained a Democratic lean in recent statewide federal elections, but its margins have sometimes been relatively narrow. Smith defeated Republican Jason Lewis by about five points in the 2020 Senate election, while Democrat Kamala Harris carried Minnesota by 4.2 points in the 2024 presidential election. What the Polls Show The InsiderAdvantage survey was conducted October 29-30 among 1,200 likely Minnesota voters using a mixed text and panel methodology. It was weighted for age, race, gender, and political affiliation and had a margin of error of plus or minus 2.83 percentage points. With Flanagan three points ahead, the candidates' individual margins of error overlap. One percent was undecided, and 4 percent supported another candidate. Research Co.'s poll was conducted online from October 30 to November 1. Its Minnesota sample included 450 likely voters, and the data were weighted by age and gender using U.S. Census figures. The margin of error was plus or minus 4.6 percentage points. Among decided voters, Flanagan received 52 percent to Tafoya's 47 percent. The KSTP/SurveyUSA survey, conducted October 24-28 among 714 likely voters, showed Flanagan at 48 percent and Tafoya at 41 percent, with 7 percent undecided and a margin of error of plus or minus 4.2 percentage points. KSTP characterized the contest as remaining within the poll's margin of error. An AtlasIntel poll conducted from October 28 to November 1 among 2,133 respondents showed Democrat Peggy Flanagan leading Republican Michele Tafoya by 2.4 percentage points. Flanagan received 48.1 percent support to Tafoya's 45.7 percent. The survey had a margin of error of plus or minus 2 percentage points. RealClearPolling's average listed Flanagan at 48.9 percent and Tafoya at 43 percent, a 5.2-point advantage, and rated the race "Leans Dem." Its recent polling list also included a New York Times/Siena survey, conducted October 19-26 among 752 likely voters, that showed Flanagan leading 54 percent to 40 percent with a 4.1-point margin of error. The final three surveys are therefore broadly consistent on the leader, but not on the size of the lead. InsiderAdvantage's three-point margin is narrower than the RealClearPolling average, Research Co.'s five-point result is close to it, and SurveyUSA's seven-point result is somewhat wider. The Times/Siena result, showing a 14-point advantage, stands noticeably above those other late polls. Inflation and the cost of living have remained the dominant election concern among Minnesota voters, with 36 percent identifying them as their most important issue in an October KSTP/SurveyUSA poll. When asked specifically what the state's next U.S. senator should prioritize, voters most often chose fighting fraud, Social Security, health care access, and lower taxes. Larry Jacobs, political scientist at the University of Minnesota, told Newsweek: "Polls indicate that the race continues to be close. Flanagan has an edge but undecided voters may matter." "Voters are casting ballots with an overwhelming concern about inflation, cost of living, and fuel prices (39 percent). This is the primary driver against Trump and GOP. Tafoya's campaign has tried to counteract this by making the race a referendum on fraud. That isn't working (9 percent). With voters casting ballots with affordability at the forefront of their minds, that reinforces Flanagan and doesn't help Tafoya." "The polling in the race between Peggy Flanagan and Michelle Tafoya is somewhat all over the place, making it difficult to determine what an accurate reading of the race might be. On one level, some polls suggest a very close race. On another, some suggest that Flanagan is pulling away," David Schultz told Newsweek. He is distinguished University professor in the Departments of Political Science, Environmental Studies, and Legal Studies at Hamline University. Schultz added: "It is important to recognize that Minneapolis and St. Paul, and the counties in which they are located, account for approximately 30 to 31 percent of the statewide vote. Democrats do well when turnout is high in these counties, and early voting suggests that turnout could be very high. However, this could simply reflect the fact that Democrats are more likely to vote early than Republicans. "This is perhaps the best chance Republicans have had to win a U.S. Senate seat in Minnesota since Norm Coleman defeated Walter Mondale in 2002. It is also among the best opportunities Republicans have had to win a statewide race in approximately 20 years. "If one looks at the activities of Tafoya and Flanagan, both are charging hard to get their supporters to the polls. This could mean that their internal polling shows a close race," said Schultz. "Alternatively, it could simply mean that both campaigns are going through the motions of an aggressive get-out-the-vote effort in the final 48 hours." What the Race Means for Control of the Senate The Minnesota contest is particularly important for Democrats because they are defending an open seat rather than attempting to gain one from Republicans. Republicans currently hold a 53-47 Senate majority, meaning Democrats need a net gain of four seats to secure a 51-seat majority. A Tafoya victory would therefore represent an additional Republican pickup Democrats would have to offset elsewhere. A Flanagan victory would keep the Minnesota seat in Democratic hands, allowing the party to concentrate on gains in Republican-held states and defending other Democratic seats. Outside ratings give Democrats an advantage in Minnesota but do not treat the outcome as certain. RealClearPolitics rates the contest "Leans Dem," while a separate race tracker lists the Cook Political Report rating as Lean Democratic and Sabato's Crystal Ball as Likely Democratic. The Senate race has also unfolded against an unusually turbulent political backdrop in Minnesota. A series of fraud cases has fueled Republican criticism of Governor Tim Walz’s administration, while Democrats have focused on the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. Minnesota also became the center of a political firestorm over federal immigration enforcement after U.S. citizens Renee Good and Alex Pretti were shot and killed by federal agents on the streets of Minneapolis in January during Operation Metro Surge. The shootings sparked nationwide protests and intensified scrutiny of the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown in the state and across the nation. The campaign has also played out amid a federal immigration investigation involving Democratic Representative Ilhan Omar, who has denounced the probe as politically motivated. Update, 11/3/26 6:19 a.m. ET: this article was updated with further polling information.
news.summary: Final polls give Flanagan the edge over Tafoya as Democrats fight to hold Minnesota’s open Senate seat.

news.title: What are the races to watch in the US midterm elections and why do they matter?
news.text:
As the name implies, midterm elections fall nearly halfway through a president’s term. They are often a telling referendum on the sitting president’s performance, something Trump is actively encouraging by telling voters “pretend I’m on the ballot”. In this case, voters will decide whether Trump’s Republican party can retain its grip on Congress.

Democrats are hoping to capitalise on growing discontent with Trump to seize control of the US House of Representatives, and possibly the Senate. Republicans are fighting to preserve their congressional majorities and prevent a fresh period of legislative paralysis and investigations into the White House.

What is being decided?

The US Congress in Washington has two chambers: the House of Representatives and the Senate. Both must approve federal legislation before it can become law and both play important roles in overseeing the executive branch.

The House is elected every two years, meaning all 435 voting seats are contested at every congressional election. The Senate has 100 members serving staggered six-year terms, so roughly a third of its seats are up for election every two years.

This year’s ballot includes:

 All 435 seats in the House of Representatives. Republicans are defending a narrow majority, with Democrats needing a net gain of four seats to take control.

 35 seats in the Senate. Thirty-three seats are up in regular elections, along with two special elections in Florida and Ohio to fill the remainder of terms that were vacated early. Republicans currently hold 53 seats, against 47 held by Democrats and independents who caucus with them. Democrats need to gain four seats to secure a majority.

 39 governorships. Voters will choose governors in 36 states and three US territories.

 Thousands of state legislative seats, as well as local offices, judicial contests and ballot measures on issues including taxes, abortion rights and voting rules.

The elections for Congress will determine which party controls Congress for the final two years of Trump’s second term. The governorships and state legislative contests will shape policymaking closer to home, from education and reproductive rights to taxation and the administration of elections.

Why do the midterms matter?

They have a long history of punishing the occupant of the White House. The president’s party has lost House seats in 18 of the past 20 midterm elections, a 90% rate of loss that stretches back to 1946.

The pattern is not inevitable. George W Bush’s Republicans gained seats in the 2002 midterms, following the September 11 attacks. But Barack Obama’s Democrats suffered a “shellacking” in 2010 and Trump’s Republicans lost the House in 2018.

Republicans enter this election with a narrow margin for error in the House and a more substantial advantage in the Senate. The RealClearPolitics average of national generic polls showed Democrats leading Republicans by 8.2 points in early October. Trump has been forced to hold campaign rallies in what should be safe Republican states.

But political polarisation and years of redistricting have reduced the number of genuinely competitive House districts, making it harder for either party to translate a national swing into a big change in seats. The Reuters news agency has estimated that only about 40 to 50 House races are truly competitive.

What are the races to watch?

Several Senate contests have emerged as key battlegrounds. In Michigan, progressive Abdul El-Sayed is seeking to hold an open seat for Democrats against Republican Mike Rogers, who received a last-minute endorsement from Democrat Haley Stevens. In Georgia, Jon Ossoff, a Democratic senator, enjoys a healthy poll lead over Republican challenger Mike Collins.

In Maine, a state won by Democrat Kamala Harris in 2024, Susan Collins, the Republican senator, is defending her seat against Democrat Troy Jackson. Ohio offers another major test, with Democrat Sherrod Brown seeking to return to the Senate against Republican Jon Husted.

 Texas has become especially closely watched. Democrat James Talarico is taking on Republican Ken Paxton, the state’s attorney general. Republicans have spent about $210m to help the scandal-plagued Paxton. No Democrat has won a statewide election in Texas since 1994. Trump won Texas by nearly 14 points in 2024.

In Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola’s Senate race against Republican incumbent Dan S Sullivan sparked controversy after Republicans accused the candidate of planting a second Dan Sullivan to confuse voters. A judge dismissed a Trump-backed lawsuit seeking to block certification of Alaska’s Senate race results if Dan Sullivan loses.

Other contests in Kansas, Iowa, North Carolina and New Hampshire could help determine which party controls the chamber (if there is a 50-50 split, JD Vance, the vice-president, a Republican, wields the tiebreaker vote). Latest polls show Democrats ahead in Maine, North Carolina and Kansas, and competitive in Ohio. Also on the map this year are South Carolina and Mississippi, two reliably Republican states that have seen aggressive Democratic challenges this year.

In the House, the contest is spread across dozens of districts. Republicans are defending vulnerable seats in places including New York, Texas and Iowa, while Democrats are also fighting to protect members in districts made more difficult by redrawn congressional boundaries. Notable gubernatorial elections include Alaska, Iowa, Florida, Georgia, Ohio and Texas.

What are the main issues?

The cost of living regularly tops opinion polls. Democrats are campaigning hard on affordability related to food prices, housing, fuel and healthcare. The war in Iran has added a further complication for Republicans.

Immigration remains another defining issue, with polls suggesting that many voters feel Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) hardline approach has gone too far. This could wipe out many of the gains that Trump made with Latino voters in 2024.

Datacentres, AI, tariffs, trade, abortion rights, voting rules and the future of democracy also remain important themes. Democratic socialists scored some notable victories in Democratic primaries, creating momentum on the left of the party.

But in closely fought races, personal credibility, local connections, the ability to appeal to independent voters and a blitz of TV advertising can outweigh the national party message.

Will the elections be free and fair?

The integrity of the midterms is under scrutiny, with concerns ranging from voter registration to the certification of results. Trump has sought to amplify these fears, putting forward a litany of misleading and false claims about threats to US elections.

The justice department has sued states for access to their unredacted voter rolls, seeking to cross-check them against a federal immigration database in an effort to identify ineligible voters. A federal judge ruled that the department’s policy was unlawful, citing limits on its authority and the risks of inaccurate data.

There are also concerns about the use of immigration-enforcement data in voter-fraud investigations, the administration’s efforts to change mail-voting rules and the prospect of federal election monitors at polling places. The NAACP has sued over the planned deployment of monitors, arguing that their presence could intimidate voters.

The risks do not end when polling stations close. Voting-rights advocates are also watching for pressure on local officials to certify results, mass challenges to ballots and legal disputes that could delay or undermine the transition of power.

What happens if Democrats win?

A Democratic victory in either chamber would significantly constrain Trump’s ability to advance his domestic agenda and hasten the president’s decline into “lame duck” status.

If Democrats take the House, Republicans would lose their ability to pass legislation through that chamber without Democratic support. A Democratic majority could launch investigations into the administration, demand documents and testimony, and subject senior officials to sustained congressional scrutiny. They might come under pressure from their support base to impeach Trump.

The Senate confirms cabinet officials, ambassadors and federal judges, including supreme court nominees. A Democratic majority could block or delay many of Trump’s appointments, and force the White House to negotiate over legislation.

Even if Republicans retain one or both chambers, a reduced majority could make governing more difficult, particularly when legislation requires near-unanimous support from the party’s own members.

Why do state elections matter?

Governors and state legislatures have influence over abortion access, education, taxation and voting procedures. State legislatures also play a central role in drawing congressional district boundaries, although the precise arrangements vary by state and some maps are subject to court challenges or independent commissions.

Voting rules are another source of contention. New restrictions on identification, registration and mail-in voting have taken effect in several Republican-controlled states. Supporters describe such measures as safeguards for election integrity; critics argue that they risk making it harder for eligible citizens to vote.

These disputes are especially significant in a political climate in which Trump has repeatedly questioned election procedures and the legitimacy of results he dislikes.

When will we know who has won?

Voting takes place on Tuesday 3 November, but the results may not be known that night. Close contests, different state rules for counting early and postal ballots, and possible recounts or legal challenges could delay the final outcome.

Once the dust has settled, there will be no respite in this – the land of the endless campaign. Attention will soon turn to the 2028 presidential election campaign, when both parties will seek to turn the results of this November into a foundation for the next fight for the White House.
news.summary: US voters will decide whether Republicans will retain control of Congress or whether Democrats will rise up to stymie Trump’s agenda

news.title: Here's what the U.S. is voting on today for the 2026 midterm elections
news.text: Voters throughout the country head to the polls on Tuesday, Nov. 3, for the midterm elections, with control of Congress, dozens of governorships, and major policy proposals all on the line. What's on the ballot today? All 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 seats in the Senate are up for grabs. Beyond Washington, 36 states will choose their next governor, while voters also decide on ballot measures on issues ranging from redistricting to abortion rights to a proposed billionaire tax in California.What is a midterm election? Midterm elections get their name because they happen in the middle of a presidential term. Although the president isn't on the ballot, the midterm elections often turn into referendums on the president and the party in power.Key races that are high-stakes today: House of RepresentativesRepublicans hold a narrow, three-seat majority in the U.S. House as voters head to the polls on Tuesday. Historically speaking, that could be a tall task for the GOP, as the party controlling the White House hasn't picked up seats in the House during the midterms since 2002. The road to a majority for both parties runs through several key districts, the most prominent of which may lie in Pennsylvania. A cluster of four suburban Philadelphia, Lehigh Valley and central Pennsylvania districts are all held by Republicans in competitive territory. With control of the House being decided by such narrow margins, Democrats can put themselves within striking distance of a majority if they're able to flip all four seats, potentially making Pennsylvania an early bellwether for how the night will go.Just to the north, in New York's 17th Congressional District in the Hudson Valley, incumbent two-term Republican Rep. Mike Lawler faces Democratic challenger Cait Conley in a race that has focused a lot of time on foreign policy, immigration and data centers. Lawler has won this seat by less than 30,000 votes in the last two cycles and the district voted for Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024, but faces a much tougher hill to climb, with the national environment blowing strongly in the face of House Republicans. Further to the west in Iowa, Republicans control all four House seats and have tight races expected in three of them. In the 1st District in the southeastern part of the state, incumbent Republican Mariannette Miller-Meeks will seek to defend herself in a seat that is no stranger to tight races, including in 2020 where Miller-Meeks won by just six votes. Another potentially vulnerable Republican incumbent lies in the 3rd District, where Rep. Zach Nunn seeks a third term in what has traditionally been Iowa's "bluest" district. The northeastern 2nd District, currently held by now-Senate candidate Ashley Hinson, is a slightly taller task for Democrats, and features two young candidates: 29-year-old GOP nominee Joe Mitchell, and 42-year-old Democrat Lindsay James.Arizona, long a bastion of tight elections, is set to feature two more in the 1st and 6th congressional districts. In the state's 1st District, which includes parts of Phoenix, Scottsdale and other suburbs, GOP nominee Jay Feely, a former NFL kicker, will face Democrat Amish Shah, a physician. Shah, who worked on the medical team for the New York Jets at the same time Feely played there, narrowly lost in 2024 to current Rep. David Schweikert. In the 6th district near the border, incumbent Republican Juan Ciscomani is seeking a third term in a seat that he has held on to by less than 3 points in each of the last two cycles. In Colorado, two House races could potentially make headlines for very different reasons on Election Night. In the deep-blue 1st Congressional District in Denver, 29-year-old Melat Kiros is a heavy favorite to become the first member of "Gen Z" to be elected to Congress, after she defeated longtime incumbent Rep. Diana DeGette in the primary. In the western part of the state, Republican Rep. Lauren Boebert faces an unexpectedly tight battle for reelection in the 4th District. This is a district with a strong Republican lean, as Mr. Trump won it by more than 17 points just two years ago, but recent polling shows Boebert in a close race with Democratic challenger Eileen Laubacher.California is also set to potentially play a major role in determining who may control the House, as Democrats try to capitalize on a set of newly redrawn districts. The new map, designed to help Democrats pick up five seats currently held by Republicans, is intended to offset gains made by the GOP redistricted states. Among them is the hotly contested Central Valley 22nd congressional district, where incumbent Rep. David Valadao faces Democrat Randy Villegas. In southern California, Republicans look to hold onto the seat in the 48th district, which is being vacated by retiring Rep. Darrell Issa.But the most intriguing races may be in South Texas, where Republicans hope to hold on to their gains among Latino voters in 2024. In the Corpus Christi border 15th District, Republican Rep. Monica De La Cruz faces Democratic challenger Bobby Pulido, a Latin Grammy-winning music artist. President Trump has made gains among Latino voters in South Texas, but after the GOP-led push to redraw districts, most of the voters are unfamiliar with De La Cruz. A bit further north, in the newly-redrawn open 35th District near San Antonio, Johnny Garcia, a longtime county sheriff's deputy, will seek to flip the seat away from Republican candidate Carlos De La Cruz, Monica's brother. There are two other border districts that Democrats are hoping to hold onto that were drawn to be more friendly to Republicans: longtime Rep. Henry Cuellar's Laredo-area 28th District and Rep. Vicente Gonzalez's 34th District. SenateThe GOP is also looking to protect a 53-47 majority in the Senate. While a total of 35 seats are on the ballot, the race is likely to come down to 11 battleground races. Democrats look set to retain their seat in Georgia, as incumbent Sen. Jon Ossoff appears to have a lead on his Republican challenger, Rep. Mike Collins, according to polling. North Carolina, a longtime Democratic target, seems poised to turn blue, as popular former two-term Democratic governor Roy Cooper has been leading polls to take the seat currently held by retiring Republican Sen. Thom Tillis.In Maine, longtime Republican incumbent Sen. Susan Collins is facing one of the toughest reelection battles of her 29-year Senate career. Collins, who chairs the Senate Appropriations Committee, is seeking a sixth term in a state Kamala Harris won by three points in 2024. She faces former state Senate President Troy Jackson, who was chosen at the state party convention to replace scandal-plagued Graham Platner on the ballot.In Alaska, Democratic challenger Mary Peltola faces not one but two Dan Sullivans, one of whom is the Republican incumbent. The other, a retired teacher named Daniel J. Sullivan, has drawn criticism from Republicans who argue his presence on the ballot could siphon votes away from the incumbent. Peltola's campaign has recently come under fire following reports that operatives linked to her campaign recruited the "other Dan Sullivan" in an alleged attempt to confuse voters. Peltola's campaign has denied those claims.Ohio, meanwhile, is a chance for Democrats to reclaim a Senate seat in a state that has moved sharply toward the GOP in recent cycles. Former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown, who lost his reelection bid in 2024, faces incumbent Republican Sen. Jon Husted in a race to finish the final two years of now-Vice President JD Vance's term. Mr. Trump won the state by more than 11 points in 2024, but recent polling shows Brown with a narrow lead heading into Election Day.Texas, Iowa and Kansas are all states where Mr. Trump won in 2024 by more than 13 points, but are squarely in play. In Texas, Democratic state Rep. James Talarico faces Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton in a race that Democrats hope will deliver their first statewide election win in more than 30 years. Although Iowa has moved to the right over the last decade, Democrats also have their eyes on the Senate seat being vacated by retiring Sen. Joni Ernst. Rep. Ashley Hinson has been locked in a tight contest with Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek for months. Kansas, on the other hand, where Democrats have not won a Senate race since 1932, has also emerged as a battleground state. In a state Mr. Trump won by more than 16 points, recent polling by The Washington Post shows Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton leading incumbent GOP Sen. Roger Marshall by as much as 9 points.Michigan could be an opportunity for Republicans to flip a seat currently held by Democrats. Former GOP Rep. Mike Rogers is making his second consecutive bid for the Senate two years after losing a tight race to Democrat Elissa Slotkin. He now faces Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive who would be the first Muslim American to serve in the Senate, in the race to replace retiring Sen. Gary Peters. If Rogers is able to win, it would mark the first Republican Senate victory in the state since 1994, although Mr. Trump has won the state twice. El-Sayed narrowly won the August primary against Democrat Haley Stevens, who then reversed course over the weekend and backed Rogers. Governors' racesVoters in 36 states will be electing governors on Tuesday, with several contests taking place in states that could also play important roles in the 2028 presidential election.In Georgia, former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms faces Republican Rick Jackson in a race to replace term-limited GOP Gov. Brian Kemp. The contest has featured heavy spending, particularly on Jackson's side, while polls have Democrats within striking distance of winning the governor's mansion for the first time since 1998. If Bottoms wins, she would also become the first Black woman elected governor in American history.Iowa presents what may be Democrats' best opportunity to flip a governor's mansion blue. State Auditor Rob Sand, the only Democrat currently holding statewide elected office in Iowa, faces Republican farmer Zach Lahn in a contest to replace retiring GOP Gov. Kim Reynolds. Sand has emphasized his bipartisan credentials throughout the campaign, and has held a consistent lead in the polls since the summer, giving his party a shot to win the governor's mansion for the first time since 2006. Elsewhere in the Midwest, two other races in traditional battleground states have drawn national attention. Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson is taking on Republican Rep. John James in the race to succeed term-limited Democratic Gov. Gretchen Whitmer. In Wisconsin, Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley and Republican Rep. Tom Tiffany are competing to replace retiring Democratic Gov. Tony Evers. Both states voted for Mr. Trump in 2024 and Biden in 2020, and both have outgoing Democratic governors.The race in Ohio, which has trended red in recent years, may have attracted the most controversy, as Republican entrepreneur and former presidential candidate Vivek Ramaswamy faces Democrat Amy Acton, the state's former health director. The race grabbed headlines in recent weeks when Ramaswamy's campaign released an ad featuring Acton's estranged mother, who accused her daughter of lying about her childhood. Acton has been estranged from her mother for nearly 50 years after her stepfather was charged with sexually abusing her. Although the ad recently drew bipartisan backlash, Ramaswamy — and then Mr. Trump — defended the ad but eventually stopped airing it just days before Election Day.Ballot measuresBeyond the race for elected office, voters will also have their say on statewide and local ballot measures. The proposals cover a broad range of issues, including abortion rights, voting requirements, redistricting, taxes and government powers.In California, one of the most closely watched proposals is Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time 5% tax on billionaires living in the state. The measure, which supporters claim would raise tens of billions of dollars, would direct the funds toward healthcare, food assistance programs and education. It's caused an intra-party fight among Democrats, with Sen. Bernie Sanders, who supports the proposal, repeatedly sparring with outgoing Gov. Gavin Newsom, who opposes it.Redistricting will also be on the ballot across the country, as states continue to fight over changes to their congressional maps mid-decade. Voters in Maryland and Missouri will consider proposals that would entail major changes to how congressional maps are drawn in their respective states. The passage of either could have significant implications for the balance of power in Washington, particularly in an era when House majorities are especially narrow.Changes to the electoral process go beyond redistricting, as election rules are also on voters' minds in several states. Voters in California, Arizona, Colorado and Nevada will consider proposals that would create more stringent voter identification requirements. In Alaska, the ballot will feature a proposal that would repeal the state's controversial ranked-choice voting system.Abortion will also take center stage in several states once again, more than four years after the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade. Missouri voters will decide whether to repeal a state constitutional amendment protecting reproductive freedoms passed just two years ago. Idaho will consider a measure that would protect abortion until fetal viability, while Virginia voters will consider a similar measure to protect reproductive rights that would allow some restrictions later in pregnancy.An emerging local ballot issue is the rapid expansion of data centers. More than 40 local ballot measures across over a dozen states will address key issues relating to data centers, including construction, zoning and approval requirements. Voters throughout Ohio will decide on more than 20 such measures, while communities in parts of Maine, Florida and Kansas will do the same.
news.summary: All 435 seats in the House of Representatives are on the ballot, while voters in 35 states will choose senators and 36 will choose governors.
